blocks.text: 1. Interpreting the Title

inline.s: The Buddha Speaks the Sutra on the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life

According to the text below, when Ānanda asked, the Buddha established two titles. The first states: This sutra is named for the contemplation of the land of Ultimate Bliss, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, and the Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta. Adding the word sutra, it totals twenty characters, named from the mind and its objects. It also says: It is also called Purifying the Karmic Obstructions and Being Born Before the Buddhas. Adding the word sutra, it totals nine characters, named from breaking through obstructions and reaping the reward. In the first title, the single character contemplation is the wisdom that contemplates; the following eighteen characters are the objects contemplated. The land of Ultimate Bliss is the circumstantial reward, which envelops the first six contemplations (1. the Sun, 2. the Water, 3. the Ground, 4. the Trees, 5. the Pools, 6. the Comprehensive). From Immeasurable Life onward is the primary reward, which envelops the last ten (7. the Lotus Seat, 8. the Sacred Images, 9. the Buddha's Body, 10. Avalokiteshvara, 11. Mahasthamaprapta, 12. the Universal Rebirth, 13. the Mixed Thoughts of Buddha and Bodhisattvas, 14. the Highest Grade, 15. the Middle Grade, 16. the Lowest Grade). Contemplating the Buddha in total matches the former three contemplations; the two Bodhisattvas in total embrace the seven contemplations. Thus this one title contains all sixteen. In the second title, Purifying the Karmic Obstructions is the power and function of the sixteen contemplations as a whole; when contemplation is accomplished and obstructions break, that is the immediate cause. Being Born Before the Buddhas is the future fruit. It does not point to Amitābha alone but says the Buddhas, because the sutra below says: Whoever sees the Buddha of Immeasurable Life sees the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions. The present translator uses only the first title, following what is concise, yet, since it accords with the Buddhas, it deeply matches the intent of the sutra. The Tiantai Commentary says: Raising the primary reward to gather in the circumstantial reward, and describing the transforming teacher to include the assembly; though the contemplations are sixteen, naming the Buddha suffices. This is an interpretation that raises the essential to embrace both the preceding and following. Master Huiyuan's Commentary says: This sutra takes contemplating the Buddha as its chief focus, so he is singled out. This is an interpretation holding that the various contemplations follow the essential aim of the sutra. Examining the two explanations, the latter meaning is the most complete. For regarding contemplation of the Buddha as the primary meaning, the land must first be set forth as the gradual entry; afterward, from contemplating the Buddha, one extends to the assembly to reveal its universality. Hence the passage on contemplating the Buddha alone is called the samādhi of recollecting the Buddha.

In the title, the upper seven characters form the specific title, specific to this text; the single lower character is the common title, extending to all scriptures. The upper two denote the Buddha who proclaims the teaching; the lower five show the practice taught.

First, in the proclaimer, Buddha is one of the ten epithets. To speak means to delight and satisfy the minds of the assembly (Note: this is said with reference to the hearers, hence to delight and satisfy the minds of the assembly. The Tiantai Commentary says: To speak is to delight what is held in mind. The Miaozong Sub-commentary explains: Delight is to be fully pleased. Mind is what is held within. As to this sutra, it is that the Tathagata, through long cultivation and realization, holds within him the samādhi of recollecting the Buddha; now that the capacity is stirred, speaking it gives full expression to what was formerly held in mind). The transforming teacher of this world is surely Śākyamuni, so only his common epithet is raised. The objects contemplated below, lest they be confused with other honored ones, have both the common and specific titles raised. According to the Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom: scriptures may be spoken by five kinds of persons — Buddhas, holy disciples, sages, gods and dragons and ghosts, and persons of transformation. To show that this sutra was spoken by the Buddha himself and to exclude other persons, so that faith and acceptance might arise. Yet within one age of the teaching, the discipline is spoken only by the Buddha, specially set forth as most profound and secret; the scriptures may be spoken by others but must receive the Buddha's seal. Still, within the scriptures, the Pure Land teaching is certainly spoken by the Buddha, showing it is beyond the knowledge of lesser sages and ordinary beings. Hence the other sutras may sometimes omit the mark, but all the Pure Land sutras must be so distinguished.

Second, in the teaching spoken, the first character above is the mind that contemplates; the four below are the objects contemplated. In the first part, both the great and lesser contemplation methods point to the sixth consciousness as the substance that contemplates. Among the five aggregates it belongs to the aggregate of volitional formations. The three preceding minds are in substance merely neutral; one must take the volitional mind that forms karma before it can recompense and draw forth rebirth. According to the text below, it is sometimes called recollection and sometimes reflection; the names differ but the substance is the same, and all point to mental intention as that which contemplates. (The above are all recorded from the Lingzhi Commentary.)

The Meaning of Mahayana, chapter two says: Coarse reflection is called applied thought and subtle reflection sustained thought. The Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom, chapter seventeen: Question: Are applied thought and sustained thought one dharma or two? Answer: They are two. The coarse mind of the first moment is applied thought; the subtle analysis is sustained thought. For example, when a bell is struck, the first loud sound is applied thought, the later subtle sound sustained thought. (Annotated Commentary)

Next, in the object contemplated, in Sanskrit it is called Amitābha, translated as Immeasurable Life and also as Immeasurable Light. Life represents merit, the virtue of liberation; light represents wisdom, the virtue of prajñā. Prajñā and liberation together adorn the dharmakāya, and this is the Buddha who saves beings in the land of shared reward. The successor Avalokiteshvara truly has a measured span of life, but with reference to ordinary and lesser beings who cannot count it, it is called immeasurable. Buddha, fully stated as buddha, is translated as the awakened one. Awakening has two meanings: the meaning of awareness, for the four fetters are like robbers that only the sage perceives so they can do no harm; and the meaning of realization, for ignorance is like sleep, and once the wisdom of the sage arises it is like waking. Confronted with the two vehicles, he is called the Great Awakened One; surpassing the stage of equal awakening, he is called the Wondrously Awakened One. Here only one aspect is set forth; for the rest see the special explanations. His bodily marks and light are fully shown in the contemplation of the Buddha. (Lingzhi Commentary)

As for sutra, in Sanskrit it is called sutra, translated as the conforming doctrine. Conforming has two meanings: above, it conforms to the principle of all Buddhas; below, it conforms to the capacities of beings. Sutra again has many meanings. The Buddha-land opens two: to string together, stringing together the teachings spoken; and to hold, holding the beings to be transformed. In this world there are four: constant, unchanging through the three times; dharma, the same standard throughout the ten directions; a path, traversed alike by past and present; and a canon, honored and observed far and near. (Direct Pointer Commentary)

This sutra is named for the Contemplation of Immeasurable Life because it specifically clarifies the primary and circumstantial adornments of the lord of the land of Ultimate Bliss, and the compassionate skillful means, without being confused with the Buddhas of other directions; it seeks to cause beings to turn their minds single-mindedly and quickly escape birth and death. Contemplation has many gates, adapted to the sharp and dull capacities of beings. Gathered up in the one Buddha, nothing is left uncovered. The nine grades are spread apart and ten thousand streams all converge; without departing from the reward and transformation bodies one suddenly penetrates the dharmakāya, and without leaving the shared land one directly ascends to the stage of successor. Such skillful means are without match or peer. Those who encounter this sutra should arouse a determined mind, firm in their vow, and within this very body hasten to be born in that land. (Concise Treatise)

I reflect that Śākyamuni in this world sends us forth and Amitābha from that land comes to welcome; that land calls and this world sends, how could one not go? One should only diligently apply himself to the Dharma, taking the end of life as the limit, and abandoning this body of reward, immediately realize the eternal bliss of that dharma-nature! (Four-Fascicle Commentary)

blocks.text: 2. Clarifying the History of Translation

inline.s: Translated by the Western Regions Tripitaka Master Kalayasas of the Liu Song dynasty

The Liu Song is so called to distinguish it from the Zhao Song. Liu Yu received the abdication of the Jin, named his state Song, and set the capital at Jiankang (present-day Jiangning in Jiangsu). It held the provinces of today's Yangtze and Pearl River basins. In all, eight sovereigns and fifty-nine years. (From year 1492 before the common era (420) to year 1433 before the common era (479).) The throne passed to the Southern Qi. (Annotated Commentary)
The name Western Regions points to the kingdoms west of Dunhuang. In ancient times it was commonly used to refer to the kingdoms of India. (Annotated Commentary)

Tripitaka means the sutras, the discipline, and the treatises. A Master of Dharma is so called because he takes the Dharma of the Tripitaka as his teacher; also, because he is deeply versed in it and teaches and transforms beings.

Kalayasas is the name of the chief translator. The Biographies of Monks say: Kalayasas means well-praised in his time; he was a man of the Western Regions, by nature upright and with few desires, thoroughly versed in the Tripitaka and especially skilled in the meditation of dhyana. In the early Yuanjia era of the Song he reached the capital. Emperor Wen deeply admired him and commanded him to reside at the Daolin Hermitage on Mount Zhongshan. The monk Seng Han requested him to translate this sutra, with the Sutra of the Medicine King and the Contemplation. Han was the amanuensis. Later he traveled in Shu and returned to die at Jiangling at the age of sixty. To translate is to turn the Sanskrit text into the Chinese text.

blocks.text: 3. Exposition of the Sutra Text

inline.s: The major divisions are three: 1. the Preface Section, 2. the Main Teaching Section, and 3. the Circulation Section.
A. First, the Preface Section has two parts
1. The confidence-verifying preface
2. The initiating preface
B. First, the confidence-verifying preface

Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was dwelling in the city of Rajagrha, on Mount Grdhrakuta, together with a great assembly of monks, twelve hundred and fifty in all, and thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas, with the prince of the Dharma Manjusri at their head.
The verification of faith has six points:

First, Thus refers to the Dharma spoken in the main teaching section. Conforming to principle is called thus and being free of what is not is called true. It can be decisively trusted, hence it says thus.

Second, have I heard means that Ānanda personally heard it from the Buddha, showing it is not his own words. All dharmas are selfless; being selfless, there is no hearer. Yet following the worldly convention of provisional designation, it is spoken of as I.

Third, at one time means from the gathering of the assembly to the end of the session. That single period of time distinguishes it from other times. When the Tathagata speaks scriptures the times are immeasurable and cannot be fixed, so it says at one time. Moreover, the years, months, days, and hours of the western region and this land differ, and when circulated elsewhere people find them hard to understand. Furthermore, in some scriptures a single sermon could not be completed, and it was only later at the council that the text was assembled, so the before and after are not uniform and hard to mark. That is, in this present sutra, King Ajatasatru committed evil, the Tathagata spoke the sutra, and Ānanda repeated it; how could these be the same time? Therefore a single phrase encompasses all.

Fourth, Buddha is the lord who proclaims the teaching, showing it is no other person. It points to the Śākyamuni master who revealed the Pure Land. Buddha is translated as awakening. Awakening oneself differs from ordinary beings; awakening others differs from the two vehicles; and the fullness of awakening differs from the bodhisattvas, hence it is called the Great Awakened One.
Fifth, in the city of Rajagrha below is the place where the sutra was spoken. (The above are recorded from the Lingzhi Commentary.)

Rajagrha: in Sanskrit it is called Rajagrha, in the kingdom of Magadha in central India. King Bimbisara moved his capital here from the old city of the Upper Reed Palace. The city is surrounded by five mountains, and Grdhrakuta is one of them. The Tiantai Commentary gives three reasons for the mountain's name: first, from the rule of the kings; second, from removing the fear of fire; third, from the place of those afraid of wrongdoing. The text is too long to record here. For detail see the Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom, chapter three, and the Records of the Western Regions, chapter nine.

Grdhrakuta is translated as Vulture Peak, where the sages and spiritual sages dwell. It is also called Vulture Head, the peak resembling a vulture; or it is where many vultures roost, and so it is named. The Tiantai Commentary gives three explanations: from the sage-spirits dwelling there; from the peak's shape resembling a vulture; and from the roosting of vultures. (Lingzhi Commentary)

Sixth, the great monks and others are the assembly of identical hearing. There are two groups: the assembly of sravakas and the assembly of bodhisattvas. If we speak of their vows, the bodhisattvas come first; here taking their deportment, the sravakas are placed first. (Lingzhi Commentary)
First is said of the assembly of sravakas

Together means in common. In Sanskrit it is called mahas, translated as great. Great has three meanings: great, many, and supreme. Revered by heavenly kings and great beings, it is called great because its merit is great. Comprehensively understanding both inner and outer scriptures, it is called many because its knowledge is vast. Rising above the ninety-five kinds of teachers, it is called supreme because its views are supreme. (Tiantai Commentary, first

A monk, by his provisional name, has three meanings: seeker of alms, one who terrifies Mara, and one who destroys evil. In the fruit stage the arhat also has three: one worthy of offerings, one who destroys the thieves (of defilements), and one beyond birth. In Sanskrit, samgha is translated as assembly. With four or more persons, harmonious and without dispute, performing the karmic rites and recitation of precepts, able to accomplish all matters of destroying evil and producing good, it is therefore called an assembly. (Lingzhi Commentary)

The twelve hundred and fifty are his retinue disciples. The three Kashyapas together had a thousand disciples, and Maudgalyayana and Sariputra together two hundred and fifty. Formerly they were all fire-worshipping heretics who long endured bitter toil without realizing anything; but once they saw the Tathagata they immediately ascended to the fruit of sainthood. Grateful for the Buddha's deep kindness, they always attended him. (Lingzhi Commentary)
Being together at one place is called accompanying.
Next is said of the assembly of bodhisattvas

A bodhisattva, fully stated as bodhisattva, is translated as an enlightened being, one who enlightens all beings in an expansive way. Thirty-two thousand is the number. (The Lingzhi Commentary says: The thirty-two thousand are the leaders and their retinue.) Manjusri is translated as Wondrous Virtue, also called Wondrous Head, and again Wondrous Auspiciousness. Entering the proper position of the Dharma, he is called prince of the Dharma. His wisdom and virtue alone stand supreme, so he is the leader. (Direct Pointer Commentary)

The Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says: The Buddha is the king of the Dharma, and the bodhisattvas, entering the proper position of the Dharma through the ten grounds, are all called princes of the Dharma. The bodhisattvas, as those raised in the home of the Buddha, king of the Dharma, are all princes of the Dharma. Yet in the scriptures Manjusri is widely called prince of the Dharma, because he sits above the two attendants of the World-honored One and is the foremost Dharma-son aiding the Buddha's teaching. The Annotations on the Lotus Sutra, Words and Sentences: The scriptures call Manjusri prince of the Dharma for two reasons: first, among the princes, virtue is deferred to Manjusri; second, in the various scriptures Manjusri is the head of the bodhisattva assembly. The head of the assembly is the leader, the principal seat of the whole assembly. (Annotated Commentary)
The above lists the great and lesser assemblies to establish confidence. All scriptures commonly have this and it is also called the common preface. (Direct Pointer Commentary)

The larger and smaller Amitābha Sutras list the assemblies very broadly, while this sutra is the most concise. The translations suited their times and each had its own intention. It should also list the assemblies of humans, gods, and the miscellaneous beings, for below in the circulation section it says: the immeasurable gods, dragons, yakshas, and so on. From this we know that in the preface too this is abbreviated. (Lingzhi Commentary)
B. Second, the initiating preface
1. First, the imprisonment of the king is made clear
2. Second, the intent to harm the mother is shown

The circumstances of the various scriptures differ according to their events. This present sutra takes killing and treason as its initiating cause for roughly two intentions: first, to reveal that the beings of this world are utterly detestable, for one would dare to harm even his own parent, let alone others; the intention is to cause beings of the latter age to delight in the Pure Land. Second, to show that the capacity of this world does not think of liberation and rebirth in that land unless it meets extreme suffering, so below Vaidehi says: Speak widely to me of a place without sorrow and distress; I shall be born there and take no delight in the defiled evil world of Jambudvipa. (Lingzhi Commentary)
C. First, the imprisonment of the king has four parts
1. Prince Ajatasatru imprisons the king his father
2. The queen consort secretly offers the porridge and ghee
3. The king requests the precepts to sustain his mind
4. Sustained by both the Dharma and food he does not die
D. First, Prince Ajatasatru imprisons the king his father

At that time, in the great city of Rajagrha, there was a prince named Ajatasatru. Following the instruction of the evil friend Devadatta, he seized the king his father Bimbisara and shut him in an inner chamber of seven walls, commanding all the ministers that none might go to him.
At that time shows that the Buddha was then at the capital preaching, distinguishing the occasion from times when he travelled to teach in other kingdoms. (Direct Pointer Commentary)

Ajatasatru is translated as the unborn enemy, because even in the womb he had conceived hatred and harm toward his father. Or it is called Balala..., translated as one with a broken finger, because at birth the king ordered him dashed to the ground, but he did not die and a finger was broken. (Direct Pointer Commentary)
Following means believing another's teaching and obeying another's intent; this is called following. (Annotated Commentary)

Devadatta, fully stated as Devadatta, is translated as heaven-heated; when he was born the hearts of all the gods were agitated with heat, knowing that when he appeared in the world he must surely destroy the Triple Gem. (Also named Heaven-given.) He was the son of King Dronodana, cousin of the Buddha and elder brother of Ānanda. He had thirty marks. On renouncing the world he recited six myriad dharma-collections and the twelve Vedas. When he saw the Tathagata revered by kings and ministers and that offerings abounded, envy arose in his heart, and he went to the Buddha to ask to lead the assembly. The Buddha reproved him, and so he plotted to harm the Buddha. Ānanda, not knowing, taught him the method of supernatural power. He entered the mountains and cultivated it, attaining the five supernormal knowledges. Then he thought: who shall be my benefactor? Prince Ajatasatru has the marks of a great king. So he manifested various transformations to delude him into belief and said to the prince: I shall become a new Buddha and you a new king; is this not a delight! Thereupon he pushed a rock down to crush the Buddha. The secret guardian Vajrapani threatened him with his vajra, and the broken rock flew out and injured the Buddha's toe, drawing the Tathagata's blood. He called himself a Buddha and taught beings with five dharmas, and the five hundred new learners such as Susima were converted by his evil teaching, forming a separate assembly to beg alms and a separate observance, which split the wheel of the Dharma-sangha. The nun Utpalavarna met him on the road and reproved him, and he struck her and put out her eye, thus killing an arhat. He committed the three heinous offenses and was born in hell. Ajatasatru killed his father and harmed his mother, together the five heinous offenses. All these are great and powerful deeds of transformation by the great ones; whether adverse or compliant, none is without benefit to beings, and all are for the sake of preventing living beings of later ages from committing heinous acts. The sutra says: He reveals that he has the three poisons and again manifests the appearance of wrong views. My disciples are like this, as skillful means to save sentient beings. The Nirvāṇa Sutra also says that Devadatta did not in truth fall into hell or commit evil, and so on. Truly this is not a state within the scope of sravakas or pratyekabuddhas; it is only the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas. (Lingzhi Commentary)

Suddenly seizing the king's person is called apprehending; having got him, not releasing him is called imprisoning. Speaking of the father specifically indicates the utmost closeness of kin; king shows his rank; Bimbisara shows his name. As for being shut in an inner chamber of seven walls, what was done was grave and the matter not trifling; it could not be a light confinement among men without any guarding at all. But since the king's palace naturally excludes outsiders, only the ministers and officials, long accustomed to attending him, could, unless strictly forbidden, find occasion for secret communication. Therefore he caused the inner and outer to have no contact and shut him within seven walls. (Four-Fascicle Commentary)

Bimbisara is translated as solid and real, and also named Stable Shadow; in both cases the name arises from the solidity of his bodily form. Some translate it as handsome in countenance. The seven-walled chamber was not a matter of going and coming; adding further restraints, he intended to starve him to death. (Lingzhi Commentary)

Such events are all the skillful devices of the great beings manifesting transformation, walking in what is not the Way yet penetrating the Buddha Way. The roots of beings differ, so their entry into the Way differs; one against and one for, both spread the Way and benefit beings. They manifest the practice of the uninterrupted hell without anger or affliction. Ajatasatru manifested the adverse in order to stop evil people of later times from committing treason. (Tiantai Commentary)

Ajatasatru had enmity before birth, the cause of the imprisonment; following the evil teaching is the condition; the seven-walled chamber with the ban on entry is the method; the seizing and confining is the deed. The sutra takes the imprisonment of the father as its initiating cause for two reasons: first, Bimbisara, formerly while hunting deer on Mount Vipula and finding nothing, saw a sage and conceived an angry mind of hatred, drove him away, and had him killed. The sage, at death, vowed to be born as his son and to harm him with heart and mouth. If the grudge were not repaid, one could not prevent people from innocent harm. The Surangama Sutra says that the retributions of hatred harm through the thought of parents, like the owl and the mirror-beetle and such classes; this is precisely that meaning. Second, if the son had not committed treason, he would have been greedy for wealth and honor and could never have been led to hear the Dharma and attain the fruit, being wearied of the suffering of this Saha world. (Direct Pointer Commentary)
D. Second, the queen consort secretly offers the porridge and ghee

The queen consort, named Vaidehi, revering the king, bathed and purified herself, mixed ghee and honey with porridge and smeared it on her body, and within her necklaces and girdles concealed a vessel of grape juice, and secretly brought it to the king.
Vaidehi was the consort of King Bimbisara and the mother of Ajatasatru. (Annotated Commentary)

Vaidehi is translated as reflection. Having received this name first, it became a portent of today's request for contemplation. She bathed to purify her body, smeared it with porridge and ghee, and the hollowed ornaments could hold fruit juice. She slipped into the deep chamber, hence it is called secretly. (Lingzhi Commentary)

Ghee is pronounced su, belongs to the class of curds, and is made from the milk of cows and goats. Bran is parched flour; wheat is steamed and ground into powder to make the bran. (Annotated Commentary)

I privately think: Of deep affection, none surpasses husband and wife. The king was imprisoned within seven walls and the ministers were forbidden to go to him; how could the lady's heart not be moved to tears? Knowing clearly he would starve to death, how could her heart bear it? Offering ghee and porridge to the king is only natural. (Commentary Elucidation)
D. Third, the king requests the precepts to sustain his mind, in three parts
1. The king requests Maudgalyayana
2. Maudgalyayana responds to the occasion 3. The Buddha sends Purnamaitrayani-putra to preach
E. First, the king requests Maudgalyayana

At that time the great king, having eaten the porridge and drunk the juice, asked for water to rinse his mouth. When he had rinsed, he pressed his palms together in reverence, and facing Mount Grdhrakuta bowed from afar to the World-honored One and said: Great Maudgalyayana is my kinsman and friend; may he rouse his compassion and confer upon me the eight precepts!

Maudgalyayana is translated as the Maudgalya clan. In antiquity a sage gathered and ate beans, and from this the clan was named. He was the king's family teacher, therefore called kinsman and friend. (Lingzhi Commentary)

Saying that the great Maudgalyayana was kinsman and friend has two meanings: while in lay life Maudgalyayana was the king's close relative; having gone forth, he became his family teacher. Going and coming within the palace, there was no obstruction at all. But being a relative in lay life and called a friend in renunciation, hence he is called kinsman and friend. (Four-Fascicle Commentary)

The eight precepts are the eight precepts of the one-day observance. The Sutra of the Ten Good Karmic Precepts says: The eight precepts' observance is what the Buddhas and Tathagatas of the past and present established for lay people as the dharma of renunciation. First, not to kill; second, not to steal; third, not to engage in sexual conduct; fourth, not to speak falsely; fifth, not to drink wine; sixth, not to sit on a high and broad bed; seventh, not to engage in song, dance, and music, nor to go to watch and listen, nor to wear perfume or adornments; eighth, not to eat beyond the midday meal. (Annotated Commentary)
E. Second, Maudgalyayana responds to the occasion
At that time Maudgalyayana, flying like a hawk or falcon, swiftly reached the king's place; he did so daily and conferred the eight precepts on the king.

Maudgalyayana, having known this, responded to the occasion and went. Like a hawk or falcon in flight was the simile for the swiftness of his supernormal powers. Falcon, pronounced xun; the dictionary says it is a bird of prey, a fierce bird. The eight precepts' observance is limited to one day and one night, so it was received anew each day. (Lingzhi Commentary)
The hawk is a bird of prey; the falcon is the smallest of the hawk class. (Annotated Commentary)
E. Third, the Buddha sends Purnamaitrayani-putra to preach
The World-honored One also sent the Venerable Purna to preach the Dharma to the king.

Purna is translated as son of Full Compassion, named from his parents. Among preachers of the Dharma he is the foremost, skilled at opening and guiding, so he was especially sent. (Lingzhi Commentary)
D. Fourth, sustained by both the Dharma and food he does not die
Thus for a period of twenty-one days the king ate the porridge and ghee and, because he heard the Dharma, his countenance became serene and joyful.

The king, by eating and hearing the Dharma, did not die over many days. This precisely clarifies that the queen long offered food to remove hunger and thirst, and the two sages again inwardly sustained him with the precepts, skilfully opening the king's mind. Food can prolong life and the precepts nourish the spirit; losing the suffering and banishing sorrow, they caused his countenance to be serene and joyful. (Four-Fascicle Commentary)
C. Second, the intent to harm the mother is shown
1. The unfilial son harms his mother
2. The compassionate mother seeks help
D. First, the unfilial son harms his mother, in three parts
1. First, he is about to harm his mother
2. Second, he is stopped by the ministers' remonstrance 3. Third, he orders her shut away
E. First, he is about to harm his mother
At that time Ajatasatru asked the gatekeeper: Does the king my father still live?

At that time the gatekeeper reported: Great king, the queen consort smears her body with ghee and honey, and hides juice in her necklaces to bring to the king; and the monks Maudgalyayana and Purna come through the air and preach the Dharma to the king, so that none can forbid it.

At that time Ajatasatru, hearing this, was angry with his mother and said: My mother is a thief! She is the companion of thieves! And those evil monks, with their deluding spells, cause this wicked king not to die for so many days! Then he seized a sharp sword and would have killed his mother.

First, the king asked whether he was still alive. Then in the passage beginning at that time the gatekeeper, they report to him with the facts. Then in the passage beginning at that time Ajatasatru, the king, having heard, was angry. I privately think: First, if a man lives beyond seven days there must be a reason: either the water of concentration sustains his spirit, or the power of the Way adds support. Had the king truly died, the gatekeeper would certainly have come to report. Now twenty-one days had passed with no tidings of death, so Ajatasatru asked: Does he still live? The words still and the question mark are the pivot of the question. Second, the gatekeeper answered with facts and said none could forbid it for two reasons: first, the queen is the mistress, so how would any dare to forbid her; second, the two sages arrived through the air, so how could they be stopped. With these two considerations he said it could not be done. Third, what Ajatasatru originally wanted was only for the king to be gone so he could face south as sovereign; hearing that he still lived, how could he not be angry? The anger within issuing from the mouth, he suddenly forgot the kindness of foster care and cursed: My mother is a thief! Thief means a robber, one who robs me of the immediate fulfillment of my sovereign wish. Those monks are also thieves, coming daily to the palace to be my mother's companions, hence she is the companion of thieves! He knew well the monks were not evil men; he wanted his father dead, and they, with their power of incantation, kept him alive, putting obstacles in my way, so he calls them evil men. He knew well the incantation's power was great; calling it deluding is also a curse. Because his rising anger could not be checked, he seized the sword to harm his mother. The commentary resolves the difficulty: He should have killed the gatekeeper, yet he wanted to harm his mother because the gatekeeper had his answer; the king had first commanded the ministers be forbidden without speaking of women, and the monks flew in through the air, which I could not prevent. Though the king coveted the kingdom and killed his father, he still did not violate the Dharma. (Elucidation)
E. Second, he is stopped by the ministers' remonstrance

At that time there was a minister named Candraprabha, intelligent and wise; together with Jivaka, they made obeisance to the king and said: Great king, we have heard it said in the Veda treatises that from the beginning of the kalpa there have been wicked kings who, coveting the kingdom, killed their fathers, eighteen thousand of them. But never have we heard of one who, without justification, killed his mother. Now, for this act of killing and treason, the king would defile the Kshatriya caste, and we cannot bear to hear of it. You are a Candala! We should no longer remain here! Then the two ministers, having spoken these words, pressed their hands upon their swords and withdrew, walking backwards.

Moonlight is the Chinese [name]; Jivaka is Sanskrit, here rendered "firmly living." At birth, in one hand he held a medicine bag and in the other a needle-case. Formerly he had vowed to be a physician, curing the sick and keeping them alive, so he was named for his virtue. He was the son of the Amra woman. Both were exceedingly wise, plainly showing them to be virtuous ministers.

The Veda scriptures are the worldly classics; sometimes written Veda, the Sanskrit differs slightly. Like the histories of this land, they record the affairs of that country. To covet the throne and kill one's father is already a great evil; to slay one's mother without the Way has never been heard of through the ages. In western India there are four castes, which gather within themselves all castes: the Ksatriya and the Brahmana are the two honored ones; the Vaisya and the Sudra are the two lowly ones. The Ksatriya is the royal caste. The Candala is here called the slayer, the sort of executioner found in this land. Since the king was without the Way, a worthy minister would not aid him, and so he could not bear to remain. Pressing his sword and stepping back, he displayed his authority so as to make him afraid. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

At that time Ajatasatru was seized with terror and panic, and said to Jivaka, "Will you not act for me?" Jivaka replied, "Great king, be sure not to harm your mother!" When the king heard these words, he repented and begged for deliverance. Straightway he put down his sword and refrained from harming his mother.

King Ajatasatru was alarmed and fearful; when a worthy minister leaves the land, the altars of state must be endangered. "Will you not act for me" are words begging for deliverance. "Act" means "to assist." (Lingzhi's Commentary)
Wu 3: The decree to confine her in seclusion.
By edict he spoke to the inner officers, confining her in the deep palace, not allowing her to come out again.
Jivaka remonstrated again and again, and the king repented and followed him. That he decreed her confinement in the deep palace is the origin of her awakening. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

The king's intent: if the mother were not confined, the father could never die; if he wished the father to die, he must confine the mother. So he decreed to the inner officers to shut her up in the deep palace. (Elaboration)
Ding 2: The compassionate mother's plea for help, in three parts.
First, because of the confinement she begs the Buddha.
Second, the Buddha knows and goes. Third, in grief she asks for the Dharma.
Wu 1: Because of the confinement she begs the Buddha.

At that time Vaidehi, having been confined, was grieved and haggard; from afar she turned toward Vulture Peak, paid homage to the Buddha, and spoke these words: "O World-Honored One, in former times you always sent Ānanda to comfort and question me. Now I am grieved, and the World-Honored One's dignity is too great for me to see. I beg you to send Maudgalyayana and the venerable Ānanda to meet with me." Having spoken these words, she wept tears like rain, and from afar bowed to the Buddha.

The commentary says: Why did Vaidehi ask to see Maudgalyayana and Ānanda? Maudgalyayana was her teacher of the gate, Ānanda the Buddha's attendant. They had formerly always taught her, so she specially sought to see them. Dwelling in the deep palace, she dared not ask in particular; inwardly detesting this defiled world, she longed to be born in the Pure Land. She wished the two of them to convey her intent and beg the Buddha. I privately reflect: the lady was confined; first, she could not save the king from death, and second, she had no way to face the golden face [of the Buddha]; there was nothing to be done. She could only bow from afar and pray, hence the words "and spoke these words." Formerly, whenever the palace had affairs, the Buddha always sent his attendant to inquire; now, in her distress and grief, the Buddha's mind-reading would surely perceive it; not daring to beg the Buddha to come in person, she wished the two to meet her. Maudgalyayana is called "teacher of the gate": he was Bimbisara's teacher. It was said earlier: "Great Maudgalyayana is my friend and kinsman; I beg you to show compassion and give me the eight precepts," so he is the teacher of the eight precepts. And that she also asked for Ānanda was to have them convey her request and beg the Buddha personally to bestow the Dharma's grace. "Having spoken these words" and the following three clauses ask for the Dharma. The commentary says: weeping tears like rain, hoping for the Buddha's compassion; bowing from afar to the Buddha. Earlier she had already bowed, and now she bows again, showing her earnestness. (Elaboration)
Wu 2: The Buddha knows and goes.

Before she had even raised her head, at that time the World-Honored One, on Vulture Peak, knew what Vaidehi had in mind, and straightway commanded Great Maudgalyayana and Ānanda to come through the sky; the Buddha vanished from Vulture Peak and appeared in the royal palace.
Knowing what was in her mind is the intellect of knowing others' minds. Riding the sky in vanishing and appearing is the transcendent power of spiritual freedom. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

At that time Vaidehi, having bowed, raised her head and saw the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Buddha, his body purple-gold in color, seated on a lotus of a hundred jewels, Maudgalyayana attending on the left and Ānanda on the right; Sakra, Brahma, the world-protectors and the various devas, in the empty sky, rained heavenly flowers everywhere and held them as offerings.

In seeing the Buddha there were four particular excellences: first, the color of his body; second, the lotus seat; third, the attendants left and right; and fourth, the offerings of the devas. Sakra is Indra; in full, Sakyamunindra... rather, Sakyamunindra means "lord of the thirty-three heavens," i.e., the lord of the Trayastrimsa heavens. Brahma is the Great Brahma king, lord of the form realm. The world-protectors are the four great kings and so on. An ancient commentary asks: Bimbisara and Vaidehi both asked for disciples; why did he first send disciples and afterwards go in person? What is the meaning? There are two explanations: first, Ajatasatru had killed his father; if the Buddha went in person, it would arouse resentment and enmity, and this was to protect his mind. Second, to carry on the Buddha-Dharma, one must entrust it to the king; since Bimbisara was certain to die and Ajatasatru to ascend the throne, if the Buddha went in person it would be obstructed and could not proceed, and this was to protect the Dharma. Vaidehi had none of these [obstructions], so going in person was no impediment. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

The Direct Pointing commentary says: "Question: The king and the queen both requested the disciples; why did the king send a messenger while the queen went herself? Answer: There are three intentions. First, Bimbisara wished to receive the precepts and hear the Dharma, so a person could be sent to transmit them; Vaidehi wished to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, which the Buddha could not open without coming himself. Second, if he went in person to the king, Ajatasatru would think that his father was plotting with him for power, and his enmity would be heavy, leading to the extinction of Dharma and Sangha, an unforgivable offense; but going in person to the queen, Ajatasatru would think the mother had no plan for rule, so his resentment would be lighter; though he confined both parents, the offense could still be repented. Third, the king is a man, so a disciple could be sent to instruct him without further resentment; the queen is a woman, and so the teacher and student must come together to overcome the doubts and slanders."
Wu 3: In grief she asks for the Dharma, in two parts.
First, asking about the cause of former lives.
Second, asking about the place of rebirth.
Ji 1: Asking about the cause of former lives.

At that time Vaidehi, seeing the World-Honored One, tore off her own necklaces, threw her whole body to the ground, and weeping loudly said to the Buddha, "O World-Honored One! For what offense in a former life have I borne this evil son? And what karmic causes did the World-Honored One have, to be related to Devadatta as kinsmen?

The cause of the former life has two meanings: first, she asks what offense in her former life gave birth to this evil, rebellious son; second, what karmic relation the World-Honored One had to be regarded as kin to Devadatta. (Elaboration)

The passage has two sections: first, making obeisance to express reverence. Imprisoned so long, she did not expect to meet the Buddha; grief and joy filled her breast, with no time for delay, so she broke the necklaces from her neck and held them to offer the Buddha. She threw her body to the ground to exhaust her sincerity. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

Next, the direct question about the former cause. Between me and my son, love issues from nature; between the Buddha and his brother-in-law, affection is like the natural bonds of kinship. Yet they turned to harming one another, so there must be a past cause. She mainly reproaches herself, and at the same time asks the Tathagata. But this is merely grieving over past karma as the ground for making her plea. The sutras and vinaya say much, that the Buddha and Devadatta, from cause to fruit, were always troubling one another. This is presumably the great expedient shadow-play, and not a real matter. That is, the Lotus Sutra says: "Because of the good friend Devadatta, I was made complete in the six paramitas," down to "in future, after immeasurable aeons, he shall attain Buddhahood, named Tathagata King of Heaven," and so on. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

Under "said," she asks to be shown the two causes. "What offense" is the past cause; "this evil son" is the present fruit, asking about the cause of her own family and kin. The relation is as explained before. Under "World-Honored," she asks about the Tathagata's relation to his kin: in former times, at the time of Dipamkara Buddha, Yajnadata wished to give his daughter in marriage, and there was an aged Brahman ascetic, Sumati, who sought to be the son-in-law, wise and with a handsome face; at that time Śākyamuni, as the young man Manava Muni... rather, as the young brahmin youth, of fine appearance, having studied with the sage of jewels and become accomplished, came from afar and met Sumati in debate; Sumati was refuted, Yajnadata rejoiced and gave his daughter in marriage, and Sumati, in furious rage, vowed that in the future, life after life, he would continually trouble [the Buddha]. Sumati was Devadatta; the daughter was Gopi, as in the Birth Sutra.

...One should know that Ajatasatru and Devadatta were both practicing the inverted [path]. First, [their action] kept evil persons from arising with the offense of inversion; second, they manifested the inverted conduct to gather in the class of evil. Hence the Mahamegha [Sutra] speaks of it as inconceivable, and the Lotus Sutra gives Devadatta the prophecy. If it were truly perpetrated, they would revolve without rest in the evil realms; how could they be companions of the Buddha life after life? (Direct Pointing commentary)
Ji 2: Asking about the place of rebirth.

"Only I beg the World-Honored One to speak widely for me of a place without sorrow and trouble; I wish to be reborn there, and take no delight in this defiled and evil world of Jambudvipa!" (Elaboration)

The passage has four sections: first, marking the gladness and loathing; second, describing what is to be loathed; third, establishing the vow of separation. Lingzhi says: these three sections set forth the essential technique of cultivation in the last age. If not for these, one would cultivate pure karma in vain and certainly not be reborn. Fourth, the direct request for the cause of rebirth.

This is the first, marking the gladness and loathing. "A place without sorrow and trouble": what Vaidehi asked, its wording is broad and inclusive; according to the Buddha's answer below, it points to the Pure Land. In the Saha world, with its five defilements, whether among men or among devas, there is sorrow and trouble. Only the Buddha's Pure Land, wherein both the subjective and objective rewards are supremely excellent, and only bliss is enjoyed, could it have sorrow? Jambudvipa is here translated "surpassing gold," specifically referring to the southern continent. According to the present context it generally refers to the great thousandfold Saha world, but it takes the near to make it easy to understand. Or perhaps among the four continents Jambudvipa's defilement and evil are the worst, so it is specially marked. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

"A place without sorrow and trouble" is to ask that the Pure Land Dharma be spoken. Only the Pure Land, where the highest good gather together, can be called without sorrow and without trouble. "I wish to be reborn there" is the vow of gladness for the Pure Land. "Taking no delight in Jambudvipa" is the mind of loathing. The two words, gladness and loathing, are what a cultivator of pure karma must never leave, and must not fail to know. (Elaboration)
"This defiled and evil place is filled with hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, and is a mass of much that is not good;"

Second, describing what is to be loathed. "Defiled" refers to the five defilements, namely wrong views, afflictions, and so on. All five are impure, so together they are called defiled. "Evil" refers to the ten evils, namely killing, stealing, and so on. The five defilements generally encompass both subjective and objective rewards, while the ten evils particularly point to the activities of the body and mind. If speaking of defilement and evil, in truth they cover all six realms; but the three evil paths of suffering are particularly raised to make the loathing clear. Throughout the great thousandfold world, hence it is said "filled." "A mass of much that is not good" is the gathering together of the evil destinies mentioned above in this place. Or it may point specifically to the small amount of good that remains among human beings, as below she wishes not to see evil persons. Whether kindred or enemy, obedient or rebellious, all are not good. Could Ajatasatru and Devadatta be a gathering of good? Above I followed the text in explanation. Now I will discuss by meaning: this defiled and evil place points to the dwellings of cities and villages in the world, where relatives and clans meet; among them the minds and actions differ in a thousand ways, and the three evil paths are filled, all being a mass of what is not good. Again, the defiled and evil place points to the present discriminating mind of we sentient beings; from beginningless time to the present, the boundless karmic seeds created by body, speech, and mind, and the three-evil-path activities daily arising, cannot be fully enumerated, hence it is said "filled" and "a mass of much that is not good." (Lingzhi's Commentary)
"May I, in a future life, not hear evil sounds, and not see evil persons."

Third, establishing the vow of separation. The five defilements and the three realms with their five rebellious acts and ten evils are all evil sounds; the sentient beings among them who commit such karma are all called evil persons. The Land of Ultimate Bliss has not even the name of evil destinies, so there are no evil sounds; the many superior good ones gather in one place, so there are no evil persons. (Lingzhi's Commentary)
"Now, to the World-Honored One I cast my five limbs to the ground, imploring compassion and repenting! Only I beg the Buddha's sun to teach me to contemplate the pure karma-ground!"

Fourth, the direct request for the cause of rebirth. Head and four limbs make the five parts of the body; the five places are all round, so they are also called the five wheels. Touching the ground is the weightiest of reverences. Because there was past offense, she suffers this affliction. Now wishing to be free of it, she must seek repentance. In Sanskrit "ksama" is here translated "repentance." Now speaking of the two, the Chinese and the Sanskrit are both used. Some say: repenting is to cut off the future, and regret is to be ashamed of the past. The Tathagata's teaching breaks through hindrances and removes doubt, like the sun illuminating the world, hence "the Buddha's sun." The subjective and objective rewards of the Land of Ultimate Bliss are all accomplished by the pure karma of the teacher and the assembly, so it is called the pure karma-ground. According to this, Vaidehi was directly seeking the method of contemplation, hence "teach me to contemplate." (Lingzhi's Commentary)

Now as to the Pure Land Dharma-gate: there are contemplation with images [visualization], contemplation of forms, upholding the Name, and contemplation of reality. Now that this lady begs to be taught to contemplate the pure karma-ground, the World-Honored One speaks for her the sixteen sublime contemplations. The four kinds above are all contained within them. The first twelve contemplations are contemplation with images; the thirteenth is contemplation of forms; the last three are upholding the Name. If one knows that the subjective contemplation and the objective contemplated are both inconceivable, that is contemplation of reality. (Elaboration)
Here ends the explanation of the introduction.

blocks.text: Jia 2: The main body, in three parts.

inline.s: First, emitting light and manifesting the lands to assess the capacities.
Second, the proper elucidation of the contemplations, the right cause of pure karma. Third, the assembly gains benefit.
Yi 1: Emitting light and manifesting the lands to assess the capacities, in three parts.
First, the Tathagata emits light and universally manifests the various lands.
Second, Vaidehi addresses the Buddha and selects a single direction. Third, Bimbisara, receiving the light, attains the fruit of the Way.
Bing 1: The Tathagata emits light and universally manifests the various lands.

At that time the World-Honored One emitted light from between his brows; that light, golden in color, universally illuminated the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, then returned and dwelt on the Buddha's head, transforming into a golden platform like Mount Sumeru. The pure and wondrous lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared within it. Some lands were formed of the seven jewels; other lands were purely lotus flowers; other lands were like the palace of the lord of autonomous heaven; still other lands were like a crystal mirror. The lands of the ten directions all appeared within it, in such ways, immeasurable Buddha-lands, magnificently displayed and visible to see, so that Vaidehi might behold them.

The Tathagata has between his brows a white-hair mark, one zhang five [feet] long, five inches in circumference; on the outside it has eight ridges and is hollow within like a tube (the Contemplation of the Buddha's Samādhi Sutra says, "The hair-mark between the brows, one zhang and five [feet] long, emits light from within"), white as snow and shell; it curls to the right, signifying that from the middle path issues forth all dharmas (the Direct Pointing commentary says, "Between the brows signifies the middle way; the light signifies wisdom"). First scattered and then gathered, it also signifies gathering the many into the one. This reveals that this sutra is the pure, perfect, ultimate one-buddha-vehicle teaching, therefore this mark appears, different from ordinary times. The platform of light rises aloft, likened to Mount Sumeru. The lands manifest are immeasurable and cannot all be enumerated; briefly four are shown, to make them visible. Formed of seven jewels speaks of their dignity; purely lotus flowers speaks of their purity; like a heavenly palace speaks of their bliss; like a crystal mirror speaks of their bright clarity. As to the various lands, their splendor is extremely abundant; the sutra text, being concise, sets forth one characteristic for each, wishing to show that the Land of Ultimate Bliss possesses all these beauties together, and to let Vaidehi see them: this is the meaning of emitting light and manifesting the lands. (Lingzhi's Commentary)
Bing 2: Vaidehi addresses the Buddha and selects a single direction.

At that time Vaidehi said to the Buddha, "O World-Honored One! Though these Buddha-lands are pure and all have light, I now wish to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, at the place of Amitābha Buddha. Only I beg the World-Honored One to teach me contemplation and teach me right concentration."

According to Vaidehi's words: the lands of the ten directions are all pure in appearance, with nowhere not good; as to my seeking rebirth, I will be born in only one place. Having received the World-Honored One's compassionate manifestation so as to contemplate, it is only to make me choose for myself. I now wish to be born in Amitābha Buddha's land. This sufficiently proves that that Buddha's bond of connection with sentient beings of this world is deep. (Elaboration)

The World-Honored One emitted light between his brows and manifested the pure lands, letting Vaidehi choose for herself: because among the Buddha-lands, pure and luminous, none surpasses the Land of Ultimate Bliss; seeing it with her own fleshly eyes, her faith and joy would be doubly deep. From this contemplation she at once obtained right concentration. (Brief Treatise)
The passage has three sections: first, a general statement that the various lands are not what she wishes.

Second, from "I now" onward, she particularly points to the Land of Ultimate Bliss as exactly matching her capacity. The reason is that sentient beings of this inferior world have minds much scattered; if one does not point to a single direction and contemplate a single Buddha fixedly, the contemplation is hard to accomplish and rebirth is much obstructed. Besides, Amitābha's light always shines and his vow is vast and deep. Therefore, being born in one land, one is connected to all lands; contemplating one Buddha, one sees all Buddhas alike. The Treatise on Ten Doubts says the Buddha answered Pukwang [spoke:] the principle is clearly evident. Shandao's exclusive practice accords with the same meaning. Third, from "only I beg" onward, she requests the contemplative method for the practice of rebirth. The first stage of practice, directing the mind toward the contemplated object, is called contemplation. When the contemplation is accomplished and harmoniously still from the wheel of itself, it is called right concentration. As the earth-contemplation says, "To have such a thought is called a coarse vision of the earth of the Land of Ultimate Bliss," which is contemplation; "if one attains samādhi, one sees that land's earth clearly and distinctly, beyond all description," which is right concentration. One may know that contemplation and right concentration both belong to the contemplative method, differing only in depth. And earlier it said: "teach me to contemplate the pure karma-ground," showing that Vaidehi only asked for contemplation. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

The Direct Pointing commentary says: measuring with a scattered mind is called contemplation, spoken with reference to wisdom; fixing the mind single-mindedly is called right concentration, spoken with reference to concentration.

The Annotated Notes say: after the mind is settled there is no thought and no thinking; but the single-minded thought before settling is called contemplation. The Four-fascicle Commentary says: contemplation is the expedient prior to concentration. Right concentration, also called samādhi, is another name for meditative absorption. Free from the wrong and scattered is called right; receiving the Dharma into the mind without thought and without thinking is called concentration, like a bright mirror reflecting objects with no mind of its own. The Profound Meaning of the Contemplation Sutra says: as to right concentration, thinking mind is entirely still, and deliberating and reflecting both vanish, corresponding to samādhi; this is called right concentration. (Annotated Notes)
Bing 3: Bimbisara, receiving the light, attains the fruit of the Way.

At that time the World-Honored One straightway smiled, and a five-colored light issued from the Buddha's mouth; each light shone on the crown of King Bimbisara's head. At that time the great king, though confined, was unimpeded in the eye of his mind; from afar he saw the World-Honored One and bowed his head in reverence; and by himself he advanced, attaining the fruit of an Anagamin.

The Tathagata's manifestation of the lands was precisely for this purpose; the capacity and the stimulus met, hiddenly communicated and secretly responding, so the Buddha smiled. The Contemplation of the Buddha's Ocean of Marks Sutra says, "It is the constant law of the Buddhas that whenever they smile, a five-colored light always issues from the mouth." The light shone on the king's crown — the Buddha's power of blessing caused him to increase in the fruit of the Way. Receiving the light and seeing the Buddha, he deeply realized impermanence, raised wisdom, and cut off delusions, and so realized the third fruit. Anagamin is here rendered "no return." His remaining fetters were nearly exhausted, and he would not return to the lower worlds. According to this, Bimbisara, seeing the Buddha and attaining the fruit, should have heard the contemplative teaching together with the lady; but later, in concluding the benefit, it says the Buddha only taught Vaidehi and five hundred maids, from which we know that Bimbisara, having realized the fruit, already passed away. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

The smile has two intentions: first, answering the lady's cause of joy, hence the happy smile; second, completing the great king's fruit of joy, hence the happy smile. (The Annotated Notes say, "The Buddha does not smile idly; only when fulfilling the fundamental purpose of his appearance in the world does he begin to smile in assent. Thus the Buddha's smile manifests his fundamental purpose in appearing in the world.") That without waiting for her reply, the light first shone upon the king: first, to let them see the Buddha and the assembly so as to cut off doubt and dissolve fetters; second, to let them realize that worldly dharmas are all like dreams and illusions; third, to let them believe that good and evil and their fruits are never mistaken; fourth, to let them know that each gains the benefit of his own cultivation and realization. The five colors signify breaking the five aggregates and becoming the joy of the five-part Dharma-body, and surpassing the five defilements to attain the five purities. (Direct Pointing commentary)

The commentary says: "That he did not directly answer the cause of her land, but again emitted light and smiled, has two intentions: first, it was to (cause the king to) progress in the Way; second, it was to let the king and the lady see one another. The king, having seen the light and progressed in the Way, knew the country was not real, and looked on death as on sleep; the lady, seeing the king without sorrow, had the fruit of the contemplative method accomplished. The smile is like when the Sakya clan was slain, the Tathagata's light and color became all the more manifest. It is precisely because the Tathagata well understands that karma and its retribution are unfailing, and that when the time comes one cannot flee. The king, though destined to die, obtained the trace of the Way; the lady's imprisonment is the very moment of manifesting the Pure Land. Having so many conditions, therefore he smiled." I privately reflect: since Bimbisara's fruit had ripened and fallen, the time had come and the principle was evident; so he first emitted light to touch him, enabling him to leave the cage and become a sage-fruit. Besides, that lesser vessel of his naturally accomplished a lesser fruit; it was not only that Vaidehi was the initiator of this sutra and also the one of the assembly, while Bimbisara had neither of these matters, hence he was made to be released first. Had Bimbisara not [been born during] Ajatasatru's [reign], he would not necessarily have attained a sage-fruit in this present life. Even if he attained it in this life, it would not necessarily be so swift. Had Ajatasatru not met an evil friend, he would not necessarily have had the thought of killing his father and seizing the kingdom; without this utmost evil mind, he would by no means commit this inverted deed. That the world's most extreme evil cause of suffering should help accomplish the good fruit of sagehood beyond the world — is this not inconceivable! Bimbisara, because his own son killed his father and sought the kingdom, from this [suffering] his worldly thoughts became like cold ashes; and when he was shut in the seven-layered chamber, not hearing the least of state affairs, at this time he returned to his original face, and together with upholding the precepts and hearing the Dharma, cultivated the three studies together — therefore he cut off delusion and realized truth; that is fitting! That the light was five-colored signifies that from the Buddha's Dharma-nature, upon the substance of the five aggregates, a wonderful light was revealed, which broke through Bimbisara's five aggregates and transformed them into the fruit of the five-part Dharma-body. Therefore though the king was confined, his body and mind within and without were all at ease. The seven-layered walls of the chamber could in no way obstruct; though it is said he saw from afar, it was as if before his eyes. At the instant of bowing, he realized the third fruit. In Sanskrit, Anagamin, in Chinese, "no return," meaning he had already cut off the nine grades of birth-causes of the desire realm, so he could no longer come to the lower worlds to take birth. (Elaboration)
The Annotated Notes say: the mind that contemplates, through its power of insight, illuminates and knows all dharmas — this is called the eye of the mind.
The Jingying commentary says: the king was first a Stream-enterer, so now he advanced and became an Anagamin.
Yi 2: The proper elucidation of the contemplations, the right cause of pure karma, in two parts.

blocks.text: First, the general statement and the promise to speak. Second, the particular exposition of the pure contemplations.

inline.s: Bing 1: The general statement and the promise to speak, in two parts.
First, the general statement.
Second, the promise to speak.
Ding 1: The general statement.
At that time the World-Honored One told Vaidehi: "Do you now know? Amitābha Buddha is not far from here. You should fix your thought and contemplate closely that land accomplished by pure karma.

First asking whether she knows is to make clear that the Pure Land is not something the Buddha speaks of by himself, with no one else knowing [the capacity]. The Amitābha Sutra says, "To the west from here, passing over a hundred thousand Buddha-lands," yet it says it is not far; there are three explanations: first, from the Buddha-eye's contemplation, as the Surangama Sutra says: the celestial eye contemplates the great thousandfold, even as looking at a fruit in the palm; how much more the Buddha-eye! For example, ascending on high and looking down, one eye takes in ten thousand leagues; this is what is meant by "ascending Mount Tai and the whole world becomes small." Second, from the swiftness of thought: the spirit-mind is unimpeded, and distant regions and foreign lands, at the very rise of a thought, are reached; this is what is meant by "thought is swifter than the wind." Third, from the Buddha's power of gathering in: though one has not attained transcendent power, riding the Buddha's spiritual power, as the Treatise on Ten Doubts says, an inferior man, mounted with a world-turning king, in one day and night traverses the four continents; this is what is meant by "a blue fly attached to a steed's tail." (Lingzhi's Commentary)

The Miaozong Sub-commentary says: "Speaking of 'not far' is because by the Buddha's power, one who cultivates contemplation sees it the moment he wishes. Therefore this passage says, 'you should fix your thought and contemplate closely that land.' Hence we know that the Buddha's power enables one who wishes to see, so that when the contemplation is accomplished he sees. Later it says, 'All sentient beings who contemplate the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, by the Buddha's power, shall see that pure land.' Therefore the Pratyutpanna [samādhi] seeing the Buddha discusses three powers: first, the Buddha's power; second, samādhi power; third, the practitioner's own fundamental merit-power."
The Annotated Notes say: "Fixing thought means to fix the thought on one place and not think of another. 'Closely' means to examine carefully."

The Jingying commentary says: "'Contemplate closely that land' encourages contemplation of the objective reward; 'accomplished by pure karma' encourages contemplation of the subjective reward." That is, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and the persons of the three grades of rebirth and so on are called those accomplished by pure karma. The Lingzhi commentary says: "Those accomplished by pure karma is a general term for the subjective and objective rewards of that land." The Direct Pointing commentary says: "Those accomplished by pure karma in that land: the immeasurable splendor of the Land of Ultimate Bliss is all the perfuming and accomplishment of taintless virtue of nature, and the accomplishment of the pure karma of blessing."

The Elaboration says: "The Buddha's meaning is this: earlier you said you wished to be born in Amitābha's Land of Ultimate Bliss; now he tells Vaidehi: 'Do you now know? Amitābha Buddha's Land of Ultimate Bliss is not far from here and not hard to be reborn in; just fix your thought on Amitābha Buddha and contemplate closely that Land of Ultimate Bliss.'"
Ding 2: The promise to speak.
"I now will speak for you widely of many similes; and also cause all ordinary people of future ages who wish to cultivate pure karma to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss."

"I now will speak for you widely of many similes" is the promise to speak. From "and also cause" onward sets forth the intention of speaking. That he speaks is to benefit sentient beings of the present and future. (Jiaxiang's Commentary)

The realm of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, sentient beings have not yet known; taking things as comparisons, hence "many similes." As below, "like a thousand million suns," "its light like flowers," and so on. Or perhaps all the words of explanation are generally called similes. "And also cause future [beings]" precisely reveals the fundamental intention, not limited to those of the present assembly. This is what is meant by a bow of a thousand catties; would it be triggered merely for a field-mouse? (Lingzhi's Commentary)

blocks.text: Bing 2: The particular exposition of the pure contemplations, in two parts.

inline.s: First, setting forth the three kinds of meritorious karma; second, explaining the sixteen contemplations.
Ding 1: Setting forth the three kinds of meritorious karma, in three parts.
First, the general heading.
Second, the particular explanation. Third, the concluding praise.

The reason for first making clear the three blessings: they are the appropriate undertakings of one who cultivates contemplation. Without contemplation there is nothing to guide his merit; without merit there is nothing to accomplish his contemplation. With contemplation and no merit, one lacks the adornments; with merit and no contemplation, one is drawn toward other destinies. Lacking adornments, the reward obtained is not supreme; drawn toward other destinies, there is no way to rebirth. The two methods support each other, and there is no place where they do not benefit. In addressing those who study, apply the mind with determination to investigate; do not be confused at the crossroads and lose the starting point of your own advance. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

The Brief Treatise says: "About to explain the pure contemplations, he first teaches beings to cultivate the three blessings: because by worldly dharmas one gradually reaches supramundane dharmas. It is like storing nectar: first clean the vessel; if the vessel is not clean, its flavor is spoiled."
Wu 1: The general heading.
"Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate the three blessings:"
The Lingzhi commentary says: "'Those who wish to be born' speaks of their aspiration; 'should cultivate' instructs that they must do so."
Wu 2: The particular explanation.
"First, to honor and care for one's parents, to serve one's teachers and elders, to be of compassionate mind and not kill, and to cultivate the ten wholesome deeds."

Since these are the cause of the Buddhas of the three times, one knows clearly they are the great practice of the Bodhisattva. The first is the karma shared with ordinary people; the second is the karma shared with the two vehicles; the third is the Mahayana karma not shared [with them]. (The Direct Pointing commentary says, "the third shares the Mahayana karma.") Within the first, the upper two clauses are the practice of repaying kindness. Parents have the kindness of giving birth and nurture; teachers and elders have the kindness of instruction. The lower two clauses are the practice of abandoning evil. Not killing is the foremost of the ten wholesome deeds, so it is particularly marked. The body avoids the three wrong-doings, the mouth leaves the four faults, and the mind cuts off the three evils. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

Honoring and caring for one's parents: sentient beings, depending on parents, have this body; depending on this body, they come to know there is a Buddha. Therefore, not revering one's own body, one does not accomplish the wisdom of all seeds; not revering one's own parents, one cannot grow all the fields of merit. Some may say: the Tathagata left his family and went forth, which seems to contradict the principle of filial care. They do not know that there is the filiality of the world and the filiality of the world-transcending. The filiality of the world: while they live, provide for them fully; when they die, sacrifice to them fully; establish one's person in the Way and make one's name known to later generations — that is all. The filiality of the world-transcending must await one's parents' escape from the three realms and realization of the unconditioned; only then is the way of the son fulfilled. Great filiality honors one's parents; what exceeds this? (Brief Treatise)

Serving one's teachers and elders: there are worldly teachers and elders and world-transcending teachers and elders. Leading one in the arts of poetry and books, urging one along the path of benevolence and duty — these are worldly teachers and elders. Awakening one by the teachings of the three jewels, advancing one by the gate of the two truths — these are world-transcending teachers and elders. That they ought to be served is one and the same. (Brief Treatise)

Of compassionate mind and not killing: the Buddha's mind is great compassion. Among the evil karmas of the Saha world, none exceeds killing life; the enmities and hatreds of age after age arise from killing. If the mind of killing is not cut off, the mind of compassion is not fulfilled; if the mind of compassion is not fulfilled, one stands opposed and separate from sentient beings; standing opposed and separate from sentient beings is to stand opposed and separate from the Tathagata. To wish to seek rebirth in the Pure Land is difficult! (Brief Treatise)
"Second, to receive and uphold the three refuges, to be complete in the various precepts, and not to transgress the rules of deportment."

The upper clause is the three refuges that turn from the false. Ordinary people from beginningless time are bound to the devil; performing the rite and taking refuge, they seek deliverance and protection. If one only takes refuge, there is good but no precepts. If one receives the many precepts, one must also take the three refuges. The lower two clauses are the reception of the precept dharmas. For householders, the five and eight; for renunciates, the ten and the complete precepts; hence "the various precepts." Receiving and upholding without deficiency, hence "complete." Deportment is also precept, subtle and light, hard to hold, which people commonly trespass, so it is particularly marked and singled out. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

If one can cultivate the ten wholesome deeds and counter the ten evil deeds, then past hindrances gradually dissolve; past hindrances dissolved, hence rebirth is unimpeded. Yet one must receive them with the three refuges and widen them with the many precepts: without receiving the three refuges, one cannot plant the seed of the world-transcending; without being complete in the many precepts, one cannot cultivate the foundation of the world-transcending. The three refuges and the many precepts are the right cause of entering Buddhahood. (Brief Treatise)
"Third, to rouse the bodhi-mind, to believe deeply in cause and effect, to read and recite the Mahayana, and to encourage those who practice."

Within it are four clauses: the first is to rouse the great mind. Bodhi is translated "the Way," that is, the mind of the supreme Way. The second is to arouse great faith. Good and evil and their cause and effect all come from one's own mind; knowing this with awe and caution, hence "believe deeply." The third is to produce great understanding. The teaching conveys the original wisdom, which is produced by recitation. The fourth is to cultivate the great practice. To encourage and entice toward cultivation, not causing one to fall back. The first three are self-practice; the last one is the conversion of others. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

Yet although one is complete in refuge and precepts, if one does not rouse the bodhi-mind, though one had merit and fortune, in the end it becomes tainted and out-flowing; because it does not correspond to the Tathagata's seal of wisdom that relies on nothing. (Brief Treatise)

Bodhi is anciently translated "the Way," newly translated "awakening." The Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom, chapter forty-one: "When a Bodhisattva first rouses the mind, anchoring on the supreme Way, thinking 'I shall become a Buddha' — this is called the bodhi-mind." The Jingying commentary: "Bodhi is the Way. The Buddha-fruit is completely perfect and penetrating, called bodhi. To raise the intention and direct toward it is called rousing the mind. To speak of it in brief: what the Buddha attained, I also shall attain." The Four-fascicle Commentary: "Bodhi is the name of the Buddha-fruit; mind is the seeking-mind of sentient beings. Hence the phrase 'to rouse the bodhi-mind.'"

Believing deeply in cause and effect: doing good obtains fortune, doing evil obtains calamity; like ginseng, which is foremost in tonifying, and rhubarb, which is foremost in purging. Toning and purging lie in the person, completely from one's fundamental endowment. Hence we know that doing good is itself fortune, and outside good there is no fortune; doing evil is itself calamity, and outside evil there is no calamity. This is called cause and effect being simultaneous. Then, in a single thought of mindfulness of the Buddha, that thought is the Buddha; thought after thought of mindfulness, there is no thought that is not Buddha. The mind being pure and the Land being pure is likewise. (Brief Treatise)

Reading and reciting the Mahayana: if one does not read the Mahayana, one does not understand the Buddha's mind; not understanding the Buddha's mind, one does not accord with the Buddha's wisdom; not according with the Buddha's wisdom, though he be born in that land, he cannot see the Buddha. If one in truth understands the Buddha's mind, and in truth accords with the Buddha's wisdom, benefiting self and benefiting others, the capacity cannot be restrained, because the Buddha and sentient beings are of one substance. (Brief Treatise)
Wu 3: The concluding praise, in two parts.
First, the conclusive statement.
Second, the praise of its excellence.
Ji 1: The conclusive statement.
"Such these three matters are called pure karma."
Ji 2: The praise of its excellence.
The Buddha told Vaidehi: "Do you now know? These three kinds of karma are the pure karma right cause of the Buddhas of the three times — past, future, and present."
The meritorious fruit of the three times is accomplished by means of this, hence it is called the right cause. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

The Brief Treatise says: "When the three blessings are cultivated together, the pure cause is complete; whether one contemplates or recites, it follows whatever one seeks. It is like holding a mirror to take an image, or raising a voice to require an echo — how far off is it?"

blocks.text: Ding 2: Clarifying the Method of the Sixteen Contemplations, Divided into Two Parts.
