inline.s: Regarding the sixteen contemplations: Jingying's commentary says: “The first is the contemplation of the sun; the second, the contemplation of water; the third, the contemplation of the ground; the fourth, the contemplation of trees; the fifth, the contemplation of ponds; the sixth is the general visualization — contemplating all the pavilions, trees, ponds, and so forth; the seventh, the contemplation of the lotus seat; the eighth, the contemplation of the images of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas; the ninth, the contemplation of the Buddha's body; the tenth, the contemplation of Avalokiteśvara; the eleventh, the contemplation of Mahāsthāmaprāpta; the twelfth, the contemplation of one's own rebirth (that is, the universal contemplation); the thirteenth, the miscellaneous contemplation of Buddhas and bodhisattvas; the fourteenth, the contemplation of the highest grade of rebirth; the fifteenth, the contemplation of the middle grade of rebirth; the sixteenth, the contemplation of the lowest grade of rebirth.” In these sixteen contemplations, the ancient commentaries divide and classify them differently. Lingzhi's commentary says: “Regarding the sixteen contemplations, they are broadly divided into two: the first type first contemplates the setting sun of this region, in order to establish the direction toward which the mind should turn; the latter fifteen types properly contemplate the two kinds of retribution — the reliant and the proper — of that other land. The first contemplation is the general one, encompassing the following fifteen. The rest are all particular and do not subsume one another. Within the latter fifteen, they are again divided into two: the first five contemplate the adornment of the reliant retribution of that other land; the last ten contemplate the excellence of its proper retribution. Within the first five, they are again divided into two: the first two contemplate the realm it relies upon, [from] contemplating water becoming ice, and seeing ice as ground. The last three contemplate the marks of its adornment. The adornment of the land does not go beyond three kinds: the trees are its shady groves; the ponds are its flowing springs; the pavilions are its terraces and towers. The contemplation of the ground is the general one, because it encompasses the other three. The trees and the rest are particular, because all are supported by the ground. Within the last ten, they are again divided into four: the first three contemplate the Buddha — the seventh contemplates where the Buddha sits; the eighth contemplates the image as an expression of the real; the ninth properly contemplates the Buddha's body. The tenth and eleventh contemplate the Buddha's attendants, divided on the left and right. The twelfth and thirteenth are the general contemplation of the Three Sages, with the universal and the miscellaneous being different. The fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth contemplate the Buddha's congregation, the distinctions among the three grades.” Jingying's commentary says: “Among these sixteen, the first seven gates contemplate the reliant retribution; the latter nine gates contemplate the proper retribution. The earlier words ‘you should contemplate that land’ [of the Buddha's speech] are the first seven contemplations. ‘One whose pure karma is accomplished’ refers to the latter nine contemplations. The contemplations differ thus. Yet in the present text, the first six contemplations are discussed in one place. The latter ten contemplation-gates are distinguished in one place. The contemplation of the lotus seat should be discussed together with the first six; because it conveniently arises in connection with the contemplation of the Buddha, it is placed later.” Now, following the textual arrangement, I divide it into two categories: first, contemplating the reliant retribution; second, contemplating the proper retribution.
Wu 1: Contemplating the Reliant Retribution, in Three Parts.
First, the Tathāgata's admonition and encouragement
Second, Vaidehī's renewed request; third, the proper display of the contemplative methods
Ji 1: The Tathāgata's Admonition and Encouragement, in Three Parts.
First, commanding to listen and granting the explanation
Second, the separate charge to Ānanda to hold and proclaim [the Dharma]
Third, narrating the circumstance of Vaidehī's seeing the Land
Geng 1: Commanding to Listen and Granting the Explanation.

The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: “Listen attentively! Listen attentively! Think upon it well. The Tathāgata now, for the sake of all sentient beings of the future world, who are harmed by the thieves of affliction, speaks of the pure karma. Good indeed, Vaidehī, that you have asked this, your welcome question!”
Below ‘the Buddha’ [the text] admonishes to listen. Below ‘the Tathāgata’ it grants the explanation. Below ‘good indeed’ it praises the previous question.

‘Telling Vaidehī and again telling Ānanda’ means: telling Vaidehī to cause her to listen attentively with single-minded intent; commanding Ānanda to cause him to transmit and transform those who have not yet heard. For this reason, both persons are addressed together. (Jiaxiang's commentary)
‘Listen attentively’ gives rise to the wisdom of hearing; ‘think upon it well’ [gives rise to] the wisdom of reflection and of cultivation. (Tiantai's commentary)

‘For the sake of the future’ refers precisely to the age of the semblance and final Dharma. ‘Harmed by the thieves of affliction’ refers to ordinary beings fully bound by the fetters. ‘Pure karma’ is the sixteen contemplations. (Lingzhi's commentary)
Affliction is called a thief because it can damage the life of wisdom and injure the Dharma-body. (Tiantai's commentary)

‘Good indeed’ is an exclamation. ‘Good’ is like ‘excellent’; ‘indeed’ is a particle. ‘That you have asked this, your welcome question’ sets forth what is being praised. Because of the previous request, [which] broadly opens forth the karma of rebirth in the Pure Land, therefore it is praised. (Jingying's commentary)

The Lingzhi commentary says: “It pleases the sage's mind, therefore it is called ‘a welcome question.’” The Jiaxiang commentary says: “Because of her question, present beings obtain benefit close at hand, and future beings are further benefited; therefore it praises the welcome question.”
Geng 2: The Separate Charge to Ānanda to Hold and Proclaim [the Dharma].

“Ānanda! You should receive and uphold it, and broadly proclaim the Buddha's words to the many assemblies. The Tathāgata now teaches Vaidehī and all sentient beings of the future world to contemplate the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; through the Buddha's power, they shall see that pure land, as if holding a bright mirror and seeing one's own face. Having seen the supremely wondrous, blissful things of that land, and being joyful in heart, at that very moment they attain the tolerance of the non-arising of dharmas.”

Ānanda was widely learned, and so is exhorted to uphold and proclaim it; because, while [the Buddha] was in the secluded palace, those who heard it together with him were still few, and later, upon returning to Vulture Peak, [the Buddha] intended that it be retold, therefore he charged him in advance. ‘The Tathāgata now’ and the rest are all the words entrusted to Ānanda to speak. (Lingzhi's commentary)

Below ‘the Tathāgata’ sets forth the reason for the admonition and charge. The Jingying commentary says: “Instructing Vaidehī who is near, and instructing all sentient beings of the future who are far, the sage's intent is universal. ‘Contemplate the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss’ sets forth the matter being taught. Below ‘through the Buddha's power’ it clarifies the benefits of the contemplation. These benefits are of three kinds: first, seeing through the Buddha's power. Because one sees it clearly and distinctly, it is like holding a bright mirror and seeing one's own face. (The Zhizhi commentary says: “‘Holding’ is a metaphor for taking up the practice and upholding it; ‘mirror’ is a metaphor for the contemplative mind; ‘face’ is a metaphor for the land and its realm.”) Second, from seeing, the heart rejoices. Third, one attains the tolerance of non-arising. Because one knows that that land manifests from the mind, and penetrates to the original non-existence of dharmas, therefore one attains non-arising. Non-arising is the principle. When the mind of wisdom abides in the principle, it is called the tolerance of non-arising.” The Zhizhi commentary says: “ ‘Attain’ means to realize. ‘Tolerance’ means wisdom. ‘Dharmas of non-arising’ means the principle. Because the mind of wisdom abides in this principle of the nature of non-arising dharmas, therefore it is called attaining the tolerance of the non-arising of dharmas. ‘At that very moment’ means entering by the perfect and sudden [path]. Seeing the land is the excellence of the realm. The joyful heart is the purity of the cause. ‘Immediately attaining’ is the ripening of the fruit.” The Lingzhi commentary says: “The attainment of the tolerance of non-arising is, in terms of stage, the stage of the initial abiding. If one goes by the contemplative method, the power of its merit is strong, and it can be realized within this present life. Following the later contemplation of the Buddha, it refers to the mark of attaining realization upon being born there. Below it says: ‘Casting off the body in another world, being born before the Buddhas, and attaining the tolerance of non-arising’ — that is it.”
Geng 3: Narrating the Circumstance of Vaidehī's Seeing the Land.

The Buddha told Vaidehī: “You are an ordinary being; your mind's thoughts are weak and inferior, you have not attained the divine eye, and cannot contemplate from afar. The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess an exceptional expedient means, which enables you to see.”

[The Buddha], in his great provisional [power], draws [beings] toward the real, therefore he displays an identity with ordinary [beings]. (The Jingying commentary says: “Lady Vaidehī was in truth a great bodhisattva; attaining the tolerance of the non-arising of dharmas at this assembly, she was clearly no small [being], and yet she also transformed to appear as an ordinary being.”) The divine eye is one of the six superknowledges; whether within or beyond the obstructions, it sees all thoroughly. Ordinary immortals and lesser sages, although they attain the divine eye, cannot contemplate the pure realms in remote regions. As for the ‘exceptional expedient means’: if it is directed to those of the appropriate capacity, it is the earlier manifestation of the land upon the radiant platform, which enabled Vaidehī to see. According to the doctrine of the Buddha's dispensation [to beings] below, it is the following sixteen contemplative methods, directed specifically to future [beings]. Wanting to make clear that the way of provisional wisdom is the same [for all Buddhas], therefore it says ‘the Buddhas.’ (Lingzhi's commentary.) The Jingying commentary says: “Teaching [them] to contemplate the sun, water, and such things of this region, and causing them to know that other region, this is called the exceptional expedient means enabling them to see.” The Zhizhi commentary says: “Exceptional means supreme, swift, and wonderful. The Qixin [Lun] says: The Tathāgata possesses a supreme expedient means, namely, that through the causal conditions of mindfulness of the Buddha, one constantly sees the Buddha.” The Yanyi says: “Supreme means transcendently superior; exceptional means extraordinarily different. Viewing the sūtra and the śāstra together, it is clear that the Pure Land is the dharma-gate of the supreme and exceptional expedient means.”
Ji 2: Vaidehī's Renewed Request.

At that time Vaidehī said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One! As for me now, through the Buddha's power, I see that land; but after the Buddha's extinction, the sentient beings, defiled, evil, and not good, pressed upon by the five sufferings — how shall they see the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha?”

The meaning of this question is: I now, through the Buddha's power, see that land; but after the Buddha's extinction, how shall sentient beings come to see it? It is a renewed question on behalf of future sentient beings. (Jiaxiang's commentary)

The Lingzhi commentary says: “This is the great compassion's expedient and clever means of benefiting beings; only thus is it seen that Vaidehī's level was not ordinary and small. ‘Defiled, evil, and not good’ has the same meaning as explained previously. As for the five sufferings: the commentary says, because all the five destinies are without bliss. The asura path, when opened out, makes six; combined, there are only five. Or one may take the five evils, the five agonies, and the five burnings of the Larger Scripture as the five sufferings. Namely, the five kinds of transgression prohibited by the five precepts are the five evils. Committing these five things, meeting with calamities and offending the law, is the five agonies. Afterwards falling into the three lower realms is called the five burnings. The future sentient beings: first, being born without encountering a Buddha; second, the defilement and evil growing ever more prevailing; third, suffering pressing upon them ever more deeply. Their karmic hindrances being thus, and doubting that there is any reason to see the land, what expedient means is there to enable them to see?”
Ji 3: Properly Displaying the Contemplative Methods, in Six Parts.

The contemplative methods are six: first, the contemplation of the sun; second, the contemplation of water; third, the contemplation of the ground; fourth, the contemplation of trees; fifth, the contemplation of ponds; sixth, the general contemplation. The Jiaxiang commentary says: “The previous one-and-a-half contemplations (the contemplation of the sun and the first half of the contemplation of water) are the expedient preparation for contemplation; the later three-and-a-half contemplations are the actual contemplation (properly contemplating the reliant retribution).” Now, following the text, I divide into six: first, contemplating the setting sun; second, the contemplation of water; third, the contemplation of the ground; fourth, the contemplation of trees; fifth, the contemplation of ponds; sixth, the general contemplation.

blocks.text: Geng 1: Contemplating the Setting Sun (the Sun Contemplation), in Two Parts.

inline.s: First, the general encouragement to practice contemplation
Second, the proper elucidation of contemplating the Sun
Xin 1: The General Encouragement to Practice Contemplation.
The Buddha told Vaidehī: “You and [all] sentient beings should concentrate your minds and fix your thoughts on a single place, and contemplate the West.”

The contemplative gate of the Pure Land has as its essential point single-mindedness; therefore one must designate a single direction to be the place upon which the mind is cast. Hence the emanation of light and the manifestation of the land had precisely this intention. (Lingzhi's commentary)

As for ‘concentrate the mind and fix your thoughts’: an ordinary mind, dim and scattered — how could it clearly see the wonderful realm of the Pure Land? Therefore [the Buddha] has me focus on contemplating the form of the setting sun. Contemplating it without ceasing, the mind then becomes settled. If the mind is still and subtle, all the various contemplative methods can be cultivated. The reason the method of fixing the mind must [use] the setting sun is to cause one's settled contemplation to tend toward the West, which is the direction of Amitābha's dwelling. (Miaozong's Notes)
Xin 2: Properly Elucidating the Contemplation of the Sun, in Two Parts.
First, raising the object to be contemplated
Second, properly elucidating the method of contemplation
Ren 1: Raising the Object to Be Contemplated.
How does one go about producing the visualization? In every case of producing a visualization, all sentient beings — those who are not blind from birth, who have eyes — have all seen the sun set.

The directions are vast and boundless, with nothing to mark them out; the setting sun of this region is seen by all who have eyes. Distinct and easy to contemplate, it can serve as a standard. The commentary says: “The setting sun, like a suspended drum, is used to mark the direction toward which one's thoughts are sent.” That is precisely this point. As for ‘producing a visualization,’ visualization is contemplation. Losing one's eyes in the womb is called being blind from birth. (Lingzhi's commentary)
Ren 2: Properly Elucidating the Method of Contemplation.

You should raise a thought and visualize: sitting upright facing west, contemplate intently the place where the sun is about to set; cause the mind to abide firmly, concentrating on the visualization without shifting. See the sun as it is about to set, its form like a suspended drum. Having seen the sun, whether with eyes closed or eyes open, cause it all to be clear and distinct. This is the contemplation of the sun, called the first contemplation.

The passage has four sections: first, the two opening sentences show the manner of practice. ‘Raising a thought’ is the arising of the contemplation. ‘Sitting upright’ is the posture of the body. Full cross-legged or half cross-legged, straightening the body and piling the hands, as in the method of sitting in meditation. Hence in the Biographies of Monks, the eminent monks of ancient Jin, sitting, did not turn their backs to the West — this is precisely in conformance with this. Second, below ‘contemplate intently’ it shows the aspect of contemplation. The mind and its object responding to each other, silently unmoving, that is the essence of concentration (samādhi). Third, the two sentences below ‘see’ reveal the mark of accomplishment. The sun sets near the ground, the clouds disperse and its light gathers, bright like the face of a drum, suspended in the sky. Fourth, below ‘having seen,’ [the text] urges constant contemplation. When the visualization is accomplished and the mark arises, thought after thought continues without interruption, flowing spontaneously without being forgotten. The last two sentences conclude and point it out. This is understandable. (Lingzhi's commentary)

This contemplation first fixes the place and direction, like the needle of a compass for seafaring, causing those who cultivate the contemplation to direct their minds toward [the West]. Question: According to the doctrine of consciousness-only, there is no realm outside the mind; here it says the realm is in the West — is this not a realm outside the mind? Answer: ‘Mind’ refers to the ālaya-vijñāna, the store consciousness; the mind of the physical body arises in dependence upon the store consciousness, and is not the mind [itself]. Since beginningless time, the ālaya-vijñāna, the store consciousness, flows on without ceasing; when a bodhisattva reaches the eighth ground, he then relinquishes this store consciousness. Before the store [consciousness] is relinquished, this consciousness takes the six destinies as its way-station, undergoing immeasurable birth-and-death of the divided [kind]. The mind of the physical body is the way-station, not the master of the station. The master's property, reaching vertically through the three times and horizontally throughout the ten directions, cannot be fully contained within the way-station. The master's power can transform and produce the sense faculties, the body, and the world of instruments; then mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all manifested by consciousness — how could the West alone be an exception? One mind encompasses the ten dharma-realms, and can even include the hells; how much less is there any barrier with respect to the Pure Land. The mind's function is vast; one should exhaust its measure: letting it extend to the six directions, it is not confined to the square inch of the heart. Now [the Buddha] teaches first to contemplate the setting sun, whose form is like a suspended drum; one should forever remember it and not forget. At the moment of death, when the ālaya-vijñāna separates from the physical body, where does this consciousness, on the vast road ahead, go? As a sūtra says: If one sees before one's eyes only felt mats of various colors, one is reborn in the continents such as Uttarakuru; or if one sees dense forests, bamboos, reeds, and rushes, one is born in a lowly family; if one sees ascending palaces, one is born in a noble family. Those who cultivate the pure karma, at death, do not see these various mixed signs; they see only, in the bright place of the evening mist, a single wheel of the setting sun, its golden radiance dazzling; and they race straight toward it and go, naturally not losing the way. If their pure merit is accomplished, the Buddha himself appears before them, and there is all the more reliance, without fear. Therefore this contemplation of the sun is not only the place and direction of the Land of Bliss, but is also, for those who have not yet seen the Buddha at the end of life, a travel guide. (Shilun)

Among the latter fifteen contemplations, within the first five [dealing with] the reliant retribution, the second, the visualization of water, seeks to accomplish this land's congealed ice [as an analogy]; the fifth, the visualization of water, properly contemplates the ponds and marshes of that region. The names are the same but their substance differs; students should know this. (Lingzhi's commentary)

blocks.text: Geng 2: The Contemplation of Water, in Two Parts.

inline.s: First, contemplating the water
Second, contemplating the ground
Xin 1: Contemplating the Water.

Next, produce the visualization of water: see the water clear and pure, and cause it also to be clear and distinct, without any intention of scattering. Having seen the water, you should produce the visualization of ice; seeing the ice transparent and clear, produce the visualization of lapis lazuli (vaidūrya).

The passage has three sections: first, properly visualizing the water. The Yanyi says: “Continuing from the accomplishment of the contemplation of the sun above, one proceeds in order to contemplate the water. It does not speak of contemplation (guān) but speaks of visualization (xiǎng), because [it marks] a change of contemplation. A beginner's cultivation of contemplation must first use visualization. Fixing the thought to settle the mind, only then can one cultivate contemplation. Now water is raised as the contemplated object; people have already seen a great pool of still water, therefore it is taught to employ the mind's visualization. One should know that visualization has two kinds: first, pure visualization; second, mixed visualization. In the beginning mind of cultivating contemplation, one uses pure visualization.” The Lingzhi commentary says: “The visualization of water is precisely for the contemplation of the ground. A jeweled ground of lapis lazuli is without precedent in the world; water freezing on the surface is something all people know. By means of this to see that, using the similar to compare with the real. Therefore first the water and ice are raised, and afterwards the jeweled ground is accomplished. The commentary says: ‘A great body of water freezing into ice in truth represents a ground of lapis lazuli’ — that is it.” It also says: “It reveals the clarity above, still and unmoving, therefore it says ‘without any intention of scattering.’ Second, the two sentences below ‘having seen’ transform the water into ice. Third, the two sentences below ‘seeing the ice’ transform the ice into lapis lazuli. Up to this point, the passage on contemplation is complete. From below this visualization, it belongs to the subsequent contemplation of the ground.”
Xin 2: Contemplating the Ground.

When this visualization is accomplished, one sees the ground of lapis lazuli, transparent and clear within and without. Below it is a golden banner of vajra and seven treasures, upholding the ground of lapis lazuli. The banner has eight sides, fully provided with eight ridges. Each side is composed of hundreds of treasures. Each gem has a thousand rays of light. Each ray of light has eighty-four thousand colors; reflected upon the ground of lapis lazuli, like billions and thousands of suns, they cannot be fully seen.

The passage has three sections: first, from below ‘this visualization,’ the substance of the ground is bright and transparent. The annotation (Jianzhu) says: “First the practitioner is taught to visualize water in order to settle the mind; to turn the water to form ice; to turn the ice into lapis lazuli; to turn the lapis lazuli into a ground of lapis lazuli.”

Second, from below ‘below it,’ the banner upholding the ground below. The passage has two sections: first, the two [sentences] ‘below it,’ [concerning] the banner's substance. The Yanyi says: “It says that below the ground there is a golden banner of vajra and seven treasures, upholding the ground of lapis lazuli. ‘Banner’ is a pillar. In fact it is a pillar; because it is bright, pure, lustrous, and transparent, exactly resembling a hollow tube, it is called a banner. ‘Vajra’ takes the meaning of solidity, and so is able to uphold the jeweled ground. Below ‘its banner,’ it clarifies its form and aspect. The banner has eight sides; each side has a ridge and four edges. (The annotation says: ‘The two characters, both pronounced léng, are interchangeable. What has sharp-cornered angles in an object is called léng. It says the banner's form is octagonal in shape.’ The Lingzhi commentary says: ‘Eight faces and eight ridges, its shape like a stūpa.’) And the eight faces and front surfaces are all composed of hundreds of treasures.” Next, from below ‘one by one,’ the light of the gems shines upward. The Yanyi continues: “Within the treasures there are gems; gem after gem has light; light after light has brightness; brightness after brightness has color; the colors number eighty-four thousand, illuminating the jeweled ground of lapis lazuli like a hundred, thousand, ten-thousand, hundred-million-blazing sun in the sky. The practitioner contemplating it with the eye of the mind cannot yet fully see it — how much less with the ordinary eye!”

Upon the ground of lapis lazuli, with ropes of gold, intermingled and interwoven, with the seven treasures as borders, the division is clear and distinct. Within each treasure there are five hundred colored lights. These lights are like flowers, and also resemble stars and the moon, suspended in empty space, forming a platform of light. There are thousands and myriads of towers and pavilions, composed of hundreds of treasures.

Third, the adornment of the ground. The passage has four sections: first, the flowered levels of the ground's surface. The Zhizhi commentary says: “First, gold ropes serve as the divisions, meaning that with golden ropes they are interspersed along the borders of the pathways. Below ‘with the seven,’ next, the seven treasures serve as the borders; ‘border’ means the stepped pathways. Upon the ground of lapis lazuli there are eight intersecting paths, all formed of the seven treasures.” The Lingzhi commentary says: “The golden ropes and the seven treasures interweave with each other, like the flowered bricks of the world.” The Yanyi says: “Indeed, the jeweled ground of the Pure Land has eight intersecting paths, that is, thoroughfares in the eight directions; all are bordered with jeweled ropes. Each rope is formed of a treasure, one treasure to one rope, rope after rope interwoven, interspersed along the thoroughfares of the intersecting paths. Gold and the other seven treasures each have their own division, clearly visible to the eye.”

Third, below ‘forming light,’ it gathers these jeweled lights to form the platforms and towers. The Yanyi says: “Above it says the gems have light, and the light within the ground reflects upward; here it says that within the treasure there are five hundred colored lights, referring to the light of the boundary paths of the ground, reflected upward into the sky. Below ‘these lights,’ it links two similes together to reveal the form of the light. Light is a borrowed color; flowers, stars, and moon are all real colors. Now it uses the real colors to illustrate the borrowed color, to show that the jeweled light of the Pure Land can be both borrowed and real. Therefore the jeweled light, suspended in the sky, transforms into a jeweled platform of light; within the platform there appear towers and pavilions of hundreds of treasures, naturally formed together.”

On both sides of the platform, there are each a hundred koṭi flower banners and countless musical instruments, as adornments. Eight kinds of pure breeze, issuing from the light, beat these musical instruments, proclaiming the sound of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self. This is the visualization of water, called the second contemplation.

Fourth, below ‘on both sides of the platform,’ the flower banners and musical instruments. The Lingzhi commentary says: “The flower banners and musical instruments surround on the four sides; the wind stirs them to produce sound, expounding the Dharma to awaken the assembly.” The Yanyi says: “The flower banners and musical instruments form the adornment outside the platform. Below ‘eight kinds,’ the wind-music expounds the Dharma. The pure breeze has eight kinds; these winds do not come from the eight directions, but issue forth from the jeweled light. The reason the light pours forth the pure breeze is that on the left and right of the platform there are flower banners and musical instruments; when the eight winds issue forth, the flowers and music sound together, singing forth the wonderful Dharma, expounding the dharma-gate of the noble truth of suffering.”
The last two sentences conclude and point it out. This is knowable [clear].

The Shilun says: “The foregoing passage could still be contemplated in terms of the real ground of this world, as when sitting by a river and contemplating the sun, one can put it into immediate practice. This, however, enters entirely into a realm of illusion, constructed only by the power of the mind. The sun fixes the place and direction; the water lays the foundation of the land. The lotus land takes the virtue of water as supreme: in its melted state it manifests the eight kinds of merit; in its frozen state it becomes the seven treasures and lapis lazuli; at rest, the flowing water is equally clear; in contemplation, the mind-flowers bloom together. The realm here truly has the quality of a spring flowing at one's side, alluring and drawing one in! The magnificent phrases and splendor of the scripture, its myriad of aspects — these are but its incidental matters. The proclamation of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self does not refer to the Pure Land; it induces those who are reborn [there] from the three realms to recall their former dust [of worldly conditions] and never again to regress. ‘Impermanence’ means the four marks of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. ‘Suffering’ means the suffering of the five destinies.
…… In the Pure Land, the truths of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self are still proclaimed; therefore those who seek rebirth in the Pure Land should especially study them beforehand. ……

Question: The real mark is without marks, yet in the Pure Land there are towers and pavilions, flower banners, numberless musical instruments, and a profusion of colored marks — how is this called pure?

Answer: In terms of principle, it is indeed said to be without marks; in terms of events, it does not fall into a stubborn emptiness. The real recompense of adornments are all the fruits of pure causes. As the Cheng Weishi Lun says: “Those who hold that the emptiness-principle of the Mahāyāna which eliminates marks is the ultimate [truth]

…… and hold that both defiled and pure causality are not real, fall into a great erroneous view. …… If all dharmas were not really existent, the bodhisattva should not, for the sake of abandoning birth-and-death, diligently cultivate the provisions for bodhi.” This may be called a direct and refreshing argument.
Question: The Buddha teaches people to be detached and without greed; why is it that the adornment of the Buddha land never departs from gold and jewels?

Answer: This has two meanings: first, because [the Buddha] conforms to sentient beings; second, because the real recompense is naturally transcendent and wonderful. The precious treasures of the world: they are fought over and seized for use, and have as their nature the poison of a deadly draught. The Broad Treatise on the Five Skandhas says: “What is greed? Namely, this [defilement] binds and enwraps one, revolving in the three realms, with the production of suffering as its karma. By the power of craving, the five aggregates of clinging are produced.” The precious treasures of the Buddha land are formed spontaneously, used in accordance with conditions, with transformation as their nature. As a scripture says: Whether one treasure or two treasures, up to numberless multitudes of treasures, according to whatever one wishes, they arrive in accordance with thought. Regarding all the myriad things in that land, there is no thought of ‘mine,’ and no thought of defiled attachment. This is how it differs from the precious treasures of the world.
Question: One gem, one treasure, with a million light-colors — so profuse and complex — how can one accomplish the contemplation of such a thing?

Answer: Those who have resolve do not fear difficulty. Following [the method] and cultivating it, whether or not one succeeds, all is called accomplishment. For a single thought is a single dharma-realm; thought following on thought in mutual concatenation is a realm of dust within dust. One gem has eighty-four thousand rays of light; one leaf has eighty-four thousand veins. The immediately-present single thought, in seeking the eighty-four thousand aspects, though it cannot obtain them, yet this single thought of seeking already possesses the eighty-four thousand natures; being naturally complete, that is accomplishment. As the Avatamsaka Sutra says: ‘The dharma-nature pervades everywhere — in all sentient beings and lands; the three times are all contained within it with nothing left over, yet there is no form or mark that can be obtained.’ If in seeking the mark one does not obtain it, then one draws the marks back into the nature, and all are accomplished. But there are four causes for which it is difficult to accomplish: first, because it is not in accord with the sūtras; second, because when the sought mark does not appear, one gives rise to affliction and doubts that oneself is unable to accomplish; third, because of deficiencies in one's precept-conduct, one gives rise to anxiety and remorse; fourth, because of hindrances of past karma. The methods for counteracting them are as follows: first, one who cultivates this contemplation takes the Contemplation Sutra exclusively as his standard; although other schools each have their own wonderful methods, none of them are adopted. Second, one possesses patience and self-confidence. Third, one strictly upholds the precepts. Fourth, one repents of past karma. Among these, the upholding of precepts is of the greatest concern. [This] will be discussed at length later.” (All of the above are recorded from the Shilun.)

blocks.text: Geng 3: The Contemplation of the Ground, in Three Parts.

inline.s: First, the proper elucidation of the method of contemplation
Second, displaying the benefits; third, distinguishing the correct and erroneous contemplation
Xin 1: Properly Elucidating the Method of Contemplation.

When this visualization is accomplished, contemplate each one, causing it to be extremely clear. With eyes closed or eyes open, do not let it be lost; except during mealtimes, always be mindful of this matter. One who visualizes thus is called one who has had a coarse sight of the ground of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. If one attains samādhi, one sees that land's ground clearly and distinctly, beyond full description. This is the contemplation of the ground, called the third contemplation.”
The contemplated realm is fully [set out] in the preceding passage. Therefore the third [contemplation] merely steps upon the preceding and concludes the exhortation. (Lingzhi's commentary)

The Shilun says: “This contemplation is the latter half of the water-visualization of the second contemplation; the various adornments of the ground's surface there described constitute the contemplation of the ground, [and] one has but a coarse sight of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. ‘If one attains samādhi,’ ‘clear and distinct, beyond full description,’ means that if one's contemplation is vigorous and reaches a wonderfully inexpressible state, only then is it the third contemplation. [Then one] immediately eradicates the sins of birth-and-death of eighty koṭi kalpas. After casting off the recompense [of this life], one will surely be born in the pure land.”

The Lingzhi commentary says: “‘Contemplate each one’ refers to the general and particular marks of the foregoing. ‘Except during mealtimes’ permits a momentary interval. There are some who, following another edition, change it to ‘during sleep.’ But examining the various ancient editions, they all make it ‘during mealtimes.’ Moreover, when ordinary people sleep, [the mind] naturally settles on its own — how would it need to be excepted? Or some say: The two vehicles, great and small, each have contemplations during meals, therefore this is excepted. But this is confined to the monastic assembly, and is not a general rule. Now I say: the other contemplative methods do not select time or place; this contemplation of the sacred realm ought fittingly to be reverent. To raise a visualization facing food is at odds with respect. Therefore the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha's Samādhi, in its section on contemplating images, says: “When the visualization is accomplished, except during mealtimes and except during the time for relieving oneself, at all times one constantly sees the Buddha's image,” and so forth — this is clear evidence. There is no need to revise it. The beginning mind gradually visualizes, and has not yet accomplished a settled mark; therefore it is called ‘coarse sight,’ meaning that it is not yet clear.

“Samādhi (sānmèi), whose proper [Sanskrit] pronunciation is samādhi (sānmódì), is here translated as ‘right concentration,’ or is sometimes called ‘equal holding.’ When the visualization is accomplished so that one sees the ground, without waiting for deliberate effort, it spontaneously accords, and one sees the realm distinctly. Like a person learning archery: at first raw, then mature; whatever is shot, none misses. It cannot be reached by words or thought; only when realized is it known, therefore it is said to be beyond full description.”
Xin 2: Displaying the Benefits.

The Buddha told Ānanda: “You should uphold the Buddha's word, and for the sake of all the great assemblies of the future world, who wish to escape suffering, speak this method of contemplating the ground.”

The passage has two sections: first, the renewed charge to transmit the teaching. [Why] the command to Ānanda: because the first two contemplations are only [concerned with] the things of this region, serving as the starting point for developing contemplation; and [once he] contemplates the jeweled ground, the mind reaches that region, and [one] is then surely able to escape suffering, break through the hindrances, and remove doubt. The intended meaning of the renewed charge to transmit the teaching lies here. (Lingzhi's commentary)

One who contemplates this ground eradicates the sins of birth-and-death of eighty koṭi kalpas. Casting off the body in another world, [he] will surely be born in the pure land, and his mind obtains [a state] without doubt.

Next, [it] properly manifests the benefits. The first two sentences break the hindrances. ‘Eighty koṭi kalpas’ — some say immeasurable kalpas, some say fifty thousand, some say fifty koṭi kalpas; it is not fixed but [given] according to what is fitting, and is not something an ordinary being can fathom. Below ‘casting off the body’ it removes doubt. If this contemplation is accomplished, rebirth [in the Pure Land] is already decided. For example, the eminent Tang monk Daxing, on Mount Tai, built a hermitage and cultivated the pure karma. Before the twenty-first day, he saw a ground of lapis lazuli, and the mind's eye shone through clearly. Later, when he fell ill, the ground appeared again. He then said: ‘I have no [active] visualization, yet the jeweled ground appears again — how could I be without connection to the Land of Peace!’ That very day he passed away in his dwelling. (Lingzhi's commentary)

The Shilun says: “One might doubt: merely contemplating the ground, how can one immediately obtain such a supreme fruit? [One] does not know that this ground has been formed by the Buddha of Immeasurable Life's pure virtue over successive kalpas, established solely for the sake of saving and delivering sentient beings. Yet if sentient beings do not cultivate the contemplation, then the two [the land and oneself] do not relate to one another, and there is no way to unite them, because the seed [of it] is lacking. According to the principle of consciousness-only: the world of instruments relied upon by sentient beings is all manifested by consciousness. Now in [teaching] each portion of the jeweled ground to be contemplated, clear and distinct, [this] is to perfumate one's consciousness, causing a deep impression to be left in the store consciousness; if one originally possesses the pure seed of transcendence, then it is perfumed so as to grow to maturity; or if one does not yet possess it, it may also be newly perfumed and arise. By this, the sense faculties, body, and world of instruments are transformed and produced, and the jeweled ground becomes one's reliant retribution. Naturally accomplished, therefore it is said ‘the mind obtains [a state] without doubt.’”
Xin 3: Distinguishing the Correct and Erroneous Contemplation.
One who performs this contemplation is called [having] the correct contemplation. One who contemplates otherwise is called [having] an erroneous contemplation.”

First, [it] manifests the correct. Saying ‘performs this’ refers to the contemplative mark of the foregoing. Because the mind and its object correspond, and the teaching and the practice do not conflict. Next, [it] distinguishes the erroneous. To deviate from the measure of the foregoing realm is called ‘contemplating otherwise.’ What is not correct is called erroneous. Although these may be the contemplative methods taught by the Buddha, whether great or small, if they are not contemplations for rebirth in the Pure Land, they are all one-sided and erroneous. This is not the same as the error of the heterodox views of the non-Buddhist schools. The rest may be analogized accordingly. (Lingzhi's commentary)

blocks.text: Geng 4: The Contemplation of Trees.

inline.s: First, concluding the preceding and giving rise to the following
Second, the proper elucidation of the contemplative practice; third, the concluding statement
Xin 1: Concluding the Preceding and Giving Rise to the Following.
The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: “Once the contemplation of the ground is accomplished, next contemplate the jeweled trees.”

First, [it] announces and instructs those of the appropriate capacity. The sentence ‘the contemplation of the ground’ concludes the preceding. The sentence ‘next contemplate’ gives rise to the following. (Yanyi)
Xin 2: Properly Elucidating the Contemplative Practice, in Two Parts.
First, broadly elucidating the contemplative realm
Second, summarizing and showing the method of contemplation
Ren 1: Broadly Elucidating the Contemplative Realm, in Two Parts.
First, summarily clarifying the essence and measure
Second, separately displaying the adornments
Gui 1: Summarily Clarifying the Essence and Measure.

For the contemplation of the jeweled trees, contemplate each one. Produce the visualization of seven rows of trees. Each tree is eight thousand yojanas high. As for these jeweled trees, their flowers and leaves of the seven treasures are all fully provided.
The first two sentences instruct [one] to contemplate [them] extensively. Because the marks of the trees are of many kinds, therefore it says ‘each one.’ (Lingzhi's commentary)

Below ‘produce,’ [it] properly sets forth the essence and measure. ‘Essence’ means composed of the seven treasures; ‘measure’ means eight thousand yojanas. As for ‘seven rows of trees,’ the Yanyi says: “Upon the ground of lapis lazuli of that land, on all sides there are rows of jeweled trees; row after row each has seven tiers. Neither rising above nor sinking below, all evenly aligned. Eight thousand yojanas high. Branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits — each and every one fully provided.” The Lingzhi commentary says: “‘Yojana (yóuxún)’ is the measure of the relaying stations of Western India. As set forth in the sūtras and the vinaya, the far and near are not fixed; most authorities take forty li as the standard. ‘Leaves fully provided’ means that they do not wither and fall.”
Gui 2: Separately Displaying the Adornments, in Two Parts.
First, the adornment of radiance
Second, the adornment of flowers and fruits
Zi 1: The Adornment of Radiance, in Two Parts.
First, the jeweled radiance of the flowers and leaves
Second, the pearl net spreading over
Chou 1: The Jeweled Radiance of the Flowers and Leaves.

Each flower and leaf produces a different jewel-colored light: within the lapis lazuli color, a golden light issues; within the crystal color, a red light issues; within the agate color, a conch-shell light issues; within the conch-shell color, a light of green pearls issues. Coral, amber, and all the various treasures serve as reflections and ornaments.

The Yanyi says: “The substance is fully formed of the seven treasures, originally possessing seven kinds of color-mark; the light that issues from them in turn changes to other colors, therefore it is called ‘producing different jewel-colored lights.’” The Lingzhi commentary says: “The jewel-colored [lights] and rays alternate in five colors: the lapis lazuli blue issues yellow light; the crystal green issues red light; the agate red issues white light; the conch-shell white issues green light. If one follows the Larger Scripture: amber and seven-treasure trees fill the whole world. Trees of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, agate, conch-shell, and so forth — some with two treasures, some with three, up to the seven treasures, are variously composed together. [It is] extensively as is there stated. That is exactly ‘all the various treasures serve as reflections and ornaments.’”
Chou 2: The Pearl Net Spreading Over.

Wondrous nets of true pearls spread over the trees. On each tree there are seven tiers of nets. Between each net there are five hundred koṭi wonderful flower-palaces, like the palace of Brahmā. Celestial youths are naturally within them. Each youth wears, as a necklace, five hundred koṭi Śakra-abhilagna-maṇi [gems]. Their maṇi light shines for a hundred yojanas. Like a hundred koṭi suns and moons combined, they cannot be fully named. The many jewels are intermingled, the most supreme in color.

The passage has four sections: first, [it] shows the number of tiers. Each tree has seven layers, each layer being one tier. Its form is like a stūpa. Second, below ‘between each net,’ the palaces within the nets, like the dwelling of Brahmā, king of the form-realm heavens. Third, below ‘the celestial youths,’ the youths within the palaces. Below ‘each one,’ the adornment of the celestial youths. ‘Śakra-abhilagna’ (Shìjiā-pílíngjiā) is translated as ‘able to surpass.’ ‘Maṇi’ (móní) is translated as ‘free from defilement,’ and is also called ‘as one wishes.’ (The annotation: ‘Maṇi is the name of a precious gem. The Śakra-abhilagna-maṇi is a precious gem that can surpass all the treasures of the world.’) Fourth, below ‘their maṇi,’ the radiance of the pearl-necklaces. ‘The many jewels intermingled’ — it is not only the pearls. ‘The most supreme in color’ — [it] differs from the ordinary. (Lingzhi's commentary)
Zi 2: The Adornment of Flowers and Fruits

As for these jeweled trees: row faces row in exact correspondence, leaf follows leaf in due order. Amid the leaves there grow wonderful flowers, and upon the flowers there naturally appear fruits of the seven treasures.
This is the general statement. The Lingzhi Commentary says: “‘Row for row in correspondence’ — ‘correspond’ means to face one another. ‘Leaf in due order’ — like scales overlapping.”
Each single leaf of these trees measures twenty-five yojanas in length and breadth alike. Its leaves are of a thousand colors, and bear a hundred kinds of pictured markings, like a celestial garland.

Below this, particular indications are given. First the leaves are clarified; then, at ‘each single leaf,’ their measure is shown; and at ‘its leaves,’ their color. The ‘hundred kinds of pictured markings’ are the vein-patterns upon the leaves; ‘like a celestial garland’ describes their figured lines. (The Lingzhi Commentary)

There are many wonderful flowers, of the color of Jambū-river gold. Like a whirling fire-wheel they turn and wind among the leaves. Fruits well up and are born, like the vessel of Indra. There is a great radiance, which transforms into banners and canopies and immeasurable jeweled parasols. Within those jeweled parasols are reflected all the Buddha-matters of the three-thousand-great-thousand worlds; and the Buddha-lands of the ten directions likewise appear within them.

Next, the flowers and fruits are clarified. At ‘there are many’ the color of the flowers is made clear. The Zhizhi Commentary says: “‘Jambū-river gold’ is here rendered ‘victorious gold.’ The water of the jambū tree’s fruit, when it touches things, turns them to gold; flowing into the rivers, it dyes the stones into gold. Its color is ruddy-yellow and carries a purple flame.” The Lingzhi Commentary says: “Its flowers revolve like a windmill.” At ‘fruits well up and are born’ the fruits are made clear. The Jianzhu says: “‘The vessel of Indra’ is the precious vase of Indra, king of the gods. Whatever is needed wells forth from it of itself; it is also called the vase of virtue.” At ‘there is a great’ the radiance transforms into banners and canopies. The Lingzhi Commentary says: “Two things are reflected: the Buddha-matters of the great thousand-world, first; the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, second. To show birth and to proclaim extinction, to speak the Dharma and save living beings — all this is called Buddha-matters.”
Ren 2: The General Indication of the Method of Contemplation
Having seen these trees, one should next contemplate them one by one in due order. Contemplate and see the trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, and cause them all to be clear and distinct.

Lest the contemplation be confused, he bids them be contemplated in order. The five kinds — trunk and the rest — are precisely the due order. ‘Trunk’ means root and stem, which necessarily includes the branches. (The Lingzhi Commentary)
Xin 3: The Concluding Statement
This is the tree contemplation; it is called the fourth contemplation.”

blocks.text: Geng 5: The Pond Contemplation, in Three Parts

inline.s: First, the general heading
second, the particular display; third, the concluding statement
Xin 1: The General Heading
Next one should visualize water. To visualize water: in the Land of Ultimate Bliss there are eight pools of water.

That the Land of Ultimate Bliss has eight pools admits of two explanations. The first holds that one land has eight pools: the Lingzhi Commentary says, “One land, eight pools, their channels intercommunicating.” The second holds that ‘eight pools of water’ means the pool of the eight merits: the Yanyi says, “To say that the Land of Ultimate Bliss has eight pools does not mean that the land possesses only eight pools; it means that one pool has eight merits — that is, within the pool there is water, and the water has eight virtues. The concluding words below, ‘the water of the eight merits,’ refer to this. Let no one do violence to the meaning for the sake of the wording.” The latter explanation is the better. The Yanyi continues: “One should know that in the land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss there is the pool of general retribution, the retribution produced by the shared karma of saints and ordinary beings alike. The Smaller Sūtra says, ‘There are pools of the seven treasures, with water of the eight merits’ — this refers to that pool. Its greatness has no comparison. When living beings of the ten directions are reborn in that land, they are born in this pool. Its waters are vast as the ocean of fragrant water. Above the water are lotuses: the one at the center is like Mount Sumeru, and the eight ranks that revolve around it are like the seven golden mountains. When a suffering being of the ten directions hears a good friend’s instruction and believes that there is a Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and that within that land there is Amitābha Buddha; when he is willing to arouse his mind and invoke the Buddha, vowing to be born in that land — then within this pool a single lotus bud pushes forth. Thus one knows that the pool of general retribution is shared not only by the saints and ordinary beings of that land, but by all living beings of the ten directions. As for the pools of particular retribution: they are made by individual karma, differing in a thousand and ten thousand ways, great and small unlike, brought about by the practitioner’s own cultivation. Their number is measureless and boundless, beyond reckoning or speech. Each stands beside a tower or pavilion, within the enclosure of the row of trees, and is what each practitioner enjoys and uses after being born in that land. What is contemplated in the present Sūtra is precisely this.”
Xin 2: The Particular Display

Each single pool of water is made of the seven treasures. Those treasures are soft and pliant, born from the wish-fulfilling pearl king. They divide into fourteen branches. Each branch is of the wonderful colors of the seven treasures, with yellow gold for its channels. Beneath the channels, sand of various-colored vajra forms the bed.

The first two sentences clarify the color of the water. The Yanyi says: “The words ‘each single’ carry on from the eight pools above. It means that within that Buddha’s land there are measureless asaṃkhyeya, inexpressible pools, and that every single pool of water is without exception made of the seven treasures.” The Lingzhi Commentary says: “The banks and steps of the ponds are composed of many treasures, and the spring water within the pools is colored likewise. Hence it says they are made of the seven treasures.” The next two sentences show the source. The Lingzhi Commentary says: “At the heart of each pool there is a pearl king; the spring issues from the king and flows down into the pool, ever brimming full.” The Yanyi says: “The treasures of that pure land differ from those of our Sahā world. In this land, though there be the seven treasures, their substance is hard; in that land the substance of its treasures is soft.”

Below, at ‘they divide,’ the branch streams are clarified. The Jianzhu says: “Whatever issues in forked fashion from a single source is called a branch.” It means that the jeweled water is born from within the wish-fulfilling pearl king; issuing from one source, it divides into fourteen streams. ‘Wish-fulfilling’ is the Sanskrit maṇi. The maṇi pearl is king among all treasures; hence the water of the seven treasures is born from it, and is also called maṇi water. Since the water is made of treasures, each portion has its own wonderful color; and all the more since yellow gold forms its channels. (The Yanyi) Below, at ‘yellow,’ the making of the channels is clarified. A channel is where water dwells, as in a ditch or a canal. The Yanyi says: “A channel is the pond itself. At the bottom of the channel there is sand, and the sand is called vajra. Then one may know that above and below it is bright and transparent.” The Jianzhu says: “‘Of various colors’ means the five colors combined together.”

Within each single pool there are six billion lotuses of the seven treasures. Each single lotus is perfectly round and measures twelve yojanas across. That maṇi water flows and pours among the flowers, winding up and down the trees. Its sound is subtle and wonderful, expounding the perfections of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self; and there are also those that praise the marks and excellences of the Buddhas.

Here the lotuses in the pools are clarified, and the water flowing among the flowers giving forth sound and expounding the Dharma. The first two sentences show the number; the next two clarify the measure. The Lingzhi Commentary says: “Twelve yojanas reckon to four hundred and eighty li. The Smaller Sūtra merely says ‘as large as a cartwheel,’ which takes up only the very smallest of them.” At ‘that maṇi’ the water flowing among the flowers is clarified. The Lingzhi Commentary says: “Because it issues from the wish-fulfilling pearl, it is called maṇi water — the Chinese and Sanskrit terms being set out side by side. ‘Winding up and down the trees’ — ‘winding’ means to follow along. ‘Trees’ means the stems. It says the water follows the flower stems, rising into the flowers, and there revolving it gives forth sound, then descends again by the stems.” The Shilun says: “This water not only flows in the pools among the flowers, but also winds up and down the trees, forming hanging cascades and flying fountains, and so is able to give forth sound and expound the wonderful truths, while a hundred birds join in harmony, praising the Three Jewels.” At ‘its sound’ the sound of the water expounds the Dharma. The Lingzhi Commentary says: “Three things are expounded: the four foundations of mindfulness, first; the six perfections, second; the praise of the Buddha’s marks and excellences, third.”

From the wish-fulfilling pearl king there well forth subtle and wonderful golden radiances. Those lights transform into birds of a hundred jeweled colors, whose harmonious calls are plaintive and elegant, ever praising the Buddha, praising the Dharma, and praising the Saṅgha.

Here the pearl king emits light, and the light transforms into birds that expound the Dharma. As for the birds of a hundred jeweled colors, the Lingzhi Commentary says: “They are the white cranes and peacocks of the Smaller Sūtra, and the wild ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks of the present Sūtra below. Thus one knows that the precious birds are not of one kind alone; here only their plumage colors are given, to gather them all in. They praise the Three Jewels in order to cause beings to turn toward them.”
Question: What kind of language and script are used in the Buddha’s land? The springs and the birds — by what do they speak?

Answer: This admits of two meanings: first, that there are names, sentences, and words; second, that there are no names, sentences, and words. As for the first: those born in the Pure Land all come from different regions, and their languages differ. The sounds of the springs and birds and the rest turn according to the consciousness of the hearer; Brahmā hears them as Brahmā sounds, and the dwellers of Jambudvīpa hear them as worldly speech. The Buddha speaks the Dharma with one sound, and living beings each understand according to their own capacity. This is what the Avataṃsaka means by ‘one word complete with all the seas of sounds, according with the sounds that living beings in their minds delight in.’ Again, the sūtras say that the Buddha attained a rare name, sentence, and word-body; yet if one takes the ultimate meaning, the Buddha has no speech, and it is living beings’ own consciousness that transforms, so that they seem to hear the Buddha speak and each give rise to understanding. The sounds of water and the sounds of birds should be known to be likewise. As for the second: the meaning is grasped through the sound, without relying on verbal explanation. As the Cheng Weishi Lun says, ‘Proceeding by this land, one speaks of names, sentences, and words as provisionally established upon sound; it is not said to be so of all other Buddha-lands.’ The notes of strings and pipes have no names, sentences, or words, yet the hearer may be moved to sorrow or to joy. Su Dongpo’s poem says, ‘The sound of the stream is itself the broad and long tongue’ — he heard the sound and thereby attained understanding.

… All such things do not await the explanation of names and sentences, yet one is able of oneself to apprehend them. It is so even in this dust-defiled world; how much more in the Pure Land, formed by the Buddha’s vow, where every thing arises in its own natural and wonderful function. To hold that the water forms sentences and phrases or that the birds utter human speech would be to carve a boat and glue the bridge — to be rigid and wooden indeed! (The Shilun)
Xin 3: The Concluding Statement
This is the contemplation of the water of the eight merits; it is called the fifth contemplation.”

The second contemplation above was originally the contemplation of ice, but because water was first taken as the object upon which the mind is fixed, it was given the name of the water contemplation. This fifth was originally the water contemplation, but because its name would be the same as the second, it was given the name of the pond. In truth it is water; hence it is concluded as the water visualization and called the fifth contemplation. As for ‘the eight merits’: merit means wonderful function. That water has eight kinds of wonderful function, hence it is called the eight virtues. First, the virtue of lightness: it is not like this water of ours, which can only flow downward and cannot flow upward; that water can rise and can descend. The Sūtra says, ‘Winding up and down the trees, flowing and pouring among the flowers.’ Second, the virtue of purity: this water grows turbid as soon as it touches sand or mud; that water remains pure and self-possessed. Third, the virtue of coolness: this water grows hot when exposed to the sun; that water remains cool and calm as it is. Fourth, the virtue of softness: this water’s substance is hard and strong, and often it bursts the dikes and banks; that water’s substance is soft and pliant, and can benefit other things. Fifth, the virtue of beauty: this water is bland with a turbid taste; that water is sweet, clear, and lovely. Sixth, the virtue of fragrance: this water has no breath of scent at all; that water is fragrant to the nostrils. Seventh, the virtue that the drinker never wearies of it: this water, drunk too much, produces aversion; that water, when drunk, brings one into harmony and ease. Eighth, the virtue of freedom from harm: this water, drunk in quantity, brings illness, and to drink it when ill makes the illness worse; that water harmonizes the spirit and opens wisdom, increases the way and diminishes birth. Hence it is called the eight merits. (The Yanyi)

blocks.text: Geng 6: The General Contemplation, in Two Parts

inline.s: The Jiaxiang Commentary says: “The Land of Immeasurable Life has measureless matters, which cannot be contemplated one and all; hence the sixth contemplation makes a general contemplation of all things. The text divides into two sections: first, the proper explanation; second, the display of benefits.
Xin 1: The Proper Explanation

In the land of many treasures, upon each and every boundary there are five hundred koṭi jeweled towers. Within those towers and pavilions measureless devas perform celestial music. Again, musical instruments hang suspended in empty space like celestial jeweled banners, and without being struck they sound of themselves. Within all those sounds is proclaimed the praising of the Buddha, the praising of the Dharma, and the praising of the Bhikṣu Saṅgha.
First, the jeweled towers and pavilions are contemplated in particular. ‘Upon the boundaries’ means upon the ground within the boundary paths. (The Zhizhi Commentary)

The Lingzhi Commentary says: “According to the Smaller Sūtra, ‘each and every boundary’ is upon the banks of the pools. The Sūtra says, ‘on the four sides are stepped walkways,’ and ‘above them are towers and pavilions,’ and so forth.” At ‘within those’ the devas in the towers make music. At ‘again’ the instruments in empty space sound of themselves. At ‘within all those sounds’ the sounds of the Three Jewels are brought forth from within the music. ‘All those sounds’ refers to the two kinds of sound, the celestial music and the music of the sky. (The Zhizhi Commentary)

When this visualization is accomplished, it is called a coarse sight of the jeweled trees, the jeweled ground, and the jeweled ponds of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is the general contemplation; it is called the sixth contemplation.

This is the concluding summary. The Shilun says: “This contemplation must take the jeweled trees, jeweled ground, and jeweled ponds of the third, fourth, and fifth contemplations set out above, and contemplate them together; only then may it be called the general contemplation. For the sixth contemplation speaks only of the towers and pavilions and of the object of sound, and so cannot be called general.” The Miaozong Notes say: “At the very first tying of the thought, one provisionally relies upon the sun and the ice of this land as an expedient; next one contemplates the ground, trees, ponds, and towers of that land. One should know that of these four, whoever gains the later necessarily gains the earlier; hence when the contemplation of the towers is accomplished, all four matters appear. Therefore at this point it receives the name of the general contemplation. Though it is called general seeing, if compared with the contemplations that follow, this is still approximate; hence it is called a coarse sight.” The last two sentences conclude and name it.
Xin 2: The Display of Benefits

If one sees this, one removes the karma of extremely grave evil of measureless koṭi kalpas. After the end of this life, one will certainly be born in that land. One who performs this contemplation is called one of correct contemplation. One who contemplates otherwise is called one of erroneous contemplation.”

The benefits are two: first, the extinction of offenses; second, rebirth in the West. To remove the extremely grave evil of koṭi kalpas is the extinction of offenses. To be certainly born in that land after the end of life is rebirth in the West. Earlier, when the ground was accomplished, eighty koṭi kalpas were removed; later, in the contemplation of the seat, five trillion kalpas were removed — all of these are spoken by the Buddha’s wisdom according to the true measure. They are not what a beginner’s mind can conceive; one has only to believe and receive them. The last four sentences display the erroneous and the correct. (The Yanyi)
Wu 2: Contemplating the Proper Retribution, in Four Parts
First, the Tathāgata admonishes them to listen and grants the explanation of the gate of contemplation
Second, the three sages manifest their bodies to awaken faith and understanding
Third, Lady Vaidehī asks on behalf of the future
Fourth, he properly explains the method of contemplation, causing them to accomplish cultivation and realization
Ji 1: The Tathāgata Admonishes Them to Listen and Grants the Explanation of the Gate of Contemplation

The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: “Listen attentively! Listen attentively! Think upon it well. I shall now for you distinguish and explain the method that removes suffering. You should remember and uphold it, and for the sake of the great assembly distinguish and explain it widely.”

First, the admonition to listen. The Lingzhi Commentary says: “Since the contemplation set out above has its aim in contemplating the proper [retribution], he again urges and entrusts it.” At ‘I shall now’ the explanation is granted. The Zhizhi Commentary says: “‘Suffering’ is the fruit — the three sufferings and the eight sufferings and the like. ‘Affliction’ is the cause — the ten fetters and the afflictions and the like. To remove suffering is to turn from birth-and-death and attain nirvāṇa. To remove affliction is to turn delusion and karma into bodhi.” The Lingzhi Commentary says: “The many sufferings of the Sahā world cannot be escaped except by the samādhi of Buddha-contemplation; hence it is called the method of escaping suffering. The three realms are the vessel of suffering, and the six destinies are the retribution of suffering.” At ‘you should’ they are urged to uphold and to speak it.
Ji 2: The Three Sages Manifest Their Bodies to Awaken Faith and Understanding

While he was speaking these words, Amitāyus Buddha stood in the air, and Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, these two great beings, stood in attendance at his left and right. Their radiance blazed so brightly that it could not be fully seen; a hundred thousand Jambū-river golds could not compare with it.

The Zhizhi Commentary says: “Now that the Buddha is about to speak of the contemplation of the Three Sages, he manifests his bodily marks to certify the faith.” The Yanyi says: “At the very moment when the Tathāgata grants the explanation, Amitābha Buddha and the two great beings all stand in the air, their whole bodies revealed; only, because their radiance blazes so brightly, a beginner cannot see them fully. Even should one take a hundred thousand koṭi of Jambū gold, it could not match them. That the holy images’ golden marks dazzle and shine may be known from this!” The Lingzhi Commentary says: “In the passage above, the land was manifested upon the radiant platform, causing Vaidehī to see it, and this was made the occasion for requesting [the teaching on] the dependent retribution; hence it says, ‘through the Buddha’s power you see that land,’ and so forth. Now the Three Sages come together, and this is made the occasion for requesting [the teaching on] the proper retribution; hence it says, ‘through the Buddha’s power you may see the Buddha,’ and so forth. The Buddha stands in the air and the two sages stand in attendance: that the Three Sages stood in bodily form is clear proof here. Even Jambū gold cannot compare with them; then one knows that their light cannot be wholly seen.”
Ji 3: Lady Vaidehī Asks on Behalf of the Future

At that time Vaidehī, having seen Amitāyus Buddha, did reverence at his feet. She said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One! I now, through the Buddha’s power, have been able to see Amitāyus Buddha and the two bodhisattvas. How shall living beings of the future contemplate Amitāyus Buddha and the two bodhisattvas?”

The Zhizhi Commentary says: “‘At his feet’ means doing homage at the feet of the Three Sages. ‘She said to the Buddha’ means looking up and speaking to the honored Śākyamuni. ‘Through the Buddha’s power’ — because she saw the contemplation with her own eyes, it is easy, and she may well delay; for those of the future, who have not seen the contemplation, it is difficult, and another must show them, and so she must ask in their place. Yet in saying ‘contemplate the Buddha and the bodhisattvas,’ she marks it off from the previous request, which asked as well for the contemplation of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.” The Lingzhi Commentary says: “The bodhisattva keeps others in mind and does not devote herself to her own sake alone; though she has caused me to see, her thought is for the future.”
Ji 4: He Properly Explains the Method of Contemplation, Causing Them to Accomplish Cultivation and Realization, in Four Parts

The Lingzhi Commentary says: “The latter ten contemplations are again divided into four: the first three contemplate the Buddha — the seventh contemplates the place where the Buddha sits, the eighth contemplates the image to represent the real, the ninth properly contemplates the Buddha’s image; the tenth and eleventh contemplate the Buddha’s attendants, distinguished as left and right; the twelfth and thirteenth contemplate the Three Sages in general, universal and mixed being unlike; the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth contemplate the Buddha’s assembly, with the three grades descending in rank.” Thus it is divided into four: first, the proper explanation of Buddha-contemplation; second, the contemplation of the Buddha’s attendants; third, the general contemplation of the Three Sages; fourth, the contemplation of the Buddha’s assembly.

blocks.text: The Seventh: The Contemplation of the Flower Seat

inline.s: Geng 1: The Proper Explanation of Buddha-Contemplation, in Three Parts
First, contemplating the place where the Buddha sits (the seventh, the contemplation of the flower seat)
Second, contemplating the holy image (the eighth, the contemplation of the holy image)
Third, properly contemplating the Buddha’s body (the ninth, the contemplation of the Buddha’s body)
Xin 1: Contemplating the Place Where the Buddha Sits (the Seventh, the Contemplation of the Flower Seat), in Five Parts
First, the proper clarification of the contemplated object

second, clarifying the original cause of the seat; third, the general indication of the method of contemplation; fourth, displaying the benefits of the contemplation; fifth, distinguishing the erroneous and the correct in contemplation
Ren 1: The Proper Clarification of the Contemplated Object, in Three Parts
First, the general indication
second, the particular explanation; third, the concluding statement
Gui 1: The General Indication
The Buddha told Vaidehī: “If you wish to contemplate that Buddha, you should raise a thought and, upon the ground of the seven treasures, form the visualization of a lotus flower.

The Yanyi says: “Vaidehī asked in her place for the method of contemplating the Three Sages, yet the Tathāgata first sets out the two contemplations of the seat and the image, meaning: the real and the image are subtle and wonderful, and it is not easy to accomplish the contemplation; and since the Buddha must sit upon a seat, one first contemplates the flower seat; and to contemplate the real image, one must first contemplate the semblance, so that the contemplative mind may flow smoothly; therefore he first speaks of the two contemplations of the seat and the image.” The Lingzhi Commentary says: “As for the contemplation of the flower seat: to gaze upon the honored object, one first contemplates the place where he sits. It is like standing before one’s lord: the eyes first rest upon the steps of the throne.”

The Zhizhi Commentary says: “What the Buddha sits upon is the lotus terrace as his seat; hence one should visualize the lotus flower.” To form the visualization of a lotus upon the ground of the seven treasures is to state in general the place upon which the terrace seat rests. The Lingzhi Commentary says: “The flower rests upon the ground, which shows that it is a terrace seat, not a lotus in a pool.”
Gui 2: The Particular Explanation, in Two Parts
First, clarifying the flower’s petals
second, clarifying the flower’s terrace
Zi 1: Clarifying the Flower’s Petals

Cause each single petal of that lotus to be of a hundred jeweled colors. It has eighty-four thousand veins, like a celestial painting. The veins have eighty-four thousand rays of light, clear and distinct, all caused to be seen. Even the smallest of the petals measures two hundred and fifty yojanas across. Such a lotus has eighty-four thousand petals, and between each single petal a hundred koṭi wish-fulfilling pearl kings serve as its reflected adornment. Each single maṇi pearl emits a thousand rays of light. Those lights are like canopies made of the seven treasures, covering the ground all around.

The Yanyi says: “First contemplate the whole lotus flower: its petals number eighty-four thousand, each petal has a hundred jeweled colors, and there are in addition fine and subtle vein-patterns, like a natural and wonderful painting. There are also eighty-four thousand rays of light. The measure of a petal is two hundred and fifty yojanas. Where two petals meet, there is a wish-fulfilling pearl as its adornment. The pearl emits jeweled light like a parasol, covering the lotus flower above.” The Lingzhi Commentary says: “The shape of the light is like a canopy, covering the ground below.”
Zi 2: Clarifying the Flower’s Terrace
The Śakra-abhilagna-maṇi jewel forms its terrace. This lotus terrace has eighty-four thousand vajra-arkacandana jewels, Brahmā-maṇi jewels, and nets of wonderful pearls as its woven adornment.

First, the substance of the terrace is clarified. At ‘this lotus’ below, the woven adornment is clarified. The Yanyi says: “This is the terrace within the flower. ‘Abhilagna’ was explained above. ‘Arkacandana’ is here rendered ‘red-colored.’ It is the name of a tree in the Western lands; its flower is red and shaped like a hand. This jewel resembles it, and so takes its name.”

Upon that terrace there naturally appear jeweled banners with four pillars. Each single jeweled banner is like a hundred thousand koṭi Sumeru mountains. The jeweled hangings upon the banners are like the palace of the Yāma heaven. Again, there are five hundred koṭi subtle and wonderful maṇi pearls as reflected adornment. Each single maṇi pearl has eighty-four thousand rays of light. Each single ray of light produces eighty-four thousand different kinds of golden color. Each single golden color pervades that jeweled land, transforming everywhere, each producing a different appearance: some become vajra terraces, some become pearl nets, some become clouds of many-colored flowers; throughout the ten directions they transform as they will, performing Buddha-matters.

Here the jeweled banners upon the terrace are clarified. That is, upon the terrace’s surface pillars are raised facing the four directions, and above they uphold nets and hangings to cover the Buddha’s head. (The Lingzhi Commentary.) The Yanyi says: “‘Sumeru’ is here rendered ‘wonderfully high.’ Being made of the four treasures, it is called wonderful; surpassing the seven golden mountains, it is called high.” The Zhizhi Commentary says: “In the contemplation above, the jeweled trees were only eight thousand yojanas high; now the jeweled banners are as high as a hundred thousand koṭi mountain kings — the contemplated object is seen to grow ever more profound and excellent.” The Yanyi says: “‘Yāma’ is here rendered ‘well-timed,’ meaning that by the opening and closing of the lotus flowers the times of day and night are well suited.” The Lingzhi Commentary says: “‘Yāma’ is the third heaven of the desire realm, dwelling in space. That heaven’s flower-light is the most excellent of adornments, and so it is often taken for comparison.” At ‘again’ below, the pearls emit light. The Zhizhi Commentary says: “Around the banners and hangings there are wish-fulfilling pearl necklaces hanging down on every side.” At ‘each single golden’ below, the transformation of the light and color is clarified. The Lingzhi Commentary says: “Its color transforms into three things: golden terraces, pearl nets, and flower clouds. There are yet other particular appearances; hence it says ‘as they will,’ and so forth.” ‘Performing Buddha-matters’ means benefiting beings according to their capacity.
