The Zhizhi Commentary says: “Seeing the terrace, one awakens to the Tathāgata’s wonderful enlightenment as fruit; seeing the net, one understands the many dharma-gates of the mind-ground; seeing the clouds, one knows the causal ten thousand practices of the bodhisattva. Hence Buddha-matters appear according to circumstance, and no capacity fails to receive its moisture.”
Gui 3: The Concluding Statement
This is the contemplation of the flower seat; it is called the seventh contemplation.”
Ren 2: Clarifying the Original Cause of the Seat
The Buddha told Ānanda: “Such a wonderful flower is brought about by the vow-power of the bhikṣu Dharmākara in a former life.

Amitābha Buddha was formerly a king. Meeting the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, he renounced his kingdom and left home, taking the Dharma-name Dharmākara, and made forty-eight vows. (See the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life in full.) The dependent-retribution realm of that land — its bodily life and radiance, its various adornments, and all its fruition-marks — are all brought about by his vows; how could it be the flower seat alone? This is touched upon here in passing, to cause one to know that the Pure Land is the very substance of the Buddha’s vow, and that the vow is issued from the mind, which is the very substance of the Buddha’s mind. Hence one knows that the principle of vow-power is utterly beyond speech and thought! (The Lingzhi Commentary)
Ren 3: The General Indication of the Method of Contemplation

If one wishes to be mindful of that Buddha, one should first form this visualization of the flower seat. When forming this visualization, one must not contemplate in a mixed manner; one should contemplate each one in order. Each single petal, each single pearl, each single ray of light, each single terrace, each single banner — cause them all to be clear and distinct, as though seeing one’s own face in a mirror.
The Lingzhi Commentary says: “Without the flower seat first, the contemplation of the Buddha cannot be accomplished.” Hence to contemplate the Buddha one must first contemplate the flower seat.

The Yanyi says: “The first sentence — ‘be mindful’ is to be taken as ‘contemplate.’ The visualization must be single-minded and undivided; a little heedlessness and the contemplation is not accomplished. Hence he charges that one must not contemplate in a mixed manner. ‘One should contemplate each one in order’ means that petals, pearls, lights, terrace, and banners advance in sequence, in due order without confusion.” The Lingzhi Commentary says: “‘Contemplate each one’ runs through the five kinds below. Both the petals and the banners have their pearls and lights. The terrace’s light is not specified, a small omission in the text. ‘Seeing one’s face in a mirror’ is a simile for its being without discrepancy.”

The Shilun says: “Clear and distinct, all caused to be seen: yet outer objects may appear all at once, taken in at a single glance, because the faculty of the eye is employed; the forming of a contemplation relies only upon the power of the mind. The use of mind and the use of eye are in inverse proportion: one must wait for the former thought to perish before the latter thought is born. It can only be a succession in time (the vertical sense), and cannot be a universality in space (the horizontal sense). The petals, veins, and lights of the lotus each number eighty-four thousand — how can they all be caused to be seen at once? This is not what the eye-faculty sees; it is the realm of concentration and wisdom. It means cultivating samādhi (also called sanmei), such as the ‘wisdom that turns according to the observer’ among the four wisdoms of the bodhisattva, which means that having attained excellent concentration, one contemplates a single object and all marks appear before one. Samādhi is divided into two kinds, great and small, as the Yogācāra says: ‘What is the lesser samādhi? It is small either because of its object, or because it contemplates few forms.

… Here the great-mind samādhi is this: beneath a single tree, one visualizes the lights of the heavens and gives rise to a resolute understanding. … Throughout the area beneath a single tree, even to the great earth and the limits of the great sea, one gives rise to a resolute understanding.’ There is also the distinction between partial cultivation and complete cultivation: ‘Partial-cultivation samādhi is when, within this, one either only attends to and reflects upon the mark of light, or only attends to and reflects upon the mark of form, and so enters concentration. Complete-cultivation samādhi is when one enters concentration attending to both, and both understands the light and sees the many forms.’ By this standard, ‘distinguishing the stages and contemplating each one in order’ is partial cultivation; if one gathers the petals, veins, and lights together and contemplates them all at once, that is complete cultivation. In every case, without borrowing the power of concentration it cannot be done. Yet by the Buddha’s original vow, whoever recollects and visualizes will certainly accomplish it. The other pearl nets, terraces, and banners are each contemplated one by one within concentration. Not adopting the methods of other schools or non-Buddhists, not giving rise to miscellaneous worldly thoughts — this is correct contemplation. Whether one succeeds or not, it is in every case a benefit in accord [with the Dharma], and never a loss.
Ren 4: Displaying the Benefits of the Contemplation
When this visualization is accomplished, one removes the offenses of birth-and-death for fifty trillion kalpas, and will certainly be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The Yanyi says: “If this contemplation is accomplished, the offenses removed are many; hence it says fifty trillion kalpas. When offenses are extinguished, merit is born; when dust departs, light is born. That one is born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss admits of no doubt.”

The Lingzhi Commentary says: “This is the Buddha-contemplation’s first expedient; the offenses removed are still few. Next, at the contemplation of the image, the offenses removed are then many. Later, at the contemplation of the Buddha, one attains the patience of non-arising, which is the destruction of ignorance.”
Ren 5: Distinguishing the Erroneous and the Correct in Contemplation

blocks.text: Xin 2: Contemplating the Holy Image (the Eighth, the Contemplation of the Holy Image), in Two Parts

inline.s: First, concluding the preceding and marking off the following
second, the proper display of the method of contemplation
Ren 1: Concluding the Preceding and Marking Off the Following
The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: “Having seen this matter, you should next visualize the Buddha.

The sentence ‘having seen’ concludes the preceding; ‘next’ marks off the following. The Lingzhi Commentary says: “Living beings from beginningless time have never known the true Buddha, and for the most part have seen his images; hence they are caused to contemplate these first. By the image one represents the real, and the contemplation of the Buddha is easily accomplished.”
Ren 2: The Proper Display of the Method of Contemplation, in Four Parts
First, the general indication of the meaning of visualizing the Buddha
second, the proper clarification of the method of visualizing the Buddha; third, the concluding statement; fourth, the display of benefits
Gui 1: The General Indication of the Meaning of Visualizing the Buddha, in Four Parts
First, clarifying that the Buddha’s body is universal and can respond to the minds of beings
Second, clarifying that when the practitioner’s visualization is accomplished, he himself possesses the Buddha’s substance
Third, raising that fruition-virtue to cause faith in the causal mind
Fourth, concluding and urging the cultivation of the cause, which must rely upon the fruition-virtue

In this passage of the Sūtra, our Buddha, the Tathāgata, wishing to make clear the contemplation of the Buddha, first sets out at the head of the contemplation of the image the merit of contemplating the Buddha; this is precisely the opening of the essential way for living beings to become Buddhas. The wonderful purport of the whole Sūtra lies in this passage alone. Later students in their discussions should exhaustively investigate it. If this is not understood, what else is there to say? (The Lingzhi Commentary)
Zi 1: Clarifying That the Buddha’s Body Is Universal and Can Respond to the Minds of Beings
Why is this so? All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the Dharma-realm body, and enter into the mind-thoughts of all living beings.

The first sentence is the question: wherein lies the benefit of contemplating the Buddha? At ‘all’ below is the answer. Here it is properly Amitābha who is spoken of; because the Dharma-body is one in substance, it says ‘all Buddhas.’ The Avataṃsaka says: ‘The bodies of all the Buddhas are one single Dharma-body; one mind, one wisdom, and the powers and fearlessnesses likewise.’ This makes clear that the Dharma-body realized by all Buddhas as fruition is nowhere not pervading; hence it is not two and not different from the causal-stage Dharma-body of living beings. Therefore when living beings form the visualization, the Buddha’s body responds accordingly. The commentary says: ‘When the minds of living beings are pure, the Dharma-body is at liberty, and so can enter into the mind-thoughts of living beings. It is like the white sun rising in the sky, its reflection appearing in a hundred rivers.’ Hence the mind that visualizes the Buddha is itself the thirty-two marks and the eighty subsidiary excellences. As Mahāsthāmaprāpta’s perfect penetration says: ‘The Tathāgatas of the ten directions pity and remember living beings as a mother remembers her child’ — this makes clear that the Buddha ever remembers living beings. ‘If the child flees away, what use is her remembering?’ — this makes clear that when living beings do not remember, there is response but no feeling. ‘If the minds of living beings recollect the Buddha and invoke the Buddha, whether now or in the future they will certainly see the Buddha and be not far from the Buddha’ — this makes clear that when living beings invoke the Buddha, response and feeling meet. This is truly the inconceivable function of Amitābha, the World-Honored One’s same-substance great compassion and the power of his roots of goodness, going to meet the feeling according to conditions and letting forms hang down in response to beings. If one understands this principle, what doubt can there be that the Buddha enters in? (The Lingzhi Commentary)
Zi 2: Clarifying That When the Practitioner’s Visualization Is Accomplished, He Himself Possesses the Buddha’s Substance
Therefore, when you and others visualize the Buddha in your minds, that mind is itself the thirty-two marks and the eighty subsidiary excellences. This mind forms the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha.

The first sentence shows the mind and its object corresponding. At ‘this mind’ below, the causal mind accomplishing the fruition-marks is made clear. The two sentences below explain and establish the meaning above. ‘This mind’ refers to the mind with which the practitioner contemplates the Buddha. By contemplating the Buddha’s marks, the marks appear within the mind, and this mind then possesses the Buddha’s marks and excellences. This is spoken with reference to the small body of one zhang and six feet; its merit is of this order. If one contemplates the eighty-four thousand marks and excellences, the mind’s possession is likewise. The teaching bids one contemplate the Buddha, and its merit is of this order. Living beings rely upon the teaching, cultivate the cause, and feel the fruit; it begins from this mind, and hence it says ‘this mind forms the Buddha.’ Lest one think that the Buddha accomplished by cultivation is obtained from outside, [it is said] that just because this mind in its very substance is the Buddha, therefore when one establishes the cultivation, nothing fails of fruition; hence it says ‘this mind is the Buddha.’ Were it otherwise, when one is born in that land and possesses the thirty-two marks and excellences of a great man, from where would they be obtained? One should know that the mind that visualizes the Buddha today already possesses in full the marks, excellences, and fruition-virtues. The substance conceived in the lotus womb is precisely this mind. So it is proved that the attainment of bodhi is not obtained from another. (The Lingzhi Commentary)

The Yue-lun Commentary says: “‘Forms’ parts from the sense of spontaneity. ‘Is’ parts from the sense of causal conditions. To know that this mind forms the Buddha but not that this mind is the Buddha is to be blind to the originally wonderful and to be stalled in one’s efforts; to know that this mind is the Buddha but not that this mind forms the Buddha is to trust to one’s natural endowment and to abandon cultivation and realization. Parting from these two extremes, one thought perfectly fused — only then is the middle way made clear.”

The Shilun says: “‘This mind forms the Buddha’ and ‘this mind is the Buddha’ — these two sentences are the confluence of the whole Sūtra. The two words ‘forms’ and ‘is’ are again the guiding cords of the two sentences, showing the meaning that mind and Buddha are not two. The Avataṃsaka Sūtra, in the elder Muktaka’s words to Sudhana, says: ‘Good man! If I wish to see the Buddha of Immeasurable Life in the Land of Peace and Bliss, I see him as I will.

… Those Tathāgatas do not come here, and I do not go there. I know that all Buddhas come from nowhere, and that I arrive nowhere. I know that all Buddhas and my own mind are all like a dream; I know that all Buddhas are like a flash of lightning, and I understand that my own mind is like an image in water. I know that all Buddhas are all like illusions, and my own mind likewise. I know that the voices of all Buddhas are like an echo, and my own mind likewise. Thus to know, thus to understand, thus to enter.’ The Avataṃsaka’s interpretation of the word ‘enter’ is as perfectly fused as this. Measured against the present Sūtra, whether one says that the Buddha’s Dharma-body enters into the mind-thoughts of living beings, or that the mind-thoughts of living beings enter into the Buddha’s mind, neither is inadmissible. There is no need to ask whether he comes or I go: not he, yet not not-he; not I, yet not not-I. Both self and other are unobtainable — this is what is called the mind being one with its object. The ancients, in their commentaries on this chapter, having said ‘response and feeling meet,’ then feared that one might hold that there is a Buddha outside the mind, and so repeatedly offered various remedial words to wipe out that view. In truth, the sentences ‘the mind forms’ and ‘the mind is’ are already perfectly fused; there is no boundary to be wiped out. The cultivation of contemplation belongs to the function of perfuming seeds; one does not seek for responses, lest one be rash and advance too quickly and be possessed by a demon (a demon meaning mental illness). Wait until one’s effort is seasoned, like water arriving and the channel forming, like spring returning and the flowers bursting open — then one obtains the effect of itself. Therefore the beginner on the path does not seek to be in accord with the Buddha, but seeks only to be in accord with the Sūtra; as it is said, ‘to be in accord with the sūtras; what is not in accord is called false thinking.’
Zi 3: Raising the fruit-virtue to bring faith in the mind of cause.
The ocean of right universal knowledge of the Buddhas is born from the mind and thought.

By 'right universal knowledge' is meant one of the ten epithets of a Buddha. The transcendent Dharma is fully and exhaustively known by it. Deep and vast without limit, therefore it is likened to an ocean. The Buddha's virtues are boundless; the text gives but a brief mention of universal knowledge in order to embrace the rest. The ten thousand virtues of the fruit-person all arise from mind and thought; the intent is to encourage lower ordinary beings to single-mindedly and diligently cultivate, so that their effort is not in vain. (Lingzhi's commentary)
Zi 4: Concluding exhortation to cultivate the cause, which must rely on the fruit-virtue.
Therefore one should single-mindedly hold the thought and contemplate intently that Buddha: Tathagata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha.

It is precisely because the virtue of the Buddha contemplated is lofty and deep that he urges the holding of the thought. The preceding passage spoke generally of all Buddhas; this one points specifically to Amitābha, concluding and returning to the true intent of this sutra. Hence it says 'contemplate intently that Buddha.' Tathagata is translated as 'Thus-come'; Arhat, 'worthy of offerings'; Samyaksambuddha, 'right universal knowledge.' These are three of the ten epithets, briefly mentioned. The detailed explanation is given elsewhere. (Lingzhi's commentary)
Gui 2: Properly clarifying the method of contemplating the Buddha, in two parts.
First, directly contemplating the three images.
Second, the realm of the accomplished contemplation.
Zi 1: Directly contemplating the three images, in two parts.
First, contemplating the image of the Buddha.
Second, contemplating the images of the two bodhisattvas.
Chou 1: Contemplating the image of the Buddha, in two parts.
First, properly clarifying the contemplation of the image.
Second, seeing the land through the image.
Yin 1: Properly clarifying the contemplation of the image.
In thinking of that Buddha, one should first visualize the image; whether the eyes are closed or open, one sees a jewel image, Jambunada golden in color, seated upon that lotus.

The image is used to represent the real, going from the easy to the difficult; therefore, whether painted or carved, according to what a person is familiar seeing, that is taken as the object. 'Seated on that lotus' refers to the lotus seat of the preceding contemplation. (Lingzhi's commentary)
Yin 2: Seeing the land through the image.

Having seen the image seated, the mind's eye opens. Clearly and distinctly one sees the Land of Ultimate Bliss adorned with seven jewels: jewel ground, jewel pools, jewel trees in rows, jewel canopies of the devas spread above, and nets of many jewels filling the sky. Seeing these things, one makes them utterly clear, as if viewing something in the palm of the hand.

Seeing the land through the image is seeing the retributive environment of the preceding contemplation. Miaozong's commentary says: 'Once the image-contemplation is accomplished, the mind's eye opens, and one sees broadly the features of the retributive environment, the ground, the trees, and so forth. One should know that these trees and so on exceed those of the preceding contemplation by countless times. Why is this? Because the present jewel image must match the lotus seat; if the trees were not tall, how could they cover the seat? All this is because the wondrous contemplation becomes ever deeper, so that what is contemplated becomes ever more excellent.' Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Viewing in the palm of the hand' speaks of its clarity.
Chou 2: Contemplating the images of the two bodhisattvas.

Having seen this, one should further create a great lotus on the Buddha's left, like the preceding lotus, identical in every way. Again create a great lotus on the Buddha's right. Visualize the image of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva seated on the left lotus seat, also golden in color, just as before, without difference. Visualize the image of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva seated on the right lotus seat.

First, contemplating the lotus seat. 'Like the preceding lotus' refers to the one the Buddha sits on. Considering the bodies of the bodhisattvas, the lotus should be reckoned as smaller. Next, contemplating the form and image. 'Also golden in color' means the bodhisattvas' bodies are the same color as the preceding Buddha. (Lingzhi's commentary)
Zi 2: The realm of the accomplished contemplation, in two parts.
First, the eye beholds the supreme realm.
Second, the ear hears the wondrous Dharma.
Chou 1: The eye beholds the supreme realm.

When this contemplation is accomplished, the images of the Buddha and the bodhisattvas all emit light. That light is golden, illuminating the many jewel trees. Beneath each tree there are also three lotuses, and upon each lotus there is one image of a Buddha and two images of bodhisattvas, filling that land completely.
First, the three images emit light, and the light-color illuminates the trees. Next, beneath each tree one sees the three images everywhere, present in every place. (Lingzhi's commentary)
Chou 2: The ear hears the wondrous Dharma.

When this contemplation is accomplished, the practitioner should hear the flowing water and light, as well as the many jewel trees, ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks, all speaking the wondrous Dharma. Whether emerging from or entering absorption, he constantly hears the wondrous Dharma. What the practitioner has heard, upon emerging from absorption, he recollects and holds without letting go, making it accord with the sutras. If it does not accord, it is called deluded thinking. If it does accord, it is called a coarse thought seeing the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

First, this clarifies hearing the Dharma within the contemplation. The flowing water and light, together with the many jewel trees, are the insentient speaking the Dharma; the ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks are the sentient speaking the Dharma. That the sentient and the insentient alike perfectly fulfill the Buddha-wisdom of the seed-nature may be seen here. (Lingzhi's commentary: 'Bitter, empty, impermanent, and no-self, the perfections, hence it is called the wondrous Dharma.') The practitioner does not merely hear it upon entering absorption; so too upon emerging from it; hence it says he constantly hears. Second, from 'the practitioner' onward, it clarifies that what is heard should accord with the sutras, otherwise it is delusion. Hence it says, 'If it does not accord, it is called deluded thinking; if it accords, it is called a coarse seeing.' This clarifies the state upon emerging from absorption. Because when hearing within absorption it necessarily accords with the sutras (Lingzhi's commentary: 'This means the dharma heard does not conflict with the scriptural teachings, hence it is called according.'). Fearing that upon emerging it might not be so, this instruction is given. If upon emerging it still accords with the sutras, then it is not emerging yet, emerging, and emerging yet, not emerging. Even so, it is still called a coarse thought, because comparing the image to the real, one must distinguish coarse from subtle. This contemplation is an expedient of the Buddha-contemplation; how could it be wholly identical with the true Buddha-contemplation? (The Yanyi) Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Contradicting the teachings is delusion; according with the Dharma is still coarse. Compared with the following samādhi, coarse and subtle are distinguished here.'
Question: The sutra says 'the heard dharma he recollects and holds without letting go.' What if one has not heard it?

Answer: One must attain superior absorption before one can hear it. If one does not hear it, then one may take up the fifth contemplation, the so-called water-sound expounding the bitter, empty, impermanent, and no-self perfections, and the birds' praise of the Three Jewels; relying on these, one recollects and holds, without contravening the scriptural teachings. (The Shilun)

The sutra says: 'In thinking of that Buddha, one should first visualize the image.' The word 'first' indicates that visualizing the image and thinking of the Buddha are two tasks. From 'next, think of the Buddha' down to 'arising from the mind of thought,' all these suggest thinking of the Buddha's awesome virtue. What are awesome virtue and virtue? 'The ocean of right universal knowledge' is the awesome; great compassion is the virtue. Having thought of the Buddha's wisdom, vast as an ocean, one then contemplates the Buddha's mind of compassion without conditions. The image must be contemplated first: mentally create a jewel image of Jambunada golden color, with the two bodhisattvas each seated upon a lotus; all the images emit light, illuminating the many jewel trees. The reflected images beneath each tree are all alike. The eighth contemplation is confined to this; one need not seek the thirty-two marks and eighty minor marks in their various parts. Contemplating the Buddha has a direct function for perfuming the seed-nature. The Record on Consciousness-Only says: 'The self-nature's immediate cause is called the equally-flowing seed; the different-nature attraction is called the ripening seed; all seeds are fully contained within these two.' The equally-flowing includes both the defiled and the undefiled; the ripening is only the defiled. Contemplating the Buddha is a transcendent Dharma, not contained in the ripening, and should belong to the equally-flowing. The Mahayana-samgraha says: 'The teachings and such that flow from the most pure Dharma-realm are called the equally-flowing of the most pure Dharma-realm.' According to this, one who contemplates the Buddha has, in the near term, the cause of rebirth in the Pure Land, and in the far term, the cause of Buddhahood after asamkhya kalpas. This is what is meant by being drawn by one's own kind, for the fruit resembles the cause. Yet the practitioner must purify his mind at all times; if the time of being tainted by habits is much while the time of contemplating the Buddha is little, the quantities being so unequal, it will lack the supreme function. The Vimalakirti Sutra says: 'As the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure' - this is truly an unchanging principle. (The Shilun)
Gui 3: Concluding statement.
This is the visualization of the image, called the eighth contemplation.
Gui 4: Manifesting the benefit.
Those who make this contemplation remove the offenses of birth and death of immeasurable millions of kalpas; in this very body they attain the Buddha-mindfulness samādhi.

The passage has two points: first, removing the obstacle of offenses; second, approaching the samādhi, which is the following Buddha-contemplation. If the image-contemplation is accomplished, the true body will surely be seen; hence it says in this very body one attains it. (Lingzhi's commentary)

blocks.text: Xin 3: Directly Contemplating the Buddha's Body (the Ninth, the Buddha-Body Contemplation), in Five Parts

inline.s: First, concluding the preceding and arousing the following.
Second, properly showing the body's marks; Third, raising the benefit and urging cultivation; Fourth, concluding the contemplation's name; Fifth, distinguishing right and wrong contemplation.
Ren 1: Concluding the preceding and arousing the following.
The Buddha told Ānanda and Queen Vaidehi: 'Once this contemplation is accomplished, next you should contemplate the marks and light of the body of the Buddha of Measureless Life.'

This sentence concludes the preceding; the next sentence arouses the following. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'This, like the image-contemplation, has the sequential text of treading on the preceding and arousing the following; the intent is that proper cultivation may not take a different path.'
Ren 2: Properly showing the marks of the body, in three parts.
First, separately distinguishing the body's marks.
Second, generally showing the marks and virtues; Third, the realm of the accomplished contemplation.
Gui 1: Separately distinguishing the body's marks.

Ānanda, you should know: the body of the Buddha of Measureless Life is like the Jambunada gold of the Yama heavens, in its hundreds of millions and billions; the Buddha's body is sixty trillion nayuta Ganges-sands yojanas in height. The white hair between the brows is coiled clockwise, like five Mount Sumerus. The Buddha's eyes are like the water of the four great oceans, clear blue and distinct. From all the pores of the body issues light, like Mount Sumeru. That Buddha's halo is like a hundred billion thousand-times-great-thousand worlds. Within the halo are a million billion nayuta Ganges-sands transformation-buddhas; each transformation-buddha also has many, countless transformation-bodhisattvas as attendants.

First, contemplating the color of the Buddha's body. Zhizhi's commentary says: 'The gold of the Yama heavens surpasses the sun and moon by doubling their radiance into thousands of millions, a splendor beyond thought!' Next, from 'the Buddha's body,' one contemplates the body's measure. Zhizhi's commentary says: 'Nayuta is a number reaching the myriad; here it means tens of thousands of millions. Yojana is a measure; the greater is eighty li, the middle sixty li, the lesser forty li. Compared with the two great bodhisattvas, the Buddha is less by twenty trillion nayutas, but more by Ganges-sands times.' Lingzhi's commentary says: 'The Buddha's body is measureless, while the capacities' perceptions differ; those cited in the text are but borrowed quantities, to show it is without quantity, and to make clear the Buddha's body cannot be fixed. Hence the passage below says: As previously said, the measure of the Buddha of Measureless Life is without bound, beyond the reach of the mind and power of ordinary beings. Again it says: Or he manifests a great body filling the sky. Citing this verifies the preceding, so one knows it is without limit. To measure the ocean with a ladle, to measure the sky with a foot-rule, is that possible? The simile makes this clear.'

Third, from 'between the brows' onward, the measure of the brow-hair. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Coiled clockwise, its shape like a pearl. One Sumeru is three million three hundred sixty thousand li high; its breadth and length likewise. Five Sumerus make sixteen million eight hundred thousand li.' Fourth, from 'the Buddha's eyes,' the measure of the eyes' color. Lingzhi's commentary: 'One great ocean is eighty-four thousand yojanas; the four great oceans together make three hundred thirty-six thousand yojanas.' Fifth, from 'all the body,' the flowing light from the pores. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'To stream is to flow; the light from each pore is like Mount Sumeru.' Zhizhi's commentary: 'The light like Mount Sumeru is because it possesses the color of many jewels.' Sixth, from 'That Buddha,' the halo's transformation-buddhas. Zhizhi's commentary: 'First, the measure. The thousand-times-great-thousand worlds, again with a hundred billion; the all-round measure can be known. Within the halo, next, the transformation-buddhas; within each, third, the transformed assemblies.'
Gui 2: Generally showing the marks and virtues.

The Buddha of Measureless Life has eighty-four thousand marks; within each mark there are eighty-four thousand subsidiary marks; within each subsidiary mark there are again eighty-four thousand lights. Each light universally illumines the beings of the ten directions who are mindful of the Buddha, gathering them without abandoning. These lights, marks, and transformation-buddhas cannot be fully told. One should only recollect and visualize them, so that the mind's eye sees them.

First, properly clarifying the marks and virtues. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'A body of sixteen feet possesses the thirty-two marks and eighty minor marks; now the measure of the body, marks, virtues, and lights of Amitābha, all of eighty-four thousand, their number is without limit, beyond counting!' Zhizhi's commentary says: 'All being eighty-four thousand is because he turns the dust-like defilement into the virtue of wisdom.' Miaozong's commentary says: 'The marks, virtues, and lights are all said to be eighty-four thousand, because manifesting virtue from the obstacle produces this number. The Buddha, dwelling at the stage of the ordinary being, is endowed with eighty-four thousand defilements; within all these defilements he sees the real marks. Since principle and wisdom accord, he can manifest the marks, virtues, and lights; hence each clause gives such a number. The practitioner contemplating now, knowing in his mind that this is so, can see the Buddha's marks within the defilements.'

Next, from 'each light,' it clarifies the gathering of beings. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Below it shows the light universally illumining and gathering beings; this is the very mind-substance of Amitābha's compassion.' Zhizhi's commentary says: 'The Buddha thinks of beings as a mother remembers her child; hence within the marks, each light illumines and gathers the one mindful of the Buddha.' Miaozong's commentary says: 'Beings and the Buddha are of one substance; although the land is vast and beings many, the gathering misses none.' The Yuelun says: 'That light universally illumines the beings of the ten directions who are mindful of the Buddha and gathers them without abandoning; hence one knows that when beings mindfully invoke the Buddha in a single thought, they are constantly within the great compassionate light of our Buddha, whether sitting, lying, or walking, without the least separation.'
Question: For those who do not invoke the Buddha, does the Buddha's light gather them?

Answer: Whether one invokes or does not invoke, there is nothing the light does not gather. But the invoker of the Buddha, being in accord with the light, is gathered for rebirth and surely never falls back. The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says: 'It is like fish roe; if the mother does not attend to them, the roe rots.' The Surangama Sutra says, 'The Buddha thinks of beings as a mother remembers her child.' It is only that the child, toward the mother, either remembers or does not. Again it is like a blind man beneath the sun: the sun illumines all, but the blind man does not see. Those who do not invoke the Buddha are likewise. (Lingzhi's commentary)

Third, from 'that light,' it generally distinguishes the inscrutable. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Its light and marks, together with the two lights of the upper body and the nape (the nape being the halo); the transformation-buddhas are what the halo manifests. Words cannot exhaust it; only by recollecting and visualizing is it seen. The mind's eye is the mind-thought.'
Gui 3: The realm of the accomplished contemplation.
Those who see this see all the Buddhas of the ten directions. Because they see the Buddhas, it is called the Buddha-mindfulness samādhi.

This clarifies that contemplating one Buddha, one sees all Buddhas. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Seeing many Buddhas, because the Dharma-body is the same. The Buddha-mindfulness samādhi gets its name from this.'

Those who make this contemplation are said to contemplate the bodies of all Buddhas. Because they contemplate the Buddha's body, they also see the Buddha's mind. The Buddha's mind is great compassion. With the unconditional compassion they gather all beings.

This clarifies that contemplating the Buddha's body, one sees the Buddha's mind. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Seeing the Buddha's mind, because the body is the mark of the mind. The Buddha has no mind of selfish inclinations; he has only great compassion. Compassion is giving joy; mercy is removing suffering. As beings are inexhaustible, the Buddha's great compassion is likewise inexhaustible. The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says: Compassion has three kinds. First, the being-referencing compassion: with no deliberate clinging to all beings, yet it naturally benefits them. Second, the Dharma-referencing compassion: with no deliberate contemplation of Dharma, yet it naturally counteracts with regard to all dharmas. Third, the unconditional compassion: with no deliberate contemplation of principle, yet it naturally abides in the equal highest truth. The last raises the principle-substance; the first two concern the functional use. Now raising the unconditional, the meaning includes all three. That is, the minds of all Buddhas abide neither in being nor in non-being, neither relying on the three times; the equal great compassion constantly illumines the Dharma-realm. With this it gathers beings, and no being is not gathered. It does not arise through conditions, hence it is called unconditional. This is what was earlier said: gathering the beings mindful of the Buddha without abandoning.' Zhizhi's commentary says: 'From contemplating, next, one contemplates the Buddha's mind. First raising the contemplation of the body, it is entirely the compassionate mind responding and manifesting; hence it says contemplating the body, seeing the mind. Affection and joyful remembrance is compassion, the virtue of giving joy; pity and distress is mercy, the virtue of removing suffering. Each has three aspects: first, the being-referencing compassion, taking hold of all beings as parents and six relatives; second, the Dharma-referencing compassion, taking hold of all dharmas as all arising from causes and conditions; third, the unconditional compassion, abiding neither in the marks of Dharma nor in the marks of beings. The three of mercy are to be understood likewise. The Buddha's mind is formless, manifesting through the virtue of inherent nature; hence it is said to be great compassion. He employs the compassion of the same body to save all beings, yet neither takes hold of the marks of beings nor limits the number of kalpas; hence it is called unconditional compassion gathering beings. The Samādhi Sutra says: The minds of all Buddhas are great compassion. That which compassion takes as its object is beings in suffering. When it sees beings experiencing suffering, it is like an arrow entering the heart, wishing to pull out their suffering. Since all Buddhas take beings as their body and mind, then outward is the Tathagata's body and inward is the mind, and beings may all follow and contemplate them accordingly.'
Ren 3: Raising the benefit and urging cultivation, in four parts.
First, properly clarifying the benefit.
Second, urging the cultivation of the contemplation; Third, showing the contemplation method; Fourth, again raising the benefit.
Gui 1: Properly clarifying the benefit.
Those who make this contemplation, when they leave this body in another life, are born before the Buddhas and attain the patience with the unborn.

Leaving this body in another life, having been born in that land, one directly realizes the unborn; hence one knows that if this contemplation is accomplished, the highest-grade highest rebirth is clear. (Lingzhi's commentary)
Gui 2: Urging the cultivation of the contemplation.
Therefore the wise one should bind the mind and contemplate intently the Buddha of Measureless Life.

The wise one is the person who cultivates the contemplation. Relying on the preceding contemplation methods, this is the intent contemplation. Because by cultivating this contemplation one is reborn and attains the patience, the merit is deep and the benefit great, hence he urges binding the mind. Thus in the Pratyutpanna Sutra, beings ask the Buddha: 'For what cause are we born in this land?' Amitābha answers: 'By cultivating the Buddha-mindfulness samādhi, one is born in that land.' (Lingzhi's commentary)
Gui 3: Showing the contemplation method.

Those who contemplate the Buddha of Measureless Life enter through a single mark. They need only contemplate the white hair between the brows, making it utterly clear. Those who see the mark of the white hair between the brows will find the eighty-four thousand marks and virtues naturally appear.

'Many marks self-endowed' - because the single mark of the brow-hair sums up all the marks. According to the sutra text, one contemplates the measure of five Sumerus. Hence it says 'the eighty-four thousand marks and virtues naturally appear.' One then knows it is not the brow-hair of the sixteen-foot body. (Lingzhi's commentary)
Gui 4: Again raising the benefit.
Those who see the Buddha of Measureless Life see the measureless Buddhas of the ten directions. Because one sees the measureless Buddhas, the Buddhas appear before one and give the prophecy.
Lingzhi's commentary says: 'The many Buddhas giving the prophecy - one receives their seal of approval and the prophecy of becoming a Buddha.'
Ren 4: Concluding the contemplation's name.
This is the universal contemplation of the marks of all the form-bodies, called the ninth contemplation.
Lingzhi's commentary says: 'The word all either refers collectively to the Buddhas seen, or specifically to the marks of Amitābha; both explanations are acceptable.'

blocks.text: Geng 2: Contemplating the Buddha's Attendants, in Two Parts

inline.s: First, contemplating Avalokiteshvara.
Second, contemplating Mahasthamaprapta.
Xin 1: Contemplating Avalokiteshvara (the Tenth, the Avalokiteshvara Contemplation), in Five Parts.
First, concluding the preceding and arousing the following.
Second, properly showing the body's marks; Third, concluding the contemplation's name; Fourth, raising the benefit and urging cultivation; Fifth, distinguishing right and wrong contemplation.
The Buddha told Ānanda and Queen Vaidehi: 'Having seen the Buddha of Measureless Life clearly and distinctly, next you should also contemplate Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva.'
Ren 2: Properly showing the body's marks.
This bodhisattva's body is eighty trillion nayuta yojanas tall. The body is purple-gold in color. On the top of the head is the fleshy top-knot.

First, clarifying the body's measure. Zhizhi's commentary says: 'Its measure is less than the Buddha's body by Ganges-sands; for example, in the realm of Pure Light Adornment of the east, the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King of Wisdom has a body of six million eight hundred thousand yojanas; Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound has forty-two thousand yojanas (see the Wondrous Sound chapter of the Lotus Sutra). In this land, our Tathagata Śākyamuni is sixteen feet, while a person is eight feet.' The Shilun says: 'This contemplation first speaks of the body's measure as eighty trillion nayuta yojanas. Now the Buddha's body is sixty trillion nayuta Ganges-sands yojanas. Speaking in trillions, eighty is more than sixty; speaking in yojanas, without the words Ganges-sands, it is reduced greatly. Yet in such places one need not cling; one should only imagine the body's height as resembling the Buddha's, only slightly lower.' 'The body purple-gold' - second, clarifying the body's color. 'On the top of the head' - third, clarifying the top-knot. The annotated commentary says: 'The fleshy top-knot, in Sanskrit ushnisha, is a mound of flesh on the top of the Buddha's head, shaped like a top-knot, hence called the fleshy top-knot. It is one of the thirty-two marks.'

At the nape there is a halo, its face on each side a hundred thousand yojanas. Within that halo are five hundred transformation-buddhas, like Śākyamuni. Each transformation-buddha has five hundred transformation-bodhisattvas and measureless devas as attendants.

Fourth, clarifying the nape-light. The Yanyi says: 'The light's measure on the four faces is each a hundred hundred-thousand (that is, one hundred thousand) yojanas. Within it are transformation-buddhas; each Buddha has transformation-bodhisattvas, and further there are devas as attendants, their number measureless.' Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Like Śākyamuni refers to the sixteen-foot body.'
Within the light of the whole body, all the forms of beings of the five paths appear.

Fifth, the body-light. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'The beings of the five paths, because the asuras are combined in. The bodhisattva manifests his form in the five paths to save suffering beings; hence within the light their forms appear.' The Shilun says: 'Within the light are not only transformation-buddhas and bodhisattvas, but also the five paths, extending to the evil destinies; because this bodhisattva's primal vow, clad in the armor of the great vow, travels through all the realms to save suffering beings. He is not like the Buddha of Measureless Life, who establishes a Pure Land and takes gathering beings as his principal task.'
On the top of the head, the Virinca mani-jewel forms the heavenly crown. Within that heavenly crown is a standing transformation-buddha, twenty-five yojanas tall.

Sixth, the heavenly crown. The Yanyi says: 'Sakyavirinca is translated as able to prevail. Within the crown is a standing Buddha, twenty-five yojanas tall.' Lingzhi's commentary says: 'The transformation-buddha within the crown represents bearing the fruit while practicing the cause.'

The face of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva is like Jambunada gold. The mark of the hair between the brows possesses the color of the seven jewels, and flows out into eighty-four thousand kinds of light; each light has measureless, countless hundreds of thousands of transformation-buddhas; each transformation-buddha has countless transformation-bodhisattvas as attendants. The transformations are free, filling the worlds of the ten directions.

Seventh, contemplating the face's color. Eighth, from 'between the brows,' the brow-mark. The hair possesses the color of the seven jewels; the color has eighty thousand lights; each light has countless transformation-buddhas; each Buddha has countless transformation-bodhisattvas as attendants. The transformations are free, filling the sky. (The Yanyi)
The Shilun says: 'The brow-mark between the brows makes the color of the seven jewels, different from the white hair.'
The arms are the color of the red lotus. There are eighty hundred-million subtle lights forming a necklace. Within that necklace all the magnificent adornments appear universally.
Ninth, the arm-mark. Its color is like the red lotus. Further there are eighty hundred-million subtle lights forming a necklace; within the necklace all the adornments appear. (The Yanyi)

The palms make the color of five hundred hundred-million mixed lotuses. On the ten finger-tips, each finger-tip has eighty-four thousand lines, like seal-inscriptions. Each line has eighty-four thousand colors; each color has eighty-four thousand lights. That light is gentle, universally illumining all. With these jewel-hands he gathers and leads beings.

Tenth, the hand-mark. The palm is like the color of mixed lotuses. The ten finger-tips each have eighty-four thousand lines; the lines have eighty-four thousand colors; the colors have eighty-four thousand lights; the light illumines all and gathers and leads beings. (The Yanyi)

The Shilun says: 'Throughout the body the parts are not all the same in color. The face is Jambunada gold, the body purple-gold, the arms lotus-red, the hands the color of five hundred hundred-million mixed lotuses; and the jewel-hands have especially many distinguishing colors, representing the virtue of direct gathering and leading. This should be noted.'

When he lifts his foot, beneath the foot is the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel, naturally transforming into five hundred hundred-million light-platforms. When the foot is set down, vajra-mani flowers scatter everywhere, filling without exception.

Eleventh, the foot-mark. If the foot were not lifted, it seems one could not contemplate it; hence one must, when the foot is lifted, contemplate the thousand-spoked wheel. (Lingzhi's commentary: 'The wheel has a thousand spokes, hence named the thousand-spoked wheel.') The wheel-mark transforms into light-platforms. When the foot is set down there are vajra-jewel flowers, spread everywhere. The marks and virtues of the whole body are in general like this. (The Yanyi)

The other marks of the body are fully endowed with the many good marks, no different from the Buddha. Only the fleshy top-knot on the head and the mark of the unseen crown are less than the World-Honored One's.

This clarifies that the other marks are the same as the Buddha's; only the fleshy top-knot differs. Miaozong's commentary says: 'The fleshy top-knot is a mark; the unseen crown is a good mark. These marks and virtues represent the ultimate fruit; now as one in the causal stage, therefore he is not equal to the Buddha.'
Ren 3: Concluding the contemplation's name.
This is the contemplation of the real form-body of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, called the tenth contemplation.
Lingzhi's commentary: 'The real form-body is the response-body.'
Ren 4: Raising the benefit and urging cultivation.

The Buddha told Ānanda: 'If one wishes to contemplate Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, one should make this contemplation. Those who make this contemplation do not meet any calamities and are cleansed of the obstacles of karma; they remove the offenses of birth and death of countless kalpas. For such a bodhisattva, merely hearing his name obtains measureless merit - how much more the intent contemplation.'

First, the exhortation on dispelling offenses through cultivating the contemplation. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Should make this means the above various marks; one may not differ. Not meeting calamities removes present difficulties; removing the offenses of countless kalpas breaks past karma.' Next, the exhortation on gaining merit through invoking the name. The Yanyi says: 'Even invoking the name, a scattered-good, still obtains measureless merit - how much more cultivating the contemplation, a concentrated-good, which can remove the grave offenses of birth and death of countless kalpas.' Gaining merit by hearing the name is widely explained in the Universal Gateway chapter.

If one wishes to contemplate Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, first contemplate the fleshy top-knot on the head, next the heavenly crown; the other marks one contemplates in order as well. Make them all clear, as if viewing in the palm of the hand.

Third, showing the order of the contemplation. Lingzhi's commentary: 'From top to bottom is taken as the order.' The Yanyi: 'This means from the crown and nape one follows the order down, right to the wheel-mark beneath the feet, making all clear and distinct, as in the palm of one's hand one sees the lines of one's own palm.' The commentary says: 'Since the body-marks are many, which mark should one first contemplate? Now it shows: first contemplate the fleshy top-knot, next the heavenly crown. Because these two can, in particular, represent Avalokiteshvara's virtue-marks. Why? The fleshy top-knot, lower than the Buddha, manifests the practice of the cause; the crown has a transformation-Buddha, manifesting the fruit accomplished of old. If the particular marks are manifest, the remaining general marks then become easy to understand. The practitioner, contemplating the crown, top-knot, brow-hair, face, body-color, and light, must each time use the mind's making and mind's being as the contemplative faculty. The teaching was given before the images, and is applied here. Since it says making the Buddha, one is the Buddha - how could one not be able to make Avalokiteshvara, and be Avalokiteshvara? Making the top-knot and the crown, being the top-knot and the crown, may all serve as examples. Not only should one use the Buddha as an example to contemplate the bodhisattvas, but one should also apply it to the universal, the miscellaneous, and the three grades; not only use the preceding as example for the following, but also use the following as example for the preceding. This is so that the practitioner may cultivate the contemplation on both the beginning and the end of the sutra text.'
Those who make this contemplation are called right contemplation. If one makes other contemplations, they are called wrong contemplation.

blocks.text: Xin 2: Contemplating Mahasthamaprapta (the Eleventh, the Mahasthamaprapta Contemplation), in Four Parts

inline.s: First, properly clarifying the contemplated realm.
Second, concluding the contemplation's name; Third, manifesting the contemplation's benefit; Fourth, jointly concluding the two contemplations.
First, contemplating the body-marks.
Second, contemplating the action-marks; Third, contemplating the sitting-mark.
Gui 1: Contemplating the body-marks.

Next, contemplate Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva: this bodhisattva's body, in size and measure, is also like Avalokiteshvara's. The halo, on each face, is a hundred twenty-five yojanas, illumining two hundred fifty yojanas. The light of the whole body illumines the lands of the ten directions, in purple-gold color. Beings with conditions all see it. Merely seeing the light of a single pore of this bodhisattva, one sees the pure and wondrous light of the measureless Buddhas of the ten directions. Therefore this bodhisattva is named Measureless Light. With the light of wisdom he universally illumines all, causing them to leave the three evil paths and obtain the supreme power; therefore this bodhisattva is named Mahasthamaprapta, Great Power Attained.

The first sentence is the general heading. Below that is the particular explanation. First, clarifying the body-measure. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Like Avalokiteshvara - also eighty trillion nayuta.'

Second, the halo. Third, the body-light, which has three: first, the light-color; second, the light's function, meaning beings with conditions see it. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Those who cultivate this contemplation are the beings with conditions.' Third, the two reasons for the name: first, named from the light; second, named from the awesome power. Lingzhi's commentary says: 'Because the light illumines beings, removing suffering and giving joy, the name is taken from the awesome power. The supreme power is the ten powers.'

The Shilun says: 'This bodhisattva's body-marks are for the most part wholly without difference from Avalokiteshvara's. Now I briefly explain the particular marks; the shared marks I will not repeat. Now the halo of Avalokiteshvara is a hundred thousand yojanas - hundred thousand, in Chinese speech is an indefinite great number, but spoken in Western terms it is one hundred thousand. Why then is Mahasthamaprapta's light only a hundred twenty-five yojanas? This is not that the lights have superior and inferior, but that their forms and functions differ. The pores are indeed minute and fine, yet seeing the light of a single pore of this bodhisattva, one sees the pure and wondrous light of the measureless Buddhas of the ten directions - it does not depend on the size of the halo-mark. Moreover, it can cause beings with conditions to all see it; then its function is wondrous indeed.'

This bodhisattva's heavenly crown has five hundred jewel-flowers. Each jewel-flower has five hundred jewel-platforms. Within each platform, the broad and long forms of the pure and wondrous Buddha-lands of the ten directions all appear.
Fourth, the heavenly crown. Zhizhi's commentary says: 'The flowers are lotuses.' The rest is as the text makes known.
The fleshy top-knot on the head is like the padma flower. Upon the fleshy top-knot there is a jewel vase holding various lights, universally manifesting the Buddha's work.
Fifth, the fleshy top-knot. First, clarifying the top-knot's color. Padma is translated as the red lotus. Next, the vase-light's transformations.
The remaining marks of the body are without difference, like Avalokiteshvara's.
Sixth, pointing out that the remaining marks are the same as Avalokiteshvara's; that is, the face, arms, hands, and so forth.
Gui 2: Contemplating the action-marks.

When this bodhisattva walks, all the worlds of the ten directions tremble. Wherever the earth quakes, there are five hundred hundred-million jewel-flowers. Each jewel-flower is adorned, lofty and manifest, like the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

This means when the bodhisattva walks, the earth of the ten directions quakes; wherever it quakes, jewel-flowers appear. The flowers' loftiness is like the Land of Ultimate Bliss and such. (The Yanyi)
Gui 3: Contemplating the sitting-marks.

When this bodhisattva sits, the land of the seven treasures quakes all at once. From the Buddha-realm of Golden Light below up to the Buddha-realm of Light-King above, in the space between them, immeasurable dust-mote numbers of emanated Amitāyus Buddhas, and emanated Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta, all gather like clouds in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, filling the sky, seated upon lotus seats, expounding the wonderful Dharma, and saving suffering sentient beings.

When the bodhisattva sits, the earth also quakes. When he walks, the quaking spreads horizontally; when he sits, the quaking penetrates vertically — the text reveals each by the other. From below to above, in between there are dust-mote numbers of emanated Three Sages, gathering like clouds and filling the sky, expounding the Dharma and saving beings. (The Yanyi) The annotated commentary says: “Gathering like clouds is a simile for the abundance of the assembly; again, it is like clouds that gather without any intent. Cè (pronounced like ‘tsuh’): cèsài, the Zhizhi commentary says, means ‘filling everywhere.’”
Question: Why is it that when this bodhisattva walks or sits, the quaking spreads horizontally through the ten directions and shakes vertically above and below?

Answer: Because this bodhisattva’s awesome power is supreme, he is named Great Power (Mahasthamaprapta). He represents virtue by firmness, while Avalokiteshvara represents virtue by gentleness. Hence the Sūtra says: “Its light is soft and gentle.” European writers also hold this view. Whether it is appropriate must await later sages; I dare not pronounce a final verdict.

Question: This bodhisattva, in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, sits upon a lotus seat, expounds the wonderful Dharma, and saves suffering sentient beings — does the Land of Ultimate Bliss then also have suffering?

Answer: The preaching of the Dharma is not confined to that land alone; the Buddhas, without moving from the place of enlightenment, extend their awesome power over worlds in the ten directions. For example, the devas and humans in the Land of Ultimate Bliss all possess the celestial ear and hear what hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas teach (see the Forty-eight Vows). This bodhisattva preaches the Dharma for suffering sentient beings so that the devas and other sentient beings with karmic ties in suffering worlds may all hear it — just as the devas and humans in the Land of Ultimate Bliss hear the Buddhas of other directions preaching the Dharma. Otherwise, those born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss would be beings already saved: what suffering would remain to be named, and whom would there be to ferry across? (The above two questions and answers are recorded from the Shilun.)
Ren 2: Concluding and pointing out the contemplation’s name.

One who practices this contemplation is said to see Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva. This is the contemplation of the bodily marks of Mahasthamaprapta, and it is called the eleventh contemplation. (This follows the circulated edition; the Taishō Tripiṭaka text reads: “This is the contemplation of the bodily marks of Mahasthamaprapta; one who contemplates this bodhisattva is named the eleventh contemplation, and removes the offenses of birth-and-death of countless kalpas and asaṃkhyeyas.”)

The Zhizhi commentary says: “In saying that all Three Sages have bodies of form-marks, [the Sūtra] makes clear that they are not the Dharma-body; for the Dharma-body has no form-marks of self and other that see one another in turn. The form-marks of the reward-body and the transformation-body are all manifested from the Dharma-body. Hence the Awakening of Faith says: ‘The Dharma-body of the Buddhas is solely the highest truth, and has no realm of worldly truth.’”
Ren 3: Revealing the contemplation’s benefits.

One who contemplates this bodhisattva removes the offenses of birth-and-death of countless kalpas and asaṃkhyeyas. One who practices this contemplation is not lodged in a womb, and constantly roams through the pure and wonderful lands of the Buddhas.

The benefits are also two: the extinction of offenses and rebirth in the West. Lingzhi’s commentary says: “The words ‘is not lodged in a womb’ and the rest mean: escaping the suffering of the Sahā world, one is born in the Buddha’s pure land, conceived in substance within a jeweled lotus, forever cut off from the womb.”
Question: Why do people in the world mostly make offerings to Avalokiteshvara and not to Mahasthamaprapta?

Answer: As explained earlier, Avalokiteshvara’s practice largely benefits worldly dharmas. One who aspires to the world-transcending and dreads womb-birth should also contemplate Mahasthamaprapta, for by contemplating this bodhisattva one is not lodged in a womb. (The Shilun)
Ren 4: Concluding Both Contemplations Together.
When this contemplation is accomplished, it is called the complete contemplation of Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta.

This concludes the two contemplations of Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta together. As for the words ‘complete’: Lingzhi’s commentary says: “It gathers up the bodily marks in their entirety, therefore it says ‘complete.’” The Zhizhi commentary says: “It means that when the above two contemplations are accomplished, then as to the bodies of the two great beings, it is called the complete contemplation of their form-bodies.” Miaozong’s commentary says: “The complete contemplation: because these two bodhisattvas differ only in two things — the transformation-Buddha and the jeweled vase — while all their other marks are the same. Same and different being clearly distinguished, it is called complete seeing.” Now I say: as for the attendants to the left and right of Amitāyus Buddha, if one contemplates only one of them, it is not complete; here both are contemplated, therefore it is called complete.

blocks.text: Geng 3: The General Contemplation of the Three Sages, in Two Parts

inline.s: First, the universal contemplation
Second, the miscellaneous contemplation
Xin 1: The Universal Contemplation (the Twelfth, the Universal Rebirth Contemplation), in Three Parts.
First, showing the method of contemplation
Second, concluding the name and meaning; third, revealing the response
Ren 1: Showing the Method of Contemplation.

When one sees these things, one should raise the thought that one’s own mind is born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, seated cross-legged within a lotus; one should form the thought of the lotus closing, the thought of the lotus opening; when the lotus opens, the thought that five hundred colored lights come to illumine one’s body; the thought that one’s eyes open and one sees Buddhas and bodhisattvas filling the sky, and that the water, birds, trees, and groves, together with the sounds issuing from all the Buddhas, all expound the wonderful Dharma in accord with the twelve divisions of the scriptures. If one emerges from concentration (this follows the circulated edition), one recollects and holds it without losing it.

Miaozong’s commentary says: “In the foregoing contemplations, the reliant [retribution] came first and the proper [retribution] next, the master first and the attendants next. Although each contemplation was accomplished, none was a universal summing-up, nor had one yet thought of one’s own body as born there and seen face to face. Therefore now one is caused to think of one’s body as ending [this life] and being born there, seeing all at once universally. Not only are the contemplated objects suddenly complete, but the thought of rebirth is also brought to accomplishment. This may be compared to the earlier contemplation of the reliant retribution: at first the trees, ponds, and the rest were contemplated separately, and when the contemplation of the pavilions was accomplished, the four things were seen together, which was called the general contemplation — yet that could only sum up the four things of the reliant retribution. Now one thinks of being born there and universally sees and universally hears all the marks of the reliant and the proper, therefore it is called the universal contemplation.”

In the text: the first sentence concludes what precedes; the next sentence arouses what follows, that is, to raise the mind and form the contemplation of being born in that Buddha-land. Next, the cross-legged sitting within the lotus. Next, the thought of the lotus opening and closing. The Zhizhi commentary says: “Closing is like being placed in the womb; opening is like emerging from the womb.” Next, the lotus opens and light illumines. Next, seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma. Lingzhi’s commentary says: “The Buddhas and bodhisattvas are the Three Sages. The water, birds, trees, and groves are the reliant retribution teaching the Dharma; and the Buddhas are the proper retribution teaching the Dharma. Still, one must accord with the teaching in order to test whether it is true or false.” The Shilun says: “The various reliant retributions above, up to the proper retribution of the Three Honored Ones, have now all been described. When the practitioner, following the Sūtra, has cultivated the contemplation to this point, he should then form the thought of his own rebirth, in order to bring it to a close. Following the precedent that this mind makes the Buddha and this mind is the Buddha, the mind made and the mind born, he is born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, sits cross-legged within a lotus, closes his eyes, and thinks: all things of the dusty world are empty; his own house and bed are also empty; only his own body and a single lotus remain. Sitting upright, he at once settles. The petals of the lotus close layer upon layer. After a moment in concentration, the petals slowly open again; five hundred colored lights touch his body, and he feels a subtle exhilaration, so he opens his eyes to look. — But one only forms the thought of opening the eyes; one must not actually open them, because opening them would bring the dusty realm into view and destroy the contemplated realm. Keeping the eyes closed preserves the contemplated mark, and one sees in thought all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas filling the sky, and hears in the mind the water, birds, trees, and groves, and the Buddhas preaching the Dharma. All sounds are constructed by the mind; the faculties of eye and ear are not used.”
Ren 2: Concluding the Name and Meaning.
Having seen these things, one is said to see Amitāyus Buddha and the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is the universal contemplation, called the twelfth contemplation.

As for the universal contemplation: Lingzhi’s commentary says: “It concludes the reliant and the proper together, therefore it receives the name ‘universal.’” The Zhizhi commentary says: “The proper retribution of the Three Sages, the reliant retribution of the Blissful Land, and one’s own body going to see them — all are thought of together at the same time, therefore it is called the universal contemplation.” The Shilun says: “What the Sūtra describes of the marks of the Pure Land is brought to an end here; joining together all the foregoing realms, it concludes with the universal contemplation.”
Ren 3: Revealing the Response.
Amitāyus Buddha, with countless transformation-bodies, together with Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta, constantly comes to where this practitioner is.”

The Zhizhi commentary says: “The Buddha’s Dharma-realm body enters into the mind-thoughts of all sentient beings; therefore, when the mind’s thought of the Buddha is accomplished, the transformation-bodies of the Three Sages constantly come to this place.”

blocks.text: Xin 2: The Miscellaneous Contemplation (the Thirteenth, the Contemplation of the Buddha and Bodhisattvas Hard to Clarify), in Three Parts

inline.s: First, the general indication
Second, the particular explanation; third, concluding the name
Ren 1: The General Indication.
The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: “If one wishes with utmost sincerity to be born in the West, one should first contemplate a sixteen-foot image standing on the water of a pond.

The Shilun says: “This is a separate gate outside the various contemplations set forth above, or else it is a guide leading into those contemplations. Because the practitioner finds the foregoing contemplations difficult to accomplish all at once, the Buddha, as an expedient, first establishes this contemplation and afterwards proceeds to the rest. The word ‘first’ indicates the order of sequence; it does not mean that one takes this one contemplation and discards all the others.” Lingzhi’s commentary says: “To accord with the capacities of this region, therefore one contemplates the sixteen-foot [image]. It does not say whether seated or standing, but it should be a standing image.”
Ren 2: The Particular Explanation, in Two Parts.
First, establishing the reason for the contemplation
Second, properly clarifying the method of contemplation
Gui 1: Establishing the Reason for the Contemplation.

As was said before: the measure of Amitāyus Buddha’s body is boundless, beyond the reach of the mental power of ordinary beings. Yet by the power of that Tathāgata’s former vows, those who recollect and think [of him] will surely accomplish it. Merely thinking of the Buddha’s image brings immeasurable merit — how much more contemplating the Buddha’s complete bodily marks.

Lingzhi’s commentary says: “What was said before refers to the preceding contemplation of the Buddha. The mind of an ordinary being is inferior, and though it cannot contemplate [him], relying on the Buddha’s vow-power, one who thinks [of him] will surely succeed.” The Shilun says: “Although the foregoing contemplations are beyond the reach of an ordinary being’s mental power, the Buddha, fearing that the practitioner might cling to this sentence, immediately uses the word ‘yet’ as a turning phrase, promising that it will surely be accomplished, because of that Buddha’s vow-power. Below ‘merely,’ he raises the image to illustrate the real.” The Shilun says: “The ‘image’ means the contemplation of the sixteen-foot [body]. The height of sixty trillion nayutas of Ganges-sands yojanas is the complete bodily marks.” Lingzhi’s commentary says: “Thinking of the image still brings merit; how much more the real — this may be known.”
Gui 2: Properly Clarifying the Method of Contemplation, in Two Parts.
First, contemplating the Buddha
Second, contemplating the two bodhisattvas
Zi 1: Contemplating the Buddha.

Amitābha Buddha’s spiritual powers are sovereign and free; in the lands of the ten directions he manifests transformations at will. Sometimes he manifests a great body filling the sky, sometimes a small body of sixteen feet or eight feet. Whatever form he manifests is all of true golden color. The transformed Buddhas in his circular halo, and the jeweled lotus, are as described above.

First, clarifying that the measure of the body is not fixed. Lingzhi’s commentary says: “The Buddha has no great or small; according to capacities there is difference.” Next, pointing to the remaining marks. Lingzhi’s commentary says: “The golden color and the circular halo are as in the preceding contemplation of the Buddha. The jeweled lotus is the contemplation of the lotus seat.” The Shilun says: “The Buddha’s body has originally no fixed measure of great or small; only its color is entirely true gold, and everything is the same as before, by which the right is distinguished from the erroneous.”
Zi 2: Contemplating the Two Bodhisattvas.

Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva and Mahasthamaprapta, in every place, make their bodies the same as those of sentient beings. One need only contemplate the head and countenance to know which is Avalokiteshvara and which is Mahasthamaprapta. These two bodhisattvas assist Amitābha Buddha in universally transforming all [beings].

The Shilun says: “In this contemplation, the bodies of the two bodhisattvas are the same as those of sentient beings, because of the expedient of responding to all sentient beings.” Lingzhi’s commentary says: “One need only contemplate the head and countenance to distinguish the two sages: Avalokiteshvara’s crown bears a standing Buddha, and Mahasthamaprapta’s top-knot bears a jeweled vase.” The Zhizhi commentary says: “As for ‘assisting in transforming all’: since the Buddha’s body follows the minds of sentient beings, the bodhisattvas likewise accord with the measure of what is known [by each].”
Ren 3: Concluding the Name.
This is the miscellaneous contemplation, called the thirteenth contemplation.”

The Shilun says: “Why is this contemplation called ‘miscellaneous’? Because it is tied to the inferior response-body, it is miscellaneous and impure when compared with the true body; because it is tied to a separate expedient gate, it is miscellaneous when compared with the superior contemplation and right absorption.” Lingzhi’s commentary says: “The Three Sages are not the same, and their sizes differ, therefore it is called the miscellaneous contemplation.”
Geng 4: Contemplating the Buddha’s Congregation, in Three Parts.

Lingzhi’s commentary says: “The three kinds from the fourteenth [contemplation] onward contemplate that land’s congregation. The three classes and nine grades are all objects of contemplation, and by them the marks of rebirth are clarified. Many people are confused about this. Now I say: what the text describes are all people who have already been born in that land; they are the marks of the fruition corresponding to the cause originally cultivated, and they serve as the three kinds of objects for the proximate contemplation.” It also says: “This is to make one recognize that the grades are upper, middle, and lower; these are precisely the three grades of the larger text [the Larger Sūtra].” Now I say: the three grades of the larger text all mark the arousing of the bodhi-mind, and can correspond only to the upper three grades of the present Sūtra; the middle and lower two grades do not correspond. Moreover, their causal practices are entirely different from the present one. Searching the Sūtra and comparing, one then knows it is not so. Now I clarify: the upper three grades are that land’s assembly of bodhisattvas; the middle three grades are its assembly of Śrāvakas; the lower three grades are its assembly of ordinary people. The three classes and nine grades gather in all the sages and ordinary beings of that land. Furthermore, within each of the three classes there are distinctions of high and low, as will be fully clarified below.”
The text is divided into three: first, contemplating the assembly of bodhisattvas; second, contemplating the assembly of Śrāvakas; third, contemplating the assembly of ordinary people.

blocks.text: Xin 1: Contemplating the Assembly of Bodhisattvas (the Fourteenth, the Upper-Grade Rebirth Contemplation), in Two Parts

inline.s: First, properly clarifying the three grades
Second, concluding the name of the contemplation
Ren 1: Properly Clarifying the Three Grades, in Three Parts.
First, the upper-grade upper-birth
Second, the upper-grade middle-birth; third, the upper-grade lower-birth.

Lingzhi’s commentary says: “In the fourteenth, the upper class has five [factors]: first, arousing the bodhi-mind — the mind of the Great Vehicle; second, understanding the highest truth — the understanding of the Great Vehicle; third, cultivating all practices — the practice of the Great Vehicle; fourth, deeply believing in cause and effect — the faith of the Great Vehicle; fifth, dedicating [merit] toward rebirth — the vow of the Great Vehicle. These five dharmas appear and disappear alternately among the upper three grades. The upper-grade upper-birth possesses all five: the Sūtra sets forth the three minds and the three practices, which is this. The upper-grade middle-birth possesses four, lacking only the great practice, as when the Sūtra says ‘skilled at understanding the purport and meaning.’ The upper-grade lower-birth possesses three, lacking understanding and practice, as when the Sūtra says ‘merely arousing the unsurpassed mind of the Way.’ Without the first, one is not of the upper grade; without the fourth and fifth, one is not reborn. Therefore the upper three grades gather in the [bodhisattvas of the] stage of supplementing the Buddha’s place, the non-regressing, the initial-mind, and all the great bodhisattvas.”
Gui 1: The Upper-Grade Upper-Birth, in Three Parts.
First, the heading
Second, the explanation; third, the conclusion
Zi 1: The Heading.
The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: “The upper-grade upper-birth:
Zi 2: The Explanation, in Four Parts.
First, cultivating the supreme cause
Second, meeting the supreme condition; third, clarifying rebirth; fourth, the benefits after rebirth
Chou 1: Cultivating the Supreme Cause.

If there are sentient beings who wish to be born in that land, they arouse three kinds of mind and forthwith are reborn. What are the three? First, the mind of utmost sincerity; second, the profound mind; third, the mind of dedication and vow. One who possesses the three minds will surely be born in that land.

First, arousing the three minds. Lingzhi’s commentary says: “The arousing of the three minds is the bodhi-mind; it is also called the unsurpassed mind of the Way. First, ‘utmost sincerity’: seeking the Buddha’s bodhi, firm and decisive, unshifting until Buddhahood.” The annotated commentary says: “The mind of utmost sincerity is the true mind that vows to be reborn [there].” The Yuelun says: “What is ‘utmost sincerity’? ‘Utmost’ means leaving no room to spare; ‘sincere’ means this one mind alone. When the practitioner first hears the instruction that this mind makes the Buddha and this mind is the Buddha, he arouses the mind of taking up the burden, proceeding straight to the unsurpassed bodhi, no longer seeking the nirvāṇa with residue or the fruits of gods and humans. He only thinks that without relying on the Buddha’s power his practice and vows will be hard to fulfill, and therefore decisively seeks rebirth in the Pure Land, single-mindedly and finely cultivating without interruption — this is called utmost sincerity.” Lingzhi’s commentary says: “Second, the ‘profound mind’: hearing, reflecting upon, and cultivating the Great Vehicle dharmas, never ceasing until Buddhahood. The Shilun (the Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom) says: ‘The great ocean of the perfection of wisdom is fathomed to the bottom only by the Buddha,’ therefore it is called profound.” The Jingying commentary says: “The seeking mind is earnest and weighty, therefore it is called the profound mind.” The Tiantai commentary says: “‘Profound’ means the Buddha-fruit is deep and lofty; one seeks it with the mind, therefore it is called the profound mind.” The Yuelun says: “What is the ‘profound mind’? The Sūtra says: ‘With the profound mind one believes and understands, constantly pure.’ The profoundly deep Dharma-store of the Buddhas cannot be understood by thought and discrimination; yet it is not apart from the mind of deluded thought of sentient beings. Therefore it is said: all sentient beings possess the Tathāgata’s wisdom. The Tathāgata’s wisdom is nothing other than the deluded thought of sentient beings; the deluded thought of sentient beings is nothing other than the Tathāgata’s wisdom. Only by illuminating with the profound mind, knowing that the Tathāgata and sentient beings are without duality and without distinction, does one not see the Buddha outside the mind — because the Buddha seen is not apart from one’s own mind. Knowing that the Tathāgata and sentient beings are without duality and without distinction, one does not seek the Pure Land outside the mind — because one understands that the Pure Land to be born in is complete within one’s own mind. And so, seeing yet without seeing, being born yet without birth, pure from the very beginning, apart from all perception and observation.
