Such faith and understanding is called the profound mind.” Lingzhi’s commentary says: “Third, dedication and vow: the merit one has cultivated is universally given to sentient beings, without end until Buddhahood.” The annotated commentary says: “The mind of dedication and vow is the mind that dedicates the merit one has cultivated and vows to seek rebirth in the Pure Land.” The Yuelun says: “What is the mind of dedication and vow? Just as Amitābha Buddha, for the sake of the Buddha-way, aroused a vast and great mind, so I likewise, for the sake of the Buddha-way, arouse a vast and great mind. Just as Amitābha Buddha, for the sake of sentient beings, took a wonderful Pure Land, so I likewise, for the sake of sentient beings, take a wonderful Pure Land. If there is a single sentient being not yet saved, then my land is not pure and my Buddhahood is not accomplished. I, the Buddha, and sentient beings are at once one and three, neither three nor one, ultimately unattainable. This is called the mind of dedication and vow.” Lingzhi’s commentary says: “If matched with the three collections [of precepts]: the first is the collection of discipline, cutting off no evil — hence it must be utmost sincere; the second is the collection of wholesome dharmas, leaving no good uncultivated — hence it must be ever more profound; the third is the collection of sentient beings, leaving no being unsaved — hence it must be dedicated and given. If matched with the three Buddhas: the first is the virtue of severance, the Dharma-body Buddha; the second is the virtue of wisdom, the reward-body Buddha; the third is the virtue of grace, the response-body Buddha. Since the fruit has three Buddhas, the cause must have three minds; not one may be lacking.”

There are further three kinds of sentient beings who will attain rebirth. What are the three? First, those of compassionate mind who do not kill and are complete in all precept-conduct; second, those who read and recite the Vaipulya scriptures of the Great Vehicle; third, those who cultivate the six recollections, dedicate [their merit], and vow, wishing to be born in that land.

Next, cultivating the three practices. Lingzhi’s commentary says: “Having aroused the above three minds, one must cultivate the three practices. Yet there are those who cultivate the three practices directly, and the meaning includes the three minds; therefore it says ‘there are further three kinds of sentient beings’ and so on.” The Yuelun says: “The three kinds of sentient beings means sentient beings who cultivate all three kinds of practice together; it does not mean each cultivates one kind. For faith and vow support each other, and understanding and practice arouse each other. If one is deficient, one cannot enter the Way.” Lingzhi’s commentary says: “First, not killing is the head of all precepts, therefore it is singled out. ‘Complete in all precept-conduct’: in this upper grade one must receive the Great Vehicle bodhisattva precepts. According to the Sūtra of Good Precepts, one first receives the five, the ten, and the full precepts, and afterwards receives the bodhisattva precepts; therefore it says ‘all precepts.’ This corresponds to the utmost sincere mind above. Second, reading and reciting the scriptures: not merely reading and reciting, but one must learn and understand, giving rise to wisdom. This corresponds to the profound mind. Third, dedication and vow: its correspondence may be known as above. To these is added the six recollections, namely recollection of the Three Jewels, and of precepts, giving, and the gods — called the Great Vehicle’s six recollections.”
Complete in these merits, [whether for] one day or up to seven days, one attains rebirth.

Third, showing the period of cultivation. The Zhizhi commentary says: “The ‘merits’ refer to the two kinds above, of mind and practice; adding one seven-day period of single-minded Buddha-recitation, at the time of death one attains rebirth.” Lingzhi’s commentary says: “At the least one day, at the most seven days. Raising the least to illustrate the most, [the Buddha] wishes to reveal the supremacy of the merit. Then one knows that a great bodhisattva practice, if one can practice it in a single thought, is still a Buddha-seed; how much more [practice] for one day or seven — how could one fail to be reborn?” The Yuelun says: “‘Complete in these merits’ is spoken with regard to a long period. ‘One day or up to seven days’ is found in the smaller text’s holding of the Name and in the Great Collection’s sustained mindfulness; both have this passage. The Sūtra speaks of it especially in order to fix the mind in single-pointedness. To set a limit and seek the effect — this is vigorous and brave.” The Shilun: “Question: How is it that one day to seven days brings rebirth — could it not be cultivated beyond that limit? Answer: This is not a delimitation; one must practice it to the end of one’s life. Yet although the various practices may be cultivated over a long time, they may be contravened or deficient and not brought to perfection; and those who accomplish it only in the last day or seven days before death, or who heard the Way rather late and die within one to seven days after hearing it, may all be included in the upper grade. As the Confucians say: ‘If one hears the Way in the morning, one may die content in the evening.’ This, however, requires not only ‘hearing’ but also ‘reflecting’ and ‘cultivating,’ and is all the more ultimate. For one who hears the Dharma late, nothing but vigorous additional practice will serve.”
Chou 2: Meeting the Supreme Condition.

When this person is born in that land — because he has been vigorous and brave — Amitābha Tathāgata, together with Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta, countless transformation-Buddhas, a great assembly of hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus and Śrāvakas, immeasurable devas, and palaces of the seven treasures: Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva holding a vajra platform, together with Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, comes before the practitioner. Amitābha Buddha emits a great brilliant light that illumines the practitioner’s body, and together with all the bodhisattvas extends his hands in welcome. Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta, with countless bodhisattvas, praise the practitioner and encourage his mind.

The first sentence clarifies the time of rebirth. It means that when this practitioner is at the point of death — whether lying down in the auspicious posture, or passing while seated or standing — at that very time. Below ‘this person’ it clarifies the condition of the upper grade. It means that because this practitioner, during life, either cultivated the three minds or also practiced the other practices, vigorous and brave, never slackening from beginning to end, therefore at the end of life the Three Sages and the assembly of sages, the reliant and the proper [retributions] together, come to extend their hands in welcome, praising and encouraging, to comfort his mind. (The Yanyi)

Lingzhi’s commentary says: “‘Vigorous and brave’ is what is able to evoke [the response]. Vigorous means not slackening; brave means not retreating. Below ‘Amitābha’ it reveals the sages’ response: the Buddha and the great assembly gather together before him. The palace of the seven treasures is the Buddha’s dwelling-place. The vajra platform is the lotus seat; what is said below, ‘this purple-gold platform, like a great jeweled flower,’ is that. But this vajra is different from the one below. The two sages hold it together and give it to him to ride upon.”
Question: That the platform seat comes to welcome him is acceptable; how is it that the palace too can move here?

Answer: The two retributions, reliant and proper, arise together at the same time. As the Yogācārabhūmi says: ‘Those devas are born together with their palaces and pass away together with them.’ It is not like the Sahā world, where there is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; and even when obtained, there is the suffering of prior decay. (The Shilun)
Chou 3: Clarifying Rebirth.
When the practitioner sees this, he is joyful and exultant; he sees his own body riding upon the vajra platform, following behind the Buddha, and in the time of a finger-snap he is born in that land.

At that time, having seen such a supreme realm, he gives rise to great joy. He sees his own body riding the vajra platform: at the very moment of casting off the retribution in this land, it is precisely the moment of rebirth in that land — neither before nor after, therefore it says ‘in the time of a finger-snap.’ (The Yanyi) Lingzhi’s commentary says: “The form remains while the spirit departs, like the sloughing of a cicada. A hundred thousand koṭi lands are reached in a single instant. By that Buddha’s awesome spiritual power and sentient beings’ karmic force, the exchange of body and change of retribution is like turning over the palm.”
Chou 4: The Benefits after Rebirth.

Having been born in that land, he sees the Buddha’s form-body complete in all its marks, and sees the bodhisattvas complete in their form-marks. The lights and the jeweled groves expound the wonderful Dharma. Having heard it, he immediately awakens to the tolerance of the non-arising of dharmas. In a moment he journeys to serve all the Buddhas throughout the ten directions, and before each Buddha receives the prophecy in turn; returning to his own land, he obtains immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dhāraṇī-gates.

Having been born in that land, the bodily marks of the Three Sages are complete in the excellences as described in the foregoing contemplations, and he sees each one face to face. He further hears the lights and the jeweled groves expounding the wonderful Dharma; having heard it, he attains the tolerance. After a short while he can journey through the ten directions, serving all the Buddhas, and receives from all the Buddhas the prophecy in turn. Having received the prophecy, he then returns to his own land and obtains hundreds of thousands of dhāraṇī-gates, ascending to the ground of the Separate Teaching and the abiding-stage of the Perfect Teaching. (The Yanyi)

The Yuelun says: “Because his precept-conduct is complete, the form-marks of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas he sees are complete; because he has faith and joy in the Great Vehicle, hearing the wonderful Dharma he immediately attains the tolerance of the non-arising of dharmas. Having received the prophecy, he immediately obtains hundreds of thousands of dhāraṇī-gates.” Lingzhi’s commentary: “Dhāraṇī is here rendered ‘total retention’: first, able to retain the good; second, able to prevent the evil; that is, to penetrate all immeasurable dharma-gates without obstruction.”
Zi 3: The Conclusion.
This is called the upper-grade upper-birth.
Gui 2: The Upper-Grade Middle-Birth, in Three Parts.
The upper-grade middle-birth:
First, clarifying the cultivation of the cause
Second, meeting the supreme condition; third, attaining rebirth; fourth, the benefits after rebirth
Chou 1: Clarifying the Cultivation of the Cause.

One need not receive, uphold, read, and recite the Vaipulya scriptures; [one should] skillfully understand the purport and meaning, and one’s mind is not startled or moved by the highest truth. Deeply believing in cause and effect, one does not slander the Great Vehicle. With these merits one dedicates [them] and vows to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Miaozong’s commentary says: “‘Need not’ refers to one who upholds by meaning and does not delight in reading and reciting; he merely takes a single sentence or a single verse from the scriptures and fathoms its purport to the depths. Before the profound and vast principle that is beyond speech and thought, his mind is not startled or moved. Again, his mind abides in the middle way and is not stirred by the two extremes. Penetrating and understanding that cause and effect are both the real mark is called deep faith. Though he does not study [the scriptures] exhaustively, when he hears the great teaching with its differing expositions suited to capacities, he knows that they reveal the one principle, and does not give rise to doubt or slander.”

Lingzhi’s commentary says: “The first clause shows the lack of practice; below ‘skilled at’ it reveals the presence of understanding. ‘The highest truth’ means penetrating and understanding that all dharmas are ultimately empty and still, because they arise from conditions and have no self-nature. It transcends all dharmas, therefore it is called ‘highest.’ ‘The mind is not startled’ means it does not waver in doubt. ‘Believing in cause and effect’ means that although all dharmas are empty, the cause and effect of good and evil is not off by a hair. Only with such faith and understanding does one accord with the Great Vehicle — how could there be slander? One turns these merits toward that adornment, therefore it is called dedication. Without seeking and vowing, even with faith and understanding one does not escape the round of rebirth.”

For one who practices this practice, when his life is about to end, Amitābha Buddha, together with Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta and an immeasurable great assembly, surrounded by his retinue, holding a purple-gold platform, comes before the practitioner and praises him, saying: “Son of the Dharma! You practice the Great Vehicle and understand the highest truth; therefore I now come to welcome you!” Together with a thousand transformation-Buddhas, he extends his hands at once.

Lingzhi’s commentary: “The purple-gold platform is also the lotus. Because one is born by transformation from the Dharma, one is called a son of the Dharma.” The Yanyi says: “This condition differs from the upper grade; it is greatly inferior to the former. There the Three Sages came to welcome him together with immeasurable transformation-Buddhas, bhikṣus, and devas, and with palaces; here [the Buddha] is accompanied by a thousand transformation-Buddhas. There it was a vajra platform; here a purple-gold platform. There the Buddha’s light shone upon and touched him; here there is only verbal praise. ‘Extending the hands’ is welcoming.”
Chou 3: Attaining Rebirth.

The practitioner sees himself seated on the purple-gold platform, with palms joined and hands clasped, praising all the Buddhas. In a single thought-moment he is born in the pond of the seven treasures in that land.

This purple-gold platform is like a great jeweled flower, and opens after a night. The practitioner’s body becomes the color of purple burnished gold, and beneath his feet there is also a lotus of the seven treasures. The Buddha and the bodhisattvas all at once emit light that illumines the practitioner’s body, and his eyes immediately open and become clear. Through his former habitual cultivation, he hears on every side a multitude of voices purely expounding the profoundly deep highest truth. He then descends from the golden platform, does reverence to the Buddha, joins his palms, and praises the World-Honored One. After seven days, at that very time he attains non-regression with respect to anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. At that very time he can fly through the air, going everywhere throughout the ten directions, serving all the Buddhas. In the presence of all the Buddhas he cultivates all the samādhis. After one small kalpa he attains the tolerance of non-arising and receives the prophecy face to face.

In the former case, one is born in that land and sees the Buddha at once, without any lapse of time; here the flower opens only after a night. There, in a moment, one journeys to serve all the Buddhas; here it takes seven days. There the Buddhas give the prophecy at once; here one must pass a small kalpa to attain the tolerance and receive the prophecy. Since the conditions met are different, the later benefits also differ. (The Yanyi) Lingzhi’s commentary says: “‘One small kalpa’ is likewise spoken with reference to one increase and decrease [of lifespan] in this land.”
This is called the upper-grade middle-birth.
Gui 3: The Upper-Grade Lower-Birth, in Three Parts.
The upper-grade lower-birth:
First, clarifying the cultivation of the cause
Second, clarifying the condition met; third, clarifying rebirth; fourth, the benefits after rebirth

Likewise believing in cause and effect and not slandering the Great Vehicle, one merely arouses the unsurpassed mind of the Way. With these merits one dedicates [them] and vows to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Miaozong’s commentary says: “The two clauses, ‘believing in cause and effect’ and the rest, are the same as in the upper-middle [grade]; therefore it says ‘likewise.’ There, understanding the highest truth was the distinctive practice; here, merely arousing the unsurpassed mind of the Way is the distinctive practice.” The Zhizhi commentary says: “Compared with the upper-middle above, it lacks the two kinds of upholding the scriptures and understanding their meaning. The merits are: arousing the mind and reciting the Buddha’s name, upholding the precepts, practicing giving, and so on.”
Chou 2: Clarifying the Condition Met.

When the practitioner’s life is about to end, Amitābha Buddha, together with Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta and all the bodhisattvas, holding a golden lotus and transforming into five hundred Buddhas, comes to welcome this person. The five hundred transformation-Buddhas extend their hands at once and praise him, saying: “Son of the Dharma! You are now pure and have aroused the unsurpassed mind of the Way; I come to welcome you!”

Lingzhi’s commentary says: “The golden lotus is likewise the platform seat. In praising him as pure: having aroused the great mind, he must be apart from all evil.” The Yanyi says: “This condition is also inferior to the preceding. Before there were a thousand Buddhas; now there are five hundred. The rest need not be discussed. In short, the lower the grade, the fainter the condition — this is an inevitable tendency.”

When he sees this, he sees his own body seated on the golden lotus. Having sat, the flower closes. Following behind the World-Honored One, he at once attains rebirth in the pond of the seven treasures.
Lingzhi’s commentary says: “It does not state a time limit; it is the same as the single thought-moment above.”

After one day and one night the lotus then opens. Within seven days he then sees the Buddha. Though he sees the Buddha’s body, his mind is not clear about the many excellences. After three weeks he then sees them distinctly. He hears all the voices, which all expound the wonderful Dharma. He journeys through the ten directions, making offerings to all the Buddhas. Before all the Buddhas he hears the profoundly deep Dharma. After three small kalpas he attains the hundred-dharma-gate of illumination and dwells on the Ground of Joy.

The text has two [sections]: first, the flower opens and the Buddha is seen. Above, the Buddha was seen as soon as one arrived; in the middle grade, he was seen after a night; here he is seen within seven days, and it is only after three weeks that the seeing becomes complete — because although the mind and vow have been aroused, one has not yet been able to truly cultivate the eighty thousand practices and transform the dust of affliction into the excellences. Below ‘he hears all the voices’ is the second, hearing the Dharma and attaining the fruit. As for making offerings to the Buddhas and hearing the Dharma: because during life one could not extensively cultivate merit and wisdom, therefore after roaming in the Land of Ultimate Bliss one journeys to serve all the Buddhas and fulfills the two adornments. (The Zhizhi commentary) The annotated commentary says: “The hundred-dharma-gate of illumination is the gate of wisdom obtained by a bodhisattva on the first ground. ‘Illumination’ is wisdom; ‘gate’ is entry, and also distinction. Wisdom can penetrate into the true nature of the hundred dharmas, therefore it is called the gate of illumination.” The Zhizhi commentary: “The hundred-dharma-gate of illumination is the five categories and hundred dharmas of the Great Vehicle schools; the names and numbers are as in the Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas. It generally reveals that all that exists in the three realms is manifested by consciousness alone. ‘Joy’ is the name of the first ground. Having first transcended the stage of ordinary beings and entered the rank of bodhisattvas; departing from the destinies of the world and entering the world-transcending path; within the Tathāgata’s lineage, one is certain to attain it. One becomes greatly delighted and rejoicing, therefore it is called Joy. The Avatamsaka clarifies that a bodhisattva on the first ground, in a single thought-moment, attains a hundred samādhis, sees a hundred Tathāgatas, [acquires] a hundred spiritual powers, shakes a hundred worlds, illumines and teaches the sentient beings of a hundred kalpas, dwells with a lifespan of a hundred kalpas, knows the events of a hundred kalpas in each of the past and future limits, enters a hundred dharma-gates, manifests a hundred bodies, and displays a hundred bodhisattvas. Dwelling on this ground, how could one not rejoice?”
This is called the upper-grade, lower-birth one.
Ren 2: Summary of the name of this contemplation.
This is called the higher-grade rebirth-contemplation; it is the fourteenth contemplation.”

blocks.text: Xin 2: Contemplating the Śrāvaka assembly (the fifteenth, the middle-grade rebirth contemplation) — in two parts

inline.s: The Ling-zhi Commentary says: “The fifteenth covers the three grades of the middle class, and this gathers in the Śrāvaka assembly of the four fruits. The Sūtra says: ‘That Buddha has immeasurable and boundless Śrāvaka disciples, all of them Arhats,’ and so on. Question: That land is a pure Mahāyāna assembly of good companions; how then can there be Śrāvakas of the Lesser Vehicle? Answer: The Śrāvakas of this world are of two kinds. First, the ‘fixed nature,’ meaning those who sink into emptiness, cling to stillness, and take the path of final nirvāṇa; the Treatise on Rebirth says ‘the two-vehicle seeds are not born there,’ and these belong to that kind. Second, the ‘unfixed nature,’ meaning those who, in between, turn their minds back and, having already been revealed, know the eternal and receive the prophecy. Though they are Śrāvakas, they do not stop at the lesser fruition. In the Lotus these are the ‘true Arhats’; in the Nirvāṇa, the ‘bodhisattvas who have left home.’ The Śrāvakas of the Pure Land are of this same kind. Having heard the great teaching and aroused the bodhi-mind, they at first studied the Lesser Vehicle; hearing of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, they stirred up their old habits and first realized the lesser fruition, but in the end they return to the Great Vehicle. Among these three grades, the upper-birth one always upholds the five, eight, ten, and full precepts — these four kinds of precept practice; the middle-birth one also upholds the four precepts, but only for one day and one night; the lower-birth one is filial, nurturing, and compassionate. The upper two exclusively uphold the Buddha’s precepts and also have the dedication of merit and the seeking of vows. The lowest relies only on worldly teaching, and so meets a good friend only at the end of life. Because the practices of the three stages differ, they are distinguished as high and low.”
First, the middle-grade upper-birth
second, the middle-grade middle-birth; third, the middle-grade lower-birth
Gui 1: The middle-grade upper-birth

The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: “The upper-birth of the middle grade: If there are sentient beings who uphold the five precepts, observe the eight-precept fast, cultivate the various precepts, commit none of the five grave offenses, and have no faults or misdeeds — with these roots of goodness they dedicate [their merit] and vow to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

First, clarifying the cause of practice. The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘The five and the eight are the precepts of the two assemblies of lay people. The ‘various precepts’ include the ten and the full precepts, the precepts of the five assemblies of renouncers. The five precepts are: first, not to kill; second, not to steal; third, not to commit sexual misconduct; fourth, not to speak falsely; fifth, not to drink alcohol. To the eight precepts three more are added: sixth, not to wear garlands and necklaces, nor anoint the body with fragrant oils; seventh, not to sit on a high [and luxurious] bed, nor sing, dance, or [be entertained by] musicians and singers; eighth, not to eat beyond the midday meal. In the matter of sexual conduct the practice severs both the illicit and the proper, and so it is added as the ‘pure conduct.’ Because it unifies the mind, it is called the ‘eight fasts’; because it confines the faculties, it is also called the ‘eight gates.’ The details are in the vinaya. Moreover, these four kinds of precepts are either upheld separately by the monastic and the lay, or observed together [by those who have gone forth]. Since one upholds the pure precepts, one must depart from all faults. The five grave offenses are the greatest among faults, hence they are singled out. What follows sets forth the dedication of merit and the seeking of vows. The roots of goodness are the cause; being born there is the fruit.’

At the moment of death, Amitābha Buddha, surrounded by an assembly of bhikṣus as his retinue, radiates golden light and comes to where that person is, preaching of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and praising the renunciation of home-life as the means to be freed from all suffering. Seeing this, the practitioner’s heart is filled with great joy. He sees his own body seated upon a lotus throne. Kneeling long with palms joined, he does reverence to the Buddha. Before he has even raised his head, he is reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The lotus opens at once. When the flower unfolds, he hears a multitude of voices praising the Four Noble Truths. In that very moment he attains the Arhat way: the three insights, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations are all complete. This is the upper-birth of the middle grade.

Next, clarifying the experienced fruit. The Yanyi commentary says: ‘The upper three all speak of the Buddha and of the bodhisattvas. That here it speaks only of the Buddha and the bhikṣus is because the transformation [assembly] is of fellow practitioners, drawing in those of the same kind. This is because they at first practiced the lesser practice, and so what is preached to them is likewise only the method of the four foundations of mindfulness.’ The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘Praising the renunciation of home-life makes clear that this grade largely gathers in the monastic assembly. “Freed from suffering” means that in what is near one departs from the entanglements of the dusty world, and in what is far one clears away the afflictions.’ Below ‘the practitioner’ clarifies the rebirth. The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘Seated on the lotus and doing reverence to the Buddha, the consciousness-body is released at once.’ Below ‘the lotus opens’ [clarifies] the benefits after rebirth. The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘(When the lotus opens) there is in fact the vision of the Buddha, but the text omits this and does not make it explicit.’ The Yanyi commentary says: ‘In this grade the flower opens and the Buddha is seen, swifter than the upper-middle and the upper-lower grades. The upper-middle [birth] takes a night, and the upper-lower takes a day and a night before the flower opens. Here it opens at once, not so much as passing a single night. The difference is only in the form of the Buddha seen.’ The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘The praise of the Four Noble Truths accords with what they were accustomed to practice. The two truths of suffering and origin are the worldly cause and effect, and are what is to be abandoned; the two truths of cessation and the path are the transcendent cause and effect, and are what is to be realized. All four dharmas are true, and so they are jointly called truths.’

Below ‘in that very moment’ clarifies the attainment of the way. The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘“A” renders [the Sanskrit] as “not,” and “lo-han” (Arhat) as “born.” When the bonds of defilement are entirely exhausted and one no longer receives a future existence, it is therefore called “not-born.” It is also called “worthy of offerings” and “destroyer of thieves,” as explained elsewhere. The three insights are: the insight [into] past lives, the insight into the extinction of defilements in the present, and the insight into the heavenly eye [of the future]. All three see through to the depths, so alone are they called “insights.” The six supernormal powers are: first, the heavenly eye; second, the heavenly ear; third, knowledge of others’ minds; fourth, knowledge of past lives; fifth, psychic power; sixth, the extinction of defilements. All six are unobstructed, hence they are jointly called “powers.” The eight liberations are also called the “eight abandons.” First, having form within while contemplating forms without — without destroying the inner bone-body, one contemplates the impurity of the outer forms; this stage is in the first dhyāna. Second, not having form within while contemplating forms without — destroying the inner skeleton, one contemplates the outer impurity and enters the second dhyāna. Third, the liberation of the ‘pure object’ realized with the body — setting aside external impurity, the concentrated mind is pure and clear, hence called ‘pure object’; with a detached mind one receives the bliss of the third dhyāna, hence called ‘realized with the body.’ Fourth, the liberation of the sphere of infinite space — extinguishing the forms of the fourth dhyāna, the mind rests on boundless space and enters concentration; knowing impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, the mind is weary and turns away. Fifth, the liberation of the sphere of consciousness — renouncing space and resting on consciousness, one enters concentration; knowing impermanence, one gives rise to weariness and turning away. Sixth, the liberation of the sphere of nothingness — renouncing consciousness and resting on nothingness, one enters concentration; knowing impermanence, one gives rise to weariness and turning away. Seventh, the liberation of ‘neither having perception nor not having perception’ — renouncing nothingness and resting on neither having nor not having, one enters concentration; knowing impermanence, one gives rise to weariness and turning away. Eighth, the liberation of the cessation of feeling and perception — turning away from and extinguishing feeling, renouncing all the mind and mental-factor dharmas, one enters concentration and rests; hence it is called ‘abandon.’ The rest are as set out in the Sequence of the Dharma-Realm.’
Gui 2: The middle-grade middle-birth

The middle-birth of the middle grade: If there are sentient beings who, for one day and one night, observe the eight-precept fast; or for one day and one night observe the novice’s precepts; or for one day and one night observe the full precepts, and their deportment is without any deficiency — with these merits they dedicate [them] and vow to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, cultivated and perfumed by the fragrance of the precepts.

First, the cause of practice. The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘The text here omits the five precepts; earlier it omitted the ten and the full precepts. The two appear alternately, so the four precepts are necessarily complete. The novice’s precepts are the ten precepts. In the earlier eight precepts, the first seven are divided into two [groups], and to them is added “not to grasp gold, silver, and precious things.” The full precepts are the precepts received by the great monks and the great nuns. The seven limbs [of body and speech] are fully aroused and extend everywhere throughout the sphere of living beings, hence they are called “full.” Observing the precepts is a pure karmic practice, undertaken for a pure retribution. Upholding the precepts accomplishes virtue, and the name is heard far and wide, hence it is likened to fragrance.’

For such a practitioner, when his life is about to end, he sees Amitābha Buddha, with his retinue, radiating golden light and holding a lotus of the seven jewels, coming before him. The practitioner himself hears a voice in the sky praising him: ‘Good man! Because you, a good person, have followed the teaching of the Buddhas of the three times, I have come to welcome you!’ The practitioner sees himself seated upon the lotus. The lotus closes at once, and he is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. In the jeweled pond, after seven days, the lotus unfolds. Once the flower has opened, he opens his eyes and joins his palms, praising the World-Honored One. Hearing the Dharma, he rejoices and attains Sotāpanna (stream-entry). After half a kalpa he becomes an Arhat. This is the middle-birth of the middle grade.

Next, the experienced fruit. First, the experienced condition. The Buddhas of the three times all encourage the upholding of precepts, the abandoning of evil, and the cultivation of good, so to uphold precepts now is to follow along with them. Next, the rebirth. The lotus closes and one is born — this too is within a single thought-moment. Third, the benefits after rebirth. First, seeing the Buddha. The text narrates the praise [of the Buddha]; accordingly the seeing [of the Buddha] must come first. Next, hearing the Dharma. This too is [the teaching of] the Four Noble Truths — suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and so on. The lower grade is likewise. Third, the realization of the fruit. ‘Sotāpanna’ is here rendered ‘countering the stream’ — that is, countering the stream of birth-and-death; it is the first fruit. (The Ling-zhi Commentary.)
Gui 3: The middle-grade lower-birth

The lower-birth of the middle grade: If there are good men and good women who are filial to and support their parents and practice kindness in the world, then when this person’s life is about to end he meets a good spiritual friend, who explains at length to him the joyful things of the land of Amitābha Buddha and also speaks of the forty-eight great vows of the bhikṣu Dharmākara. Having heard these things, he immediately passes away. Just as a mighty warrior bends and extends his arm, in that instant he is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. After seven days he meets Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta; hearing the Dharma, he rejoices and attains Sotāpanna. After one small kalpa he becomes an Arhat. This is the lower-birth of the middle grade.

First, the cause of practice. To do labor and serve, to comply with [one’s parents’] countenance and support their aspirations — this is why it is called ‘filially nourishing one’s parents.’ Confucianism regards this as the root of the hundred conduct. Extending love to all beings and giving broadly to succor the many — hence it is called ‘practicing kindness in the world.’ The Confucian tradition regards this as the virtue of the gentleman. Because in life one accumulated goodness, therefore at death one meets the [good] condition. Below ‘this person’ [comes] second, meeting the condition. To transform others through goodness — this is what the many ‘know and recognize’: knowing his virtue, recognizing his appearance. The Lotus Sūtra, the chapter on King Wonderful-Adornment, says: ‘A good spiritual friend is a great sustaining condition’; it points to wife and children as a good spiritual friend. Therefore one knows that so long as one can guide [others], one is not restricted to the monastic or the lay. The joyful things of the land are as the dependent retribution described above and as stated in the Larger and the Smaller Sūtras of Amitāyus. The bhikṣu Dharmākara is the former name of Amitābha in [the time of] his practicing [the path]. Formerly a king, he met the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, renounced his kingdom, and went forth from home; right before the Buddha he made the forty-eight vows. The details are as in the Larger Sūtra. Third, below ‘having heard these things’ [comes] the gaining of rebirth. Here there should be such events as, at death, holding the lotus and welcoming [the practitioner], but the text abbreviates and does not narrate them. ‘As a mighty warrior bends and extends his arm’ is also only a brief moment; the wording before and after varies. (The Ling-zhi Commentary.) The Yanyi commentary says: ‘The two lines below “having heard” precisely set forth that the mind aroused at the end of life is fierce and keen, and so he immediately passes away. At the very moment of death in this world is exactly the time of rebirth in that land. The simile of the mighty warrior’s extending his arm shows the swiftness of that rebirth: dying here and being born there, without passing through the intermediate state, is like the mighty warrior’s bending and extending his arm. That the lotus is not mentioned is because it can be inferred by analogy — the three grades below all have a lotus; how could this grade have none? There is no such case. Fourth, below ‘after seven days’ clarifies the later benefits. In the preceding grade, after seven days the lotus unfolded; here it says ‘after seven days,’ which is somewhat later in time. It certainly will not reach fourteen days for the flower to open. Previously it said ‘praising the World-Honored One, hearing the Dharma and rejoicing’ — that was hearing the Buddha preach; here he meets the two great bodhisattvas preaching. Previously he passed half a kalpa; here he passes one small kalpa. This shows that the earlier ‘half a kalpa’ is also a small kalpa. That the present [grade] is inferior to the former is logically so.’
This is called the middle-class-rebirth contemplation; it is the fifteenth contemplation.”

blocks.text: Xin 3: Contemplating the assembly of the people (the sixteenth, the lower-grade rebirth contemplation) — in two parts

inline.s: First, the lower-grade upper-birth
second, the lower-grade middle-birth; third, the lower-grade lower-birth

The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘The three grades of the lower class all have no cause of cultivation; they are all people who did evil throughout their lives and meet a good [friend] at the end of life. According to the Ten Doubts Treatise, if there were no good roots from the past, they would not meet [him] now either; hence these three grades are not without a remote cause. The upper-birth one merely commits transgressions at random, knowing no shame. What the middle-birth one describes is mostly the five assemblies of renouncers who covet fame and profit and break the precepts. The lower-birth one commits the ten evil acts, the five grave offenses, and all the exceedingly heavy crimes. Since the crimes are light or heavy, they are divided into three classes.’
Gui 1: The lower-grade upper-birth

The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: “The upper-birth of the lower grade: If there are sentient beings who do many evil acts — though they do not slander the Vaipulya scriptures — such foolish people commit many evil dharmas and know no shame. When their life is about to end, they meet a good spiritual friend who explains to them the titles of the twelve sections of the Mahāyāna scriptures. Because they hear such [scriptural] names, they remove the exceedingly heavy evil karma of a thousand kalpas. The wise friend further teaches them to place their palms together and invoke ‘Namo Amitābha Buddha’; by invoking the Buddha’s name, they remove the karma of birth-and-death for five billion kalpas. At that time that Buddha sends a transformation-Buddha, a transformation-Avalokiteshvara, and a transformation-Mahasthamaprapta to come before that practitioner, who praises him: ‘Good man! Because you invoked the Buddha’s name, all your offenses are destroyed; I have come to welcome you!’ Having spoken these words, the practitioner sees the light of the transformation-Buddha filling his whole room. Seeing it, he is overjoyed and passes away at once. Riding on a jeweled lotus, he follows behind the transformation-Buddha and is born in the jeweled pond. After seven sevens (forty-nine days), the lotus unfolds. When the flower opens, the great compassionate Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva emit great light and stand before him, preaching the profound twelve sections of the scriptures. Having heard them and understood, he arouses the unsurpassed bodhi-mind. After ten small kalpas he perfects the hundred dharma-gates of illumination and enters the first stage. This is the upper-birth of the lower grade.”

The Shi-lun Commentary says: ‘The upper-birth ones of this grade are ordinary and [non-Buddhist] people who commit comparatively lighter offenses, and it is only at the end of life that they happen upon the opportunity to be told the names of the twelve Mahāyāna sections. This is by no means an easy matter. In China, where the Buddha’s instruction has flourished most, although Buddhist followers are many, those who know the names and meanings of all twelve divisions of the teaching are still rarely met. How much more [difficult] when this evil person, in the haste of death, encounters them by chance — unless his good roots from former lives happened to ripen at just this moment, how could he gain such a fortunate encounter? Even if someone could explain [the scriptures] in detail, in his pain and bewilderment he would hardly be able to listen attentively. Hence it is said that this matter is by no means easy. Hearing the scripture names and removing the heavy offenses of a thousand kalpas is already a fortunate matter; but compared with invoking the Buddha’s name, which removes the karma of birth-and-death for five million kalpas, the difference is still great. Moreover, invoking the Buddha’s name is simple, easy to practice, and the mind becomes concentrated; but as for hearing the scripture names, since he does not understand them they do not enter [his mind] and are rejected, so the efficacy is inferior. To get a person to explain the scripture names, though one may find such a person, is something one can meet but cannot seek; whereas to teach the invoking of the Buddha’s name — everyone can do it well. Some among the heterodox missionaries, when a convicted criminal is about to suffer the death penalty, take the opportunity to explain taking refuge to him; that is an excellent plan, and Buddhists too should adopt this method.’
Gui 2: The lower-grade middle-birth

The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: “The middle-birth of the lower grade: If there are sentient beings who transgress against the five precepts, the eight precepts, and the full precepts — such foolish people steal the property of the Saṃgha and the property of the Saṃgha present before them; they preach the Dharma impurely and know no shame. They adorn themselves with all their evil karma. Such offenders, because of evil karma, should fall into hell. When their life is about to end, the manifold fires of hell come together all at once. They meet a good spiritual friend, who, with great compassion, at once praises the ten powers and awesome virtues of Amitābha Buddha, extols at length the light and the spiritual power of that Buddha, and also praises precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge-and-vision of liberation. Having heard this, they remove the karma of birth-and-death for eight billion kalpas. The fierce fires of hell turn into a cool breeze, blowing heavenly flowers. On every flower are transformation-Buddhas and bodhisattvas, welcoming this person. In a single thought-moment he is reborn within a lotus in the pond of the seven jewels. After six kalpas the lotus unfolds. Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta, with brahmic-voiced sounds, comfort that person and preach to him the profound scriptures of the Great Vehicle. Having heard this Dharma, he at once arouses the unsurpassed bodhi-mind. This is the middle-birth of the lower grade.”

The Yanyi commentary says: ‘The practitioners of this grade are of two kinds, monastic and lay: lay people may transgress the five and eight precepts, while bhikṣus may violate the great full precepts (the Ling-zhi Commentary says: “the text omits the novice’s precepts”). These two kinds are all unwise fools.’ The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘The property of the Saṃgha is the heaviest [to steal], hence it is singled out. ‘Saṃgha’ is here rendered ‘great assembly’ — that is, the perpetual property. Of this there are two kinds. First, the ‘perpetual, perpetual’ — the monastery buildings, grain, and rice, and so on. (The Miao-zong Commentary says: “First, the ‘perpetual, perpetual,’ meaning the monks’ kitchen and storehouse, the monastery halls and furnishings, flowers, fruits, trees, fields, gardens, servants, and cattle, and so on; because their substance is common to the ten directions, they cannot be divided up.”) Second, the ‘ten-direction perpetual’ — the food and drink offered to the monks, and so on. (The Miao-zong Commentary says: “Second, the ‘ten-direction perpetual,’ such as the monks’ ordinary meals offered to the Saṃgha; their substance is common to the ten directions, being limited only to the present place.”) The property of the Saṃgha present-before [one] is also of two kinds. First, the ‘present, present’ — what is divided according to the count. (As today’s lay people give to the monks of that place clothing, medicine, rooms, and utensils, etc. — see the Lecture Record of the Precepts.) Second, the ‘ten-direction present’ — what is broadly given with a communal intention. (As when the Saṃgha receives a gift, and the belongings of deceased [monks].) To steal any of these four kinds of Saṃgha property forms an offense. The Sūtra says: ‘The five grave offenses and the four heavy [offenses] I am still able to save; but one who steals the property of the Saṃgha I do not save.’ This is an extreme warning! The ‘impure preaching’ means borrowing the Buddha’s Dharma to seek gain and support. ‘Knowing no shame’ means openly doing [evil], within having no sense of shame. When evil traces are full to overflowing, it is therefore called ‘adorned [with them].’ ‘Should fall into hell’ — ‘should’ still means ‘necessarily.’ The manifold fires of hell are the cauldron of boiling water, the furnace of coals, molten copper, iron pellets, and so on. In [the description of] meeting the good friend, the merits of the Buddha spoken of are three: first, the ten powers; second, the light; third, the fivefold body of the Dharma. Hearing the Dharma extinguishes offenses, and the saints are moved to come and welcome; because he hears the Buddha’s virtues and in a single thought believes and accepts, he turns evil into good and the fire changes into a cool breeze. The world changes with the mind — its swiftness is like this!’

The Shi-lun Commentary says: ‘The middle-birth of the lower grade is [for] those who, being already followers of the Buddha, commit evil karma and add to it the offense of breaking the precepts, and moreover steal the common property of the Perpetual [Saṃgha] and the private property of the Saṃgha — this is to injure the [precious] Saṃgha. To preach the Dharma impurely is to confuse the [precious] Dharma. Fortunately, through good roots from former lives, at the end of life they hear the Buddha-Dharma extensively and can remove the karma of birth-and-death for eight billion kalpas. Yet because their offenses are comparatively heavy, they must be shut within the lotus for six kalpas. The Sūtra does not state the measure of the kalpa. According to [a reckoning] one small kalpa is 16,800,000 years, a middle kalpa is 336,000,000 years, and a great kalpa is 1,344,000,000 years. Thus a small kalpa is sixteen million years — how much more a middle or a great kalpa. This is not a punishment imposed by the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, but the offender’s own karma forming the obstacle. The world should realize: heavy offenses must never be committed, and the Pure Land too does not depart from the law of cause and effect. What the Buddhas and bodhisattvas can save people from is [only] their not falling into evil destinies. To be nurtured for a long time within the flower-bud — this is, amidst misfortune, a great good fortune. The difference between the lotus-womb and hell is: first, the lotus-womb has no suffering while hell has extreme suffering; second, the opening of the flower has a fixed time whereas there is no time to escape from the Avīci hell. Unless one is utterly foolish, one should know what to choose and what to reject!’
Gui 3: The lower-grade lower-birth
The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: “The lower-birth of the lower grade:

The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘Among the headings, the upper and middle classes mark “the Buddha told [Ānanda and Vaidehī]” and so on only at the upper grade; only the three grades of the lower class each mark it one by one, because evil-doing [leading to] rebirth is contrary to the norm and startles the assembly — it is easily doubted and hard to believe — so the text repeatedly marks it, intending to make them listen and accept.’

If there are sentient beings who do unwholesome karmic deeds — the five grave offenses, the ten evil acts, with all unwholesome [deeds] complete — such foolish people, because of evil karma, should fall into the evil destinies, pass through many kalpas, and suffer without end.

In the explanation, first, the evil done in life. As for the five grave offenses: killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an Arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and drawing blood from the Buddha’s body. Violating and betraying debts of kindness, they are called the ‘five grave offenses.’ The retribution in this very life is to fall into Avīci [hell], so they are called the ‘five uninterrupted karmic deeds.’ The ten evil acts are the three of body, the four of speech, and the three of mind; all evil karma is gathered up in the ten. Having done the extremely heavy, nothing else goes undone — hence it says ‘all unwholesome [deeds are] complete.’ Question: The Larger Sūtra says: ‘Even [down] to ten thoughts, if they are not born in my land, I will not attain right enlightenment — only [those who commit] the five grave offenses and slander the right Dharma are excluded.’ Here the Sūtra [says] that even those [who commit] the five grave offenses can be reborn? Now [we] explain: If one relies on the power of Amitābha’s vows, how could it bar those who have committed offenses? Expediently responding to their capacities, the words differ but the purport accords. That [text] reveals the transcendent wonder of the Blissful Land, wishing to draw forward the good person; this [text] shows that the merit of the pure karma is deep and does not abandon even the extremely evil. So long as one holds the name and dedicates the vow, there is none whose offenses are not extinguished and who is not reborn. Hence the Sūtra of the Buddha-Contemplation Samādhi says: ‘The four assemblies [of disciples] who slander the Vaipulya scriptures, commit the five grave offenses, and violate the four grave prohibitions — if such people are able, with utmost sincerity for one day and one night, with sustained mindfulness to contemplate a single auspicious mark of the Buddha, all their evil offenses and hindrances are entirely extinguished.’ Citing that to prove this — that the offenses are extinguished, what is there to doubt? Below, [the text] shows the retribution to come. Upon committing a single grave offense, [one is in] Avīci for a kalpa; how much more for committing many — hence [the text] says ‘many kalpas.’ (The Ling-zhi Commentary.)

The Shi-lun Commentary says: ‘The lower-birth of the lower grade is [for] the extremely evil kind, whose deeds are the five uninterrupted karmic deeds — also commonly known in the world. Yet there are [offenses] that the world overlooks and easily commits: seducing and defiling monks and nuns, or not doing it oneself but causing others to do it — such as actors performing on the stage, and vulgar literati writing novels and chanted tales, treating [these] as elegant and amorous romances; this defiles the Buddhist gate and ruins the pure conduct of others, and also belongs to the karma of the uninterrupted hell. Let the foolish not bring sorrow upon themselves!’

Such a foolish person, at the end of life, meets a good spiritual friend who consoles him in every way, teaches him the wonderful Dharma, and instructs him to recite the Buddha. That person, pressed by suffering, has no leisure to [contemplate] the Buddha. The good friend says to him: ‘If you cannot contemplate that Buddha, you should invoke [his name:] Amitāyus Buddha.’ Thus, with utmost sincerity, he lets the sound never cease, and completes ten thoughts, invoking ‘Namo Amitābha Buddha.’

Next, meeting the conditions at the end of life, in two [parts]. First, the friend’s guidance. To ‘explain the wonderful Dharma’ is to praise the Pure Land; to ‘instruct him to recite the Buddha’ is to [teach] the [mental] contemplation. (The Zhizhi Commentary says: “Pressed by suffering — the evil signs of hell appear.”) ‘Leisure’ means spare time. Contemplation of the mind [alone] is ‘recitation’; recitation of the mouth is ‘invocation.’ (The Zhizhi Commentary says: “Utterly undivided is called ‘utmost sincerity’; continuing so as to form a whole, hence it never ceases.”) ‘Ten thoughts’ means ten sounds. (The Ling-zhi Commentary.)

The Shi-lun Commentary says: ‘The world always takes invoking the name to be Buddha-recitation; yet the Sūtra says: “That person, pressed by suffering, has no leisure to [contemplate] the Buddha. The good friend says to him: if you cannot contemplate that Buddha, you should invoke [his name:] Amitāyus Buddha.” According to this, Buddha-contemplation and name-invocation are clearly different. Before we reach the end-of-life pressing of suffering, besides not abandoning recitation with the mouth, we should also contemplate the Buddha — that is, to bind the mind to it in sustained contemplation. Those who take oral recitation as the exclusive practice and all else as impure [mixed] practice fall into the error of pointing at the finger while mistaking it for the moon!’
By invoking the Buddha’s name, in every thought-moment he removes the karma of birth-and-death for eight billion kalpas.

This clarifies that reciting the Buddha extinguishes offenses. The Zhizhi Commentary says: ‘Question: How is it that ten thoughts can extinguish the offenses of eight billion kalpas? Answer: Because it possesses three powers. First, the power of the originally-inherent Buddha-nature — like fire, like a boat. Second, the power of invoking the name with utmost sincerity — like a drill, like a sail and an oar. These two are the fierce and keen power of one’s own effort. Third, the power of the Buddha’s vow to gather [beings] in — like a person, like a favorable wind. This one is the strong power of another. Since the cause is advantageous, the condition strong, the object sublime, and the mind fierce, [this power] is able to burn up the wood of offense and reach the lotus pond. Dharmākara’s eighteenth vow says: ‘Even [for] ten thoughts, if they are not born [there], I will not attain right enlightenment.’ Again, the Larger Sūtra says: ‘Even to a single thought, with utmost sincerity dedicating [the merit] and vowing to be born in that land, one is immediately reborn.’ The Mahāprajñāpāramitā says: ‘If one person invokes “Namo Buddha,” even to the end of suffering, his merit is not exhausted.’ The Buddha-Name Sūtra says: ‘Upon once hearing the Buddha’s name, one extinguishes the birth-and-death karma of countless kalpas.’ This is like the kindling of a hundred carts of firewood that a single spark can burn; an unlit room of ten thousand years that a single lamp can break through; a single awl piercing a thousand sheets of paper; a single wind [moving] ten million lands. Thus Devadatta, in hell, upon one invocation of the Buddha, transformed manifold suffering into the bliss of the third dhyāna; Zhang Shanhe, before completing ten recitations at death, saw the evil signs destroyed and the Buddha come to welcome him; Zhong Kui set up a Buddha image and removed the suffering of being pecked on the face by a flock of chickens; Xiong Jun, believing in Buddha-recitation, became one who slipped through the net of hell. If a single or three invocations are already thus, how much more ten thoughts and many thoughts?’

The Miao-zong Commentary says: ‘This fierce and keen mind arises from two conditions: first, encountering a good friend; second, being pressed by suffering. The mind fears the evil destinies, and the ear hears the Buddha’s name; hence it is firm and strong and invokes with utmost sincerity. Since the object is sublime and the mind fierce, little time [yields] great merit, able to surpass the drifting vow-power of a hundred years. If these two conditions do not arouse a fierce mind, this person is one who should fall into hell.’

At the moment of death he sees a golden lotus, like the orb of the sun, standing before him. In a single thought-moment he is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Within the lotus, for a full twelve great kalpas, the flower opens. Then Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta, with voices of great compassion, explain at length to him the reality of all dharmas and the method that extinguishes offenses. Having heard it, he rejoices and in that very moment arouses the bodhi-mind. This is the lower-birth of the lower grade.

Next, the excellent sign appears. The flower being like the sun’s orb is a simile for its size. If one follows the Abhidharma-kośa, the sun’s disk is fifty-one yojanas in diameter; here it merely takes what [beings] dwelling on earth look up to see — the size is not necessarily as [that] treatise [states]. Below ‘in a single thought-moment’ [the text] clarifies the gaining of rebirth. Below ‘within the lotus’ [it clarifies] the benefits after rebirth. Offenses arise from conditions and have no self-nature; all dharmas are likewise, hence [the truth] is called ‘reality.’ The Samantabhadra Practice says: ‘All the seas of karmic hindrances arise from false thinking; if one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate reality’ — this is [the point]. (The Ling-zhi Commentary.) The Yanyi commentary says: ‘This grade is especially long! It takes twelve great kalpas before the lotus opens. The flower opens and the hindrances are cleared away, like the clouds parting and the sky clearing. [He] hears the two great bodhisattvas explaining at length the wonderful Dharma. As for “the reality of all dharmas” — this means pointing to ignorance as the wonderful brightness, realizing the deluded awareness as true awareness, making clear that all dharmas are in their very essence reality.

… “All offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dispel them” — this is no idle saying. Therefore in that very moment he arouses the bodhi-mind.’ With this the last sentence concludes [the section].
This is called the lower-class-rebirth contemplation; it is the sixteenth contemplation.”

The Shi-lun Commentary says: ‘Among the lower grade, only the upper-birth one, after ten small kalpas, attains entry into the first stage; the other two are not described as to their fruition — they are presumably of the class of devas and humans in the Pure Land.’

The Yue-lun Commentary says: ‘The text of the nine grades, collectively called “contemplations,” is so that the practitioner may possess the wisdom of discernment and arouse a mind of vigor; to forsake the lower and rise to the higher, to turn away from the small and direct toward the great; and also that he may know that, upheld by the power of the Tathāgata’s vows, no gift [of capacity] is left unspread.’ With this, [the commentary] explains the meaning of ‘contemplation’ from the standpoint of the cause of practice. If one distinguishes by way of the fruit, it is entirely as said before. As for clarifying the [spiritual] stages, the Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘According to the Profound Meaning of the Four-Fascicle Commentary, the masters of old all used the three worthies and ten sages of the Great Vehicle to correspond to the upper three grades; the two kinds of [ordinary beings and] the four fruits of the Lesser Vehicle to correspond to the middle three grades; and the beginning-learners, ordinary people of the Great Vehicle, according to the gravity of their offenses, to correspond to the lower three grades. That passage (meaning the Profound Meaning division of the Four-Fascicle Commentary) refutes [these opinions] at length, and I do not quote it all again. Now I hold: according to the text of the nine grades, it is after being reborn in that land that the stages are discussed, so [the masters] may be followed. And according to the scripture text, those who seek rebirth from this world are all ordinary people; one must follow the Profound Meaning.

…’ The Profound Meaning of the Four-Fascicle Commentary says: ‘The overall purport of the three classes of the Contemplation Sūtra, above and below, is always [the case of] ordinary people in the five turbidities after the Buddha’s passing. Only because they meet different conditions are the nine grades made to differ. Why? The three of the upper grade are ordinary people who meet the Great [Vehicle]; the three of the middle grade are ordinary people who meet the Small [Vehicle]; the three of the lower grade are ordinary people who meet evil [conditions]. Because of their evil karma, at the end of life they rely on a good [friend] and, riding the power of the Buddha’s vows, are able to be reborn; only on reaching [that land] and [the time of the] flower’s opening do they arouse the mind. How can it be said that they are people who are beginning to study the Great Vehicle? …’ The details are in the commentary; the text is lengthy and is not transcribed.
Yi 3: The assembly benefits [from hearing]

While he was speaking these words, Vaidehī and the five hundred maidservants, hearing what the Buddha said, at once beheld the wide and long features of the Land of Ultimate Bliss; they saw the Buddha’s body and the two bodhisattvas. Their minds were filled with joy and they exclaimed at what had never been before! They awakened with sudden comprehension and attained the patience of non-arising. The five hundred maidservants aroused the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and vowed to be born in that land. The World-Honored One prophesied of them all: they would all be reborn there. Having been born in that land, they would obtain the samādhi of the Buddhas appearing before them. Countless devas aroused the unsurpassed bodhi-mind.

The text [has] two [sections]. First, the assembly sees the pure adornments of the dependent and the proper [retribution] of that land. Previously only Vaidehī alone saw it; now the whole assembly beholds it. Next, below ‘their minds,’ according to capacity they obtain benefits — in three [parts]. First, the queen enters realization. She ‘awakened with sudden comprehension’ — destroying ignorance; she ‘attained the patience of non-arising’ — realizing the Dharma-nature. Second, below ‘the five hundred,’ the maidservants arouse the mind and receive the prophecy. Question: The Treatise on Rebirth says that women and those with defective faculties are all unable to be born [there] — how is this not contradicted here? Answer: It does not say that the women of this world and those with defective faculties cannot be born in that land; it means that those who are born in that land do not receive the retribution of being a woman or of defective faculties. For Amitābha vowed: ‘If any woman, having come to be born in my land, again receives the form of a woman, I will not attain right enlightenment.’ It further says: ‘If any of the humans and devas of my land do not possess the thirty-two marks of a great man, I will not attain right enlightenment.’ From this one knows that in that land there are no women nor defective faculties. The rest is as explained in the Ten Doubts Treatise. Third, below ‘countless,’ the devas arouse the mind. The Buddha, in the secluded palace, spoke this method of contemplation with Ānanda and Maudgalyāyana attending at his side. There were only the queen, the maidservants, and the devas as the audience — no others heard it. Later, returning to Vulture Peak, Ānanda repeated it, and only then did the great assembly of bodhisattvas together hear it. (The Ling-zhi Commentary.)

blocks.text: Jia 3: The section of the Propagation — in two parts

inline.s: First, at the palace in the royal city, entrusting the propagation
second, returning to Vulture Peak, Ānanda retells it
The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘Through these two places, the assembly hears, believes, and accepts; transmitted and handed on from one to another, it flows without end.’
Yi 1: At the palace in the royal city, entrusting the propagation — in four parts
First, establishing the name and teaching its upholding
second, raising the benefits and urging the practice; third, concluding the name and entrusting it; fourth, the assembly hears and rejoices
Bing 1: Establishing the name and teaching its upholding
At that time Ānanda rose from his seat, and said to the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One! By what name should this Sūtra be known? And how should the essentials of this Dharma be received and upheld?’
First, Ānanda’s two questions about the name and the upholding. First, he asks the name of the Sūtra; second, he asks the method of upholding.

The Buddha told Ānanda: ‘This Sūtra is called the Contemplation of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, of Amitāyus Buddha, of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, and of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva. It is also called the Complete Purification of Karmic Obstructions and Being Born before the Buddhas. You should receive and uphold it, and let it not be lost.

Next, within the Buddha’s answer, first, setting forth the name of the Sūtra. There are two [aspects]. First, the name is taken from the one who contemplates and the object contemplated; it includes both the [three] objects [of contemplation], but omits the assembly. The opening title avoids prolixity and takes only five characters, yet its inclusiveness is complete. Second, [the name] is taken from its function. The extinguishing of offenses and [the bringing about of] rebirth are the power and use of the Sūtra. Second, below ‘you should uphold,’ [the Buddha] teaches its upholding. The Treatise on Wisdom says: Through the power of faith one receives; through the power of mindfulness one upholds. Having both received and upheld, one does not forget or lose it. (The Ling-zhi Commentary.)
Bing 2: Raising the benefits and urging the practice

Those who practice this samādhi, in this very life, see Amitāyus Buddha and the two great bodhisattvas. If good men and good women merely hear the name of that Buddha and the names of the two bodhisattvas, they remove the karma of birth-and-death for countless kalpas — how much more so if they recollect [them]. If one practices Buddha-recitation, know that such a person is the puṇḍarīka (white lotus) among humans. Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva are his excellent companions. He will sit at the place of enlightenment and be born in the family of the Buddhas.’

The text [has] five [points]. First, the excellence of the object seen. The [chapter on] Mahasthamaprapta’s perfect penetration says: ‘If the minds of sentient beings recollect the Buddha and recite the Buddha, whether now [in this life] or in the future, they will certainly see the Buddha.’ Second, below ‘merely hear,’ the excellence of extinguishing offenses. To cite [the mere] hearing to make [the case for] recollection — its superiority is knowable. Third, below ‘if one practices,’ the excellence of the person himself. ‘Puṇḍarīka’ is here [rendered] ‘white lotus.’ First, it is a rare auspicious [flower] in the human world; second, its nature is pure and free of defilement — hence it is used as the comparison. Fourth, below ‘Avalokiteshvara,’ the excellence of companions. To have a Buddha-to-be as a friend, it is fitting not to slight oneself. Fifth, below ‘he will sit,’ the excellence of the retribution. ‘Sitting at the place of enlightenment’ means becoming a Buddha. The place where the way is attained is therefore called the ‘place of enlightenment.’ All the Buddhas, beneath the bodhi tree, sit cross-legged, cut off defilements, defeat the Māras, and attain the way. The Dharma-body is one substance, realized alike by all Buddhas, hence [they are] of the ‘Buddha family.’ The Mahasthamaprapta chapter says ‘Not far from the Buddha,’ and the Smaller Sūtra says all of them attain the non-regressing anuttara [bodhi] — these point to the same meaning. (The Ling-zhi Commentary.)
Bing 3: Concluding the name and entrusting it
The Buddha told Ānanda: ‘Uphold these words well; one who upholds these words is hereby upholding the Name of Amitāyus Buddha.’
The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘The intent is to state by way of contrast: the merit of upholding the Name is great, and so too is upholding the Sūtra.’
Bing 4: The assembly hears and rejoices
When the Buddha spoke these words, the venerable Maudgalyāyana, the venerable Ānanda, and Vaidehī and the rest, hearing what the Buddha said, all rejoiced greatly.

The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘As for “rejoicing”: first, [what they] had never heard before, they now hear it; second, they are able to be reborn in the pure land; third, [this teaching] can be shown and explained on and on, benefiting living beings without end. Possessing all these meanings, they hold great joy.’
Yi 2: Returning to Vulture Peak, Ānanda retells it
At that time the World-Honored One, treading in the sky, returned to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak).

First, the Buddha returns to his place. Since the Buddha spoke the Sūtra for a long time in the royal palace, either the assembly did not disperse and waited for the Buddha to return, or they gathered again — neither can be known. (The Ling-zhi Commentary.)

At that time Ānanda explained at length to the great assembly the matters as above. Countless devas, nāgas, and yakṣas, hearing what the Buddha said, all rejoiced greatly; and, paying reverence to the Buddha, they withdrew.

Next, Ānanda retells it. The repeated entrusting to remember and uphold [the Sūtra] — its purport appears here. Third, the assembly hears, does reverence, and disperses. Referring to the assembly listed above, the text here abbreviates the nāgas and devas. Ānanda himself heard [it] and, on behalf [of the Buddha], transmitted the Buddha’s words — hence it says ‘hearing the Buddha say [this].’ (The Ling-zhi Commentary.)
Completed as the first draft, on the morning of the day before the Buddha’s birthday, in the xinchou year of the Republic of China, in the Huayan retreat.
